finding.finding_summary: The review concludes that behavioral parent training and classroom behavioral interventions improve child behavior, ADHD symptoms, and related functioning, with sustained benefits in some studies over about a year. It notes that behavioral parent training shows small-to-medium effects depending on outcome, and that improvements in engagement can strengthen outcomes.
finding.measure: ADHD symptoms, child behavior, parenting behavior, parenting sense of competence, parental mental health, engagement
finding.effect_size: small to medium (range reported qualitatively); d=1.06 and d=0.74 cited for one digital-therapeutic comparison

finding.finding_summary: Organizational skills training is described as improving organization, time management, planning, planner use, and adolescent impairment. The review specifically notes that school-delivered OST led to improvements in organization, time management, and planning skills, as well as homework-related behavior based on parent report.
finding.measure: Organization, time management, planning, planner use, homework behavior, adolescent impairment

finding.finding_summary: The review states that classroom behavioral supports such as the Daily Report Card improve classroom functioning and are among the most cost-effective interventions. It also reports that behavior-therapy-first treatment sequences reduced discipline referrals and disruptive classroom behavior and cost less than sequences including medication in a SMART study.
finding.measure: Discipline referrals, disruptive classroom behaviors, cost of treatment sequence, classroom functioning

paper_profiles.title: Interventions for children and adolescents with specific learning disability and co-occurring disorders
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This review examines what is known about school-based and related interventions for children and adolescents with specific learning disabilities (SLD) that co-occur with other difficulties, especially mathematics difficulties, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), and anxiety. The paper is motivated by the observation that many students with SLD have more than one area of need, yet intervention research often targets only a single academic domain without considering co-occurring conditions.

The article synthesizes evidence from prior systematic reviews, meta-analyses, randomized trials, and individual studies on Tier 1, Tier 2, and Tier 3 supports within a multi-tiered systems of support (MTSS) framework. It discusses reading interventions, combined reading-math interventions, anxiety management, ADHD-related pharmacological and non-pharmacological supports, and data-based individualization. Across these areas, the strongest evidence is for word-level reading interventions for students with co-occurring reading and attention difficulties, while evidence is mixed or limited for improving reading via ADHD medication or anxiety management alone. The review also highlights promising but still preliminary findings for integrated interventions targeting both reading and mathematics or reading and anxiety, and emphasizes the need for more research on older students, dosage, sequencing, and implementation feasibility.

finding.finding_summary: The review finds strong evidence that word-level reading interventions improve word-level reading outcomes for students with co-occurring reading and attention difficulties, with a meta-analysis reporting large effects (ES = 1.11) on standardized reading outcomes for interventions delivered for at least 30 hours in regular classrooms. However, evidence is weak or mixed for reading comprehension interventions, and ADHD medications show little consistent benefit for reading outcomes.
finding.measure: Word-level reading, reading comprehension, and standardized reading outcomes
finding.effect_size: ES = 1.11 (for word-level reading interventions in students with ADHD and reading difficulties); other studies reported ESs = 0.39 to 0.56 and 1.22 for specific combined interventions

finding.finding_summary: For students with co-occurring reading and mathematics difficulties, combined reading-and-mathematics intervention outperformed business-as-usual and reading-only conditions on calculation outcomes in a randomized study of U.S. first graders (n = 277), with effect sizes of 0.60 versus BAU and 0.57 versus reading only. A second study (n = 221) found large domain-aligned gains for mathematics interventions on math outcomes (ESs = 1.05–1.36) and cross-domain transfer from math to reading (ESs = 0.54–0.91).
finding.measure: Calculations, calculations fluency, and word-problem solving

finding.finding_summary: The review reports that anxiety management interventions can reduce anxiety symptoms in some studies, but effects on reading-related anxiety and academic outcomes are mixed. In one group-design study of Canadian students (n = 36), a relaxation-based intervention did not improve word-level reading, reading comprehension, or anxiety during reading/non-reading tasks; in a 2-year combined reading-anxiety intervention (n = 128), general and social anxiety improved, but reading-anxiety effects were mixed and some academic effects depended on baseline reading anxiety.
finding.measure: Anxiety symptoms, reading anxiety, general anxiety, social anxiety
finding.effect_size: ES = 1.22 (reading comprehension at end of Year 2 for combined intervention vs BAU); ES = 0.77 (vs math-reading condition)

finding.finding_summary: The article does not test operational efficiency directly, but it identifies data-based individualization (DBI) as a promising framework for intensifying support through ongoing progress monitoring and adaptation of intervention features such as dosage. The paper presents DBI as an efficient problem-solving process for tailoring instruction, while noting that more research is needed on feasibility and acceptability.
finding.measure: Progress monitoring / intervention adaptation feasibility

finding.finding_summary: The review argues for a unified MTSS framework that integrates academic, behavioral, and social-emotional supports across tiers and emphasizes that co-occurring difficulties require coordinated, multimodal intervention planning. This is a conceptual and implementation-oriented contribution rather than an outcomes trial, but it highlights system-level implications for school organization, special education continuum design, and cross-domain support.
finding.measure: MTSS / special education implementation and coordination

paper_profiles.title: Life Course Health Development in Autism Spectrum Disorders
paper_profiles.venue: Handbook of Life Course Health Development
paper_profiles.population: Not directly an education sample; synthesis focused on children, adolescents, and adults with autism spectrum disorders
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This book chapter reviews autism spectrum disorders (ASD) through the lens of life course health development. Rather than testing a specific intervention, it synthesizes evidence on ASD epidemiology, genetic and environmental contributions, diagnostic stability, developmental course, adult outcomes, quality of life, and predictors of later functioning. The chapter is explicitly framed as a conceptual and narrative review aimed at understanding how ASD develops over time and how outcomes vary across the lifespan.

The chapter emphasizes that ASD is an early-onset neurodevelopmental condition with strong genetic contributions, some environmental influences, and wide variation in developmental trajectories. It summarizes evidence that early language, intellectual functioning, joint attention, and adaptive skills are important predictors of later independence and quality of life, while also noting that symptom severity often persists but may change over time. The authors argue that traditional outcome definitions focused narrowly on adult independence are insufficient and that future work should attend more to quality of life, supports, and developmental context across childhood through adulthood.

Because the chapter is a broad synthesis rather than an empirical study, it does not evaluate an educational program or instructional intervention. Its main contribution is to organize the ASD literature around developmental timing, context, and trajectories, with implications for early identification, intervention planning, and long-term support.

paper_profiles.title: Mindfulness Training for Adolescents with Learning Disabilities
paper_profiles.venue: University of Toronto Master of Arts thesis
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This thesis evaluates whether a 20-week Mindfulness Martial Arts (MMA) program improves executive functioning, behavior, social skills, and mindfulness in adolescent boys with learning disabilities (LD), many of whom also had ADHD or anxiety symptoms. The study was motivated by the high overlap between LD and ADHD, the associated executive-function and self-regulation difficulties, and the need for non-stigmatizing intervention options for youth with co-occurring behavioral and emotional concerns.

The intervention combined mindfulness meditation, cognitive-behavioral therapy, and mixed martial arts in weekly 1.5-hour group sessions. Sixty-five boys ages 12-18 from a Toronto children’s mental health center were assigned to either MMA or a waitlist control group; because assignment was not randomized, the design is quasi-experimental. Outcomes were assessed using parent and adolescent standardized questionnaires at pre-test and post-test, with follow-up data collected only for the MMA group.

In the full sample, the study found no intervention-specific effects relative to waitlist, although both groups changed over time on several measures. Exploratory subgroup analyses suggested benefits for adolescents with comorbid ADHD, especially those with elevated hyperactive/impulsive symptoms, who showed improvements in parent-rated monitoring and social problems and in parent-rated externalizing, oppositional, and conduct problems for the comorbid LD/ADHD subgroup. Adolescents with elevated anxiety symptoms also showed reduced self-reported DSM anxiety problems after MMA. However, the mindfulness scale did not show a significant pre-post increase, and some self-reports in the hyperactive/impulsive subgroup worsened, making the overall pattern mixed rather than uniformly positive.

finding.finding_summary: Across the full sample, there were no significant Group or Group × Time effects attributable to MMA on behavior problems, but several parent- and self-reported scales improved over time in both groups. In subgroup analyses, youth with comorbid LD/ADHD showed significant MMA-related reductions in parent-rated externalizing behavior, oppositional defiant problems, and conduct problems (e.g., externalizing F(1,19)=5.97, p<.05; conduct F(1,19)=9.91, p<.01), while boys with high hyperactive/impulsive symptoms showed improved parent-rated monitoring and social problems (monitoring F(1,22)=6.90, p<.05; social problems F(1,22)=10.20, p<.01).
finding.measure: CBCL externalizing, oppositional defiant, conduct, and social problems; BRIEF monitoring problems
finding.study_size: n=65 total; subgroup analyses n=21 LD/ADHD, n=24 hyperactive/impulsive parent-rated analyses, n=25 anxious parent-rated analyses
finding.effect_size: partial η2=.24, .28, .34, .24, .32; other effect sizes not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The study focused heavily on executive function, particularly behavioral regulation and metacognition. In the full sample there were no MMA-specific effects, but in the comorbid LD/ADHD subgroup the MMA group improved on BRIEF behavioral regulation-related subscales including shift, emotional control, working memory, plan/organize, and monitor, with significant time effects but no significant between-group interaction reported on the BRIEF. In the hyperactive/impulsive subgroup, MMA produced a significant Group × Time effect on BRIEF monitoring problems, F(1,22)=6.90, p<.05, partial η2=.24.
finding.measure: BRIEF behavioral regulation index, metacognition index, shift, emotional control, working memory, plan/organize, monitor
finding.study_size: n=65 total; subgroup BRIEF analyses n=22 LD/ADHD, n=24 hyperactive/impulsive, n=27 inattentive
finding.effect_size: partial η2=.24; other effect sizes not_reported

finding.finding_summary: Among adolescents with clinically elevated anxiety symptoms, MMA was associated with reduced self-reported DSM anxiety problems at post-test compared with waitlist, F(1,24)=7.65, p<.05, partial η2=.24. Parent-rated anxiety-related scales did not show significant Group or Group × Time effects, though several anxiety measures improved over time in both groups.
finding.measure: YSR DSM anxiety problems; CBCL anxious/depressed and DSM anxiety problems
finding.study_size: n=29 anxiety subgroup overall; self-report analysis n=26 (11 MMA, 15 WL)

finding.finding_summary: The program’s mindfulness outcome did not improve significantly over time in the small phase-5 pilot sample. On the Modified Mindful Attention Awareness Scale (MMAAS), 10 MMA participants showed no significant pre-post change, t(9)=.396, p=.70.
finding.measure: Modified Mindful Attention Awareness Scale (MMAAS)

paper_profiles.title: Executive functions mediate the association between ADHD symptoms and anxiety in a clinical adolescent population
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines why attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is so often associated with anxiety in adolescents. The authors test whether ADHD symptoms, executive dysfunction, and functional impairment predict anxiety symptoms, and whether executive functions and functional impairment mediate the ADHD-anxiety relationship.

The study analyzed baseline data from 100 adolescents aged 14–18 years recruited from two outpatient child and adolescent psychiatry units in Norway. All participants had prior ADHD/hyperkinetic disorder diagnoses, and most were receiving ADHD medication (91%). Adolescents and parents completed rating scales for ADHD symptoms (ADHD RS-IV), executive function (BRIEF), functional impairment (WFIRS), and anxiety (SCARED); analyses used regression and serial mediation models with age and sex as covariates.

Results showed that self-rated inattentive symptoms predicted anxiety, whereas parent-rated ADHD symptoms did not. Executive dysfunction and functional impairment each predicted anxiety, but in mediation analyses ADHD symptoms did not directly predict anxiety once the mediators were included. Instead, executive dysfunction was the key mediator, and functional impairment operated mainly through executive dysfunction. The authors conclude that executive dysfunction is an important treatment target for adolescents with impairing ADHD symptoms and comorbid anxiety, especially in medication-treated clinical samples.

finding.finding_summary: In a clinical sample of adolescents with ADHD symptoms (n=100), self-rated inattentive symptoms predicted higher anxiety (p=0.002), while parent-rated ADHD symptoms did not. Executive dysfunction and functional impairment both predicted anxiety in regression analyses, but the clearest pathway in mediation models was through executive dysfunction, which mediated the ADHD-anxiety association (parent-report indirect effect coefficient=0.466, 95% CI 0.013 to 1.024; self-report indirect effect coefficient=0.478, 95% CI 0.025 to 0.947).
finding.measure: SCARED total anxiety score; ADHD RS-IV; BRIEF global executive composite/indices; WFIRS total score
finding.confidence_interval: parent indirect effect 0.013 to 1.024; self indirect effect 0.025 to 0.947

finding.finding_summary: Executive function difficulties were strongly associated with anxiety and were the central mediator of the ADHD-anxiety relationship. Across parent and self reports, BRIEF global executive composite, metacognitive index, and behavior regulation index predicted anxiety in step-1 regressions, and the serial mediation results indicated that ADHD symptoms influenced anxiety through executive dysfunction and then functional impairment.
finding.measure: BRIEF (Global Executive Composite, Metacognitive Index, Behavior Regulation Index); serial mediation with WFIRS and SCARED

finding.finding_summary: Functional impairment predicted anxiety in both parent- and self-report analyses, but functional impairment alone was not a significant mediator of the ADHD-anxiety relationship. In serial mediation, functional impairment contributed indirectly after executive dysfunction, suggesting that day-to-day impairment is linked to anxiety largely through executive problems rather than acting as an independent pathway.
finding.measure: WFIRS parent-report/self-report total mean score; SCARED total score
finding.confidence_interval: functional impairment only: parent CI -0.275 to 0.0241; self CI -0.199 to 0.261

paper_profiles.title: Dual-task Coordination in Children and Adolescents with Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examined whether children and adolescents with ADHD show deficits in dual-task coordination, a core executive-function ability involving simultaneous performance of two tasks. The authors also asked whether dual-task performance depends on task difficulty, whether a paper-and-pencil dual-task measure produces results comparable to a computerized version, and whether performance is influenced by general motor ability or comorbid conditions.

The study included 91 children/adolescents with ADHD and 91 typically developing controls aged 6-16 years from schools and a pediatric neurology clinic in Tbilisi. Participants were matched on age and years of education, and groups were assessed with WISC-III, ADHD diagnostic ratings, the SCQ, CBCL/TRF, and the MABC-2. They completed computerized and paper-and-pencil dual-task paradigms combining serial digit recall with motor tracking, including variants with manipulated task difficulty.

Results showed that dual-task coordination was generally preserved in ADHD and did not differ significantly from controls on most measures, although some computerized motor-tracking indices favored controls. The paper-and-pencil version produced broadly similar group patterns and correlated moderately with the computerized version. General motor functioning, especially balance, predicted some dual-task outcomes in controls but not ADHD, and comorbidity mattered for some computerized motor outcomes. Overall, the paper concludes that children with ADHD do not show a strong generalized dual-task deficit, and that dual-task performance is influenced more by method and motor factors than by ADHD diagnosis alone.

finding.finding_summary: Dual-task coordination was largely intact in children and adolescents with ADHD compared with matched controls. On the computerized version, the group effect for the combined μ score was small and not statistically significant at conventional levels (controls M=101.51, SD=10.34; ADHD M=98.43, SD=12.01), and on the paper-and-pencil version there were no significant group differences in percentage change or μ scores.
finding.measure: Dual-task coordination performance (combined μ score; percentage change on digit span + motor tracking tasks)
finding.std_deviation: controls SD=10.34; ADHD SD=12.01 for computerized μ score

paper_profiles.title: School value-added models for multivariate academic and non-academic outcomes: A more rounded approach to using student data to inform school accountability
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether school accountability systems can be improved by moving beyond a narrow focus on attainment and instead jointly modelling academic and non-academic student outcomes. The authors argue that school value-added models usually rely on exam results alone, which can miss important dimensions of school performance such as absenteeism and exclusions.

Using administrative data from England’s National Pupil Database, the study analyzes a random sample of 300 secondary schools (n=45,103 students) who took GCSEs in 2017/2018. The authors estimate multilevel multivariate models for three outcomes: Attainment 8, total absences (log-transformed), and exclusion status. They compare a sequence of models that progressively adjust for prior attainment, prior absences/exclusions, student background, and school characteristics.

The main conclusion is that school effects are only weakly aligned across the three outcomes. After adjustment, the correlation between school effects on attainment and absences is small (e.g., -0.12 in the contextual value-added model), indicating that schools effective at raising attainment are not necessarily effective at reducing absences or exclusions. The paper concludes that school accountability systems should incorporate multiple outcomes, including non-academic measures, because singular attainment-based summaries provide an incomplete picture of school performance.

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly models Attainment 8, a composite secondary-school academic attainment measure, across 45,103 students in 300 English secondary schools. After controlling for prior attainment and student background, school effects on attainment remained but were only partly explained by school characteristics; the final contextual value-added model retained a school variance of 0.037 with VPC=9% and R-squared=0.56.
finding.measure: Attainment 8 score (standardized on a common response scale)

finding.finding_summary: The paper treats absences as an indicator of student disengagement/school connection and models total absences (log transformed) for the same sample of 45,103 students. In the final contextual value-added model, school effects on log absences were weakly related to attainment (school-effect correlation -0.12) and the model explained 28% of the variance, with school variance 0.037 and VPC=5%; the results suggest absences capture a distinct non-academic dimension of school performance.
finding.measure: Total absences across secondary school (log transformed)

finding.finding_summary: The study is centrally about implications for school accountability and governance, not an intervention effect. It finds that incorporating non-academic outcomes changes how schools are evaluated: after adjustment, school effects on attainment, absences, and exclusions are only modestly correlated, and adding school characteristics reduces some school-level variance (e.g., attainment variance from 0.059 to 0.037; exclusions from 0.086 to 0.076 in Model 4).
finding.measure: School value-added effects, school variance components, and correlations across outcomes for accountability modeling

paper_profiles.title: Cognitive characteristics of intellectually gifted children with a diagnosis of ADHD
paper_profiles.population: Elementary through High School (ages 6.0 to 16.9 years)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the cognitive profile of “twice exceptional” children who are both intellectually gifted and diagnosed with ADHD. The authors ask whether giftedness changes the way ADHD appears cognitively, whether gifted children with ADHD are being misdiagnosed, and whether comorbid specific learning disorder (SLD) meaningfully differentiates gifted-ADHD subgroups.

Using WISC-IV data from a large Italian clinical sample of 1,051 children diagnosed with ADHD, the study identifies 82 children with a General Ability Index (GAI) of at least 125 as intellectually gifted (2e-ADHD). These children are compared with children with average ADHD profiles and with a separate gifted SLD sample. The authors also simulate expected profiles from the broader ADHD distribution to test whether the observed gifted-ADHD profile matches what would be expected statistically from the upper tail of the ADHD population.

The main finding is that intellectually gifted children with ADHD do show the typical ADHD pattern of relative weakness in working memory and processing speed, despite high verbal and reasoning scores. Their profile closely resembles that of average-IQ children with ADHD, which supports the validity of the ADHD diagnosis rather than suggesting misdiagnosis due to boredom or giftedness alone. The study also finds little difference between gifted-ADHD children with versus without SLD, and concludes that giftedness appears more common among children with ADHD than expected from population norms when intelligence is measured with GAI rather than full-scale IQ.

finding.finding_summary: The study is not an academic achievement intervention study, but it directly examines cognitive profiles relevant to school functioning in 2e-ADHD children. Gifted children with ADHD showed strong reasoning abilities (GAI M=130.24, SD=5.58; VCI M=127.15, PRI M=126.05) alongside weaker working memory and processing speed (WMI M=97.37, PSI M=95.88), a pattern associated with learning challenges in school contexts. The authors conclude that these cognitive strengths and weaknesses have educational implications, including the need for personalized classroom support and accommodations.
finding.measure: WISC-IV indices and subtests relevant to school learning and cognitive functioning
finding.study_size: n=82 gifted ADHD; comparison groups n=675 average ADHD and n=129 gifted SLD
finding.std_deviation: GAI SD=5.58; FSIQ SD=8.21; WMI SD=11.54; PSI SD=15.24

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively analyzes working memory, processing speed, and attentional control as cognitive processes underlying learning and task performance. Compared with average ADHD children, gifted ADHD children still had notable deficits in working memory and processing speed (e.g., WMI 97.37 vs 85.19; PSI 95.88 vs 88.19), and the authors interpret these as persistent weaknesses that affect the ability to manage tasks, sustain focus, and respond efficiently. No formal effect sizes are reported for the main group comparisons, but the subgroup comparisons within gifted ADHD showed small, non-significant differences (e.g., GAI d=0.17, FSIQ d=0.29).
finding.measure: WISC-IV working memory and processing speed subtests/indexes; subgroup comparisons and simulated profiles
finding.study_size: n=82 gifted ADHD; subgroup comparison n=32 without SLD and n=35 with SLD
finding.effect_size: d=0.17 to 0.29 for subgroup comparisons; otherwise not_reported
finding.std_deviation: WMI SDs 11.45 and 10.60; PSI SDs 14.03 and 16.67

paper_profiles.title: Academic Writing with GPT-3.5: Reflections on Practices, Efficacy and Transparency
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how GPT-3.5 can be used in academic writing, how effective it is, and how researchers can use it transparently and responsibly. Rather than testing a pedagogical intervention, the author conducts a personal experience experiment while writing the article itself, using OpenAI’s text-davinci-003 model in the OpenAI Playground and reflecting on the process.

The paper describes five writing workflows: Chunk Stylist, Bullet-to-Paragraph, Talk Textualizer, Research Buddy, and Polisher. The author reports that GPT-3.5 helped with motivation, productivity, and reducing friction in the writing process, but also required substantial human revision and raised concerns about accuracy, authorship, transparency, and ecological cost. The strongest practical value was found in approaches where the model formalized the author’s own ideas (Chunk Stylist and Talk Textualizer), while approaches that generated more text independently required more correction and carried more risk of factual drift.

The context is a design-research perspective piece aimed at researchers and academic writers, not K-12 learners. The main conclusion is that GPT-3.5 can support academic writing when used as a drafting, transcription, or copy-editing aid, but it should be accompanied by explicit documentation of prompts, outputs, and edits to preserve transparency. The paper is reflective and exploratory rather than evaluative of learner outcomes, and it does not provide generalizable causal evidence of educational impact.

finding.finding_summary: The author reports that GPT-3.5 made the writing process smoother, reduced interruptions, and improved perceived productivity, but it was not a purely time-saving tool because extensive revision was still required. In one example, drafting an introduction took about 10 minutes, while revisions took about 90 minutes, and preparing the comparison report took about 5 additional hours.
finding.measure: Self-reported writing speed, revision time, and perceived productivity/motivation

finding.finding_summary: The author states that using GPT-3.5 had a largely positive effect on motivation and reduced the burden of writing, helping maintain focus on ideas rather than mechanics. The reflection is based on personal experience rather than a standardized instrument, so no statistical estimate is reported.
finding.measure: Self-reported motivation and writing comfort

finding.finding_summary: GPT-3.5 was portrayed as helpful for organizing ideas and formalizing text, which supported writing-related metacognitive work, but it also created uncertainty about authorship, factual reliability, and critical evaluation of outputs. The author explicitly notes the need for constant critical thinking when using Research Buddy-style prompts.
finding.measure: Self-reflection on critical thinking, metacognition, and authorial control during writing

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that GPT-3.5 can improve academic writing by helping draft, rewrite, transcribe, and polish text, especially when the user already has clear ideas. However, the author also reports that some methods produced inaccurate or weakly grounded text and required substantial manual editing, so the writing gains were contingent on the method used and the amount of human oversight.
finding.measure: Quality of generated/revised academic prose; percentage-difference comparisons between original, model output, and final text

paper_profiles.title: Quantifying the Academic Quality of Children’s Videos using Machine Comprehension
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether the academic quality of children’s YouTube Kids videos can be quantified automatically, and whether popular channels differ in how much textbook-aligned academic content they contain. The authors frame the problem as evaluating learning value rather than safety or entertainment value, arguing that parents and platforms need a scalable metric for educational quality.

To do this, they combine multi-modal video retrieval with reading comprehension. They build a large dataset of 85,976 videos from the top 100 YouTube Kids channels, plus a smaller manually labeled CVQA set (about 100 videos, 653 factual questions) and evaluate against the Textbook Question Answering (TQA) science dataset drawn from middle-school CK-12 materials. Their pipeline retrieves relevant videos using transcripts and video-frame captions, then applies Longformer-based question answering and multiple-choice answer extraction to see how many textbook questions can be answered correctly.

The main conclusion is that YouTube Kids videos from top channels can answer a substantial share of textbook questions when selected appropriately, with the best multi-modal retrieval pipeline reaching about 78.09% accuracy on TQA questions. Transcript-based retrieval generally outperforms caption-only retrieval, while combining transcripts and captions performs best overall. The paper also finds that some popular channels have relatively low academic quality, though there is a positive association between channel popularity and the amount of textbook-aligned content captured by their metric.

finding.finding_summary: The study finds that YouTube Kids videos from top channels can support answering middle-school science textbook questions at above-chance levels, indicating substantive alignment with scientific learning content. The best pipeline, Multi-modal Retriever + Longformer + CLEM, achieved 78.09% accuracy on TQA questions, compared with 32.01% baseline on random text and 76.27% using transcript-only retrieval.
finding.measure: Accuracy on Textbook Question Answering (TQA) science questions
finding.study_size: n=26,260 TQA questions; 85,976 YTK videos in retrieval corpus

finding.finding_summary: The paper proposes and validates a proxy metric for the academic quality of children’s videos relative to middle-school curriculum content. Across the top 100 YouTube Kids channels, some channels such as Sesame Street and Ryan’s Toys Review scored better on this metric than many others, while several highly viewed channels had low academic quality scores.
finding.measure: Channel-level academic quality score (percentage of TQA questions answered correctly per video)

finding.finding_summary: The proposed retrieval-plus-reading-comprehension pipeline is presented as a scalable way to evaluate large video libraries without manually inspecting each video. The authors argue that using retrieval to narrow to top-k videos and then applying Longformer-based question answering substantially reduces the computational burden compared with running question answering over all videos directly.
finding.measure: Feasibility/efficiency of automated video quality assessment pipeline

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests the method could help parents, platform owners, and policymakers monitor and rank children’s content by academic quality. It reports that academic quality varies substantially across channels, implying that platform-level quality guidelines and ranking systems could use such a metric to promote more educational content.
finding.measure: Comparative academic quality across channels and proposed platform-level monitoring metric

paper_profiles.title: Classification of ADHD and Healthy Children Using Multi-Band and Spatial Features of EEG
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of distinguishing children with ADHD from healthy controls using EEG signals and machine-learning methods. The motivation is to support early, objective, and non-invasive diagnosis of ADHD, since behavioral diagnosis can be difficult and subjective.

The study used a benchmark EEG dataset with 61 children diagnosed with ADHD and 60 healthy controls, ages 7 to 12. EEG was recorded from 19 channels during a visual attention task in which children counted cartoon characters. The authors extracted multi-band Power Spectral Density and Spectral Entropy features across delta, theta, alpha, beta, and gamma bands, then trained classifiers including SVM and XGBoost.

Results showed that SVM with an RBF kernel performed best, reaching 99.2% mean cross-validation accuracy with standard deviation 0.0079, outperforming XGBoost (96.92% accuracy). The paper concludes that multi-band EEG features combined with machine learning can classify ADHD vs. control children with very high accuracy, suggesting potential for non-invasive diagnostic support. However, the work is a classification study rather than an intervention study, and it does not evaluate academic outcomes or moderators of medication benefit.

paper_profiles.title: Microsoft Academic automatic document searches: Accuracy for journal articles and suitability for citation analysis
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper evaluates how accurately Microsoft Academic can identify journal articles and whether its citation counts are suitable for large-scale citation analysis. The author asks whether document searches can reliably retrieve specific articles using combinations of title, author, journal, and year, and whether Microsoft Academic citation counts track Scopus citation counts closely enough to be used as a substitute.

The study uses a large sample of Scopus-indexed journal articles published in 2012 (n=126,312 across 323 Scopus subfields) and tests several Microsoft Academic query strategies. The key approach is to search by title and then filter out false matches using DOI or metadata checks. The paper finds that title-only searches are the most effective: on average they recover 89.6% of DOI-matched articles with 93.8% precision, and 89.1% of non-DOI articles after metadata filtering. Adding author, journal, or year generally reduces recall without improving correctness.

The paper also compares citation counts from Microsoft Academic and Scopus for the matched articles. Overall, the two sources are highly correlated (average Spearman r=0.948), suggesting that Microsoft Academic is broadly usable for citation analysis of journal articles from this period. However, the paper highlights important limitations, especially lower retrieval rates for non-English or dual-language titles and substantial national and journal-level biases in coverage.

finding.finding_summary: The paper shows that Microsoft Academic can efficiently retrieve journal articles for citation-analysis workflows using automated queries. The best strategy was title-only searching followed by DOI/metadata filtering, which achieved mean recall of 89.6% for DOI-checked matches and 89.1% for non-DOI matches, indicating fairly efficient large-scale document retrieval.
finding.measure: Document retrieval precision and recall for Microsoft Academic search strategies
finding.study_size: n=126,312 journal articles across 323 Scopus subfields

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests Microsoft Academic can be used as a substitute citation source for research evaluation in many settings, because citation counts closely matched Scopus (average Spearman r=0.948). However, the paper also shows systematic coverage biases by language and country, with title-search match rates ranging from 77% (Brazil) to 95% (Australia), which has implications for institutional and national research assessment.
finding.measure: Spearman correlations of citation counts; field- and country-level retrieval rates

paper_profiles.title: A Network Theory Investigation into the Altered Resting State Functional Connectivity in Attention-Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether adults with attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) show altered resting-state functional connectivity (RS-fMRI) compared with healthy controls. The motivation is to identify abnormal brain network organization in ADHD using network-theoretic methods rather than task-based activation alone.

The study uses the UCLA Consortium for Neuropsychiatric Phenomics/OpenfMRI resting-state dataset and analyzes 40 adults with ADHD and 40 matched healthy controls. The authors preprocess the fMRI data in SPM12, denoise the time series, and then apply three connectivity approaches: random field theory-based seed/voxel inference, functional network connectivity (FNC) using ICA, and network-based statistic (NBS).

Across methods, the main finding is that ADHD is associated with altered connectivity in default mode and attention-related regions. Relative to controls, ADHD participants show lower average connectivity in the supramarginal gyrus and superior parietal lobule, and higher average connectivity in the lateral occipital cortex and inferior temporal gyrus. Network analyses also show increased connectivity between medial prefrontal cortex and inferior/middle temporal regions, alongside decreased connectivity between medial prefrontal cortex and intraparietal sulcus/superior parietal regions. The paper concludes that network theory can help characterize atypical resting-state brain organization in ADHD, but it does not evaluate educational interventions or academic outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: Academic Lobification: Low Performance Control Strategy for Long-planed Academic Purpose
paper_profiles.population: Not a human-subject study; conceptual discussion of students and scholars across middle school, college, graduate, post-doctoral, and faculty contexts
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces and defines the concept of "academic lobification," which the author describes as the deliberate hiding of academic behavior, lowering of performance, or delaying of academic returns for long-term strategic purposes. The paper argues that such behavior is an important but under-recognized factor that biases student evaluation, academic risk prediction, and the identification of gifted underachievers.

Rather than testing an intervention, the article is a conceptual and interdisciplinary essay. It draws on social psychology, economics, game theory, data science, behavioral science, and pedagogy to explain why lobification might occur, how it might be detected, and where it may matter in educational settings. The author proposes that academic lobification can be studied through mobile sensing, behavior computing, anomaly detection, and interpretable machine learning methods.

The paper’s context is broad and largely theoretical, spanning middle school students, college students, graduate students, postdoctoral researchers, and scholars/teachers. Its main conclusion is that academic lobification should be treated as a distinct research object and that future work should build an interdisciplinary field—"Lobificationlogy"—to study behavior, exposure, and group dynamics. No empirical data, intervention, or outcome evaluation is reported.

finding.finding_summary: The paper is conceptual and does not report empirical institutional outcomes; instead, it argues that recognizing academic lobification could improve student evaluation, academic risk prediction, and incentive design. It presents these as proposed applications rather than measured effects, with no sample size or effect estimate reported.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The article discusses delayed gratification, self-control, and strategic behavior as theoretical antecedents of academic lobification, but it does not measure these skills empirically. No participants, measures, or statistical results are reported.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper theorizes that self-worth, self-concealment, self-discrepancy, and self-efficacy may motivate lobification, linking the concept to student self-protection and self-esteem. However, these claims are purely conceptual and are not tested with data.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: Does methylphenidate improve academic performance? A systematic review and meta-analysis
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether methylphenidate improves academic performance in children with ADHD, and whether any benefits are better explained by improved attention symptoms or classroom behavior. The authors also examine whether effects differ by academic domain (math, reading, spelling) and by implementation conditions or subgroup characteristics such as age, sex, ADHD subtype, comorbidity, dose, formulation, titration method, and trial duration.

The review synthesized 34 placebo-controlled studies of mostly primary school children with ADHD (N=1777 in meta-analysis). Outcomes were separated into academic productivity and accuracy for math and reading, with spelling handled narratively because too few studies reported comparable data. The meta-analysis found small but significant benefits for math accuracy (3.0%) and math productivity (7.8%), and a medium effect for reading items attempted (SMD/d=0.47), but no significant effect for reading accuracy. Spelling findings were inconclusive. None of the tested mediators or moderators significantly explained variation in methylphenidate efficacy.

Overall, the paper concludes that methylphenidate produces specific and modest short-term academic gains, especially on productivity measures and especially in math, but these gains are much smaller than symptom improvements and do not appear to be driven by the measured moderators or by teacher-rated symptom change. The authors caution that medication should not be assumed to improve all forms of academic performance equally, and that longer-term educational outcomes remain uncertain.

finding.finding_summary: Methylphenidate did not significantly improve reading accuracy (9 studies, N=207; risk difference=0.062, 95% CI -0.009 to 0.134, p=.089), but it did improve the number of reading items attempted (5 studies, N=100; d=0.47, 95% CI 0.302 to 0.637, p<.001). The review’s narrative synthesis of spelling was inconclusive, with only 1 of 3 studies reporting significant spelling gains.
finding.measure: Reading accuracy, reading number attempted, and spelling accuracy
finding.study_size: Reading accuracy n=207; reading attempted n=100; spelling not_reported
finding.effect_size: Reading accuracy RD=0.062; reading attempted d=0.47; spelling not_reported
finding.confidence_interval: Reading accuracy 95% CI -0.009 to 0.134; reading attempted 95% CI 0.302 to 0.637; spelling not_reported

finding.finding_summary: Across 29 studies (N=1528), methylphenidate significantly improved math accuracy by 3.0% (risk difference=0.030, 95% CI 0.012 to 0.048, p=.001). Across 17 studies (N=912), it also improved math productivity by 7.8% (risk difference=0.078, 95% CI 0.043 to 0.112, p<.001).
finding.measure: Math accuracy and math productivity
finding.study_size: Math accuracy n=1528; math productivity n=912
finding.effect_size: Math accuracy RD=0.030; math productivity RD=0.078
finding.confidence_interval: Math accuracy 95% CI 0.012 to 0.048; math productivity 95% CI 0.043 to 0.112

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly analyzed academic productivity as the amount of work completed under timed conditions, which is an efficiency-oriented outcome. Methylphenidate improved math productivity by 7.8% (17 studies, N=912) and increased reading items attempted by a medium amount (5 studies, N=100; d=0.47), indicating more work completed in the same time period.
finding.measure: Math productivity and reading items attempted
finding.study_size: Math productivity n=912; reading attempted n=100
finding.effect_size: Math productivity RD=0.078; reading attempted d=0.47
finding.confidence_interval: Math productivity 95% CI 0.043 to 0.112; reading attempted 95% CI 0.302 to 0.637

paper_profiles.title: Treating attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder beyond symptom control alone in children and adolescents: a review of the potential benefits of long-acting stimulants
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This review examines whether ADHD treatment, especially long-acting methylphenidate formulations, should be evaluated beyond short-term symptom reduction alone. The paper argues that ADHD affects not only classroom behavior but also social functioning, family relationships, quality of life, adherence, and after-school functioning, and therefore treatment should cover the full day rather than only school hours.

The review centers on long-acting stimulants, especially OROS methylphenidate, and synthesizes evidence from randomized trials, open-label studies, and observational reports in children and adolescents with ADHD. It compares OROS methylphenidate with immediate-release methylphenidate and atomoxetine, and discusses how extended symptom control may help with homework, peer interactions, driving, and family functioning while potentially reducing stigma and improving adherence.

The authors conclude that full-day coverage with long-acting stimulant medication may provide benefits beyond symptom control, including improvements in academic productivity, social competence, and everyday functioning. They also note concerns about long-term stimulant treatment, such as growth, sleep, tics, cardiovascular effects, psychiatric adverse events, and abuse potential, but generally describe these risks as manageable and emphasize the need for further long-term research.

finding.finding_summary: Across multiple studies summarized in the review, OROS methylphenidate improved academic productivity and homework-related functioning compared with placebo and, in some studies, compared with immediate-release methylphenidate. The paper cites a 28-day double-blind trial in 282 children and other laboratory school studies showing better school-day and homework-period performance, but the review does not report a single pooled effect size for academic outcomes.
finding.measure: Academic productivity, homework performance, classroom behavior ratings

finding.finding_summary: The review reports that extending stimulant coverage into the late afternoon and evening improves peer interaction, self-esteem, and overall social functioning in children and adolescents with ADHD. It cites open-label follow-up data showing sustained improvements up to 12 months and notes that symptom control throughout the day may reduce embarrassment, stigma, and family conflict, though no pooled effect size is provided.
finding.measure: Peer interaction, self-esteem, global assessment, parent-reported social functioning

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that all-day symptom control may improve skills such as persistence, cooperation, and regulation of behavior across settings, and it cites studies showing improvements in working memory and classroom/task engagement with methylphenidate. However, these are presented as mixed individual-study findings within a narrative review rather than as a quantified aggregate effect.
finding.measure: Working memory, sustained attention, persistence of effort, cooperation

finding.finding_summary: A major theme of the review is that long-acting methylphenidate improves adherence and reduces dosing burden, with once-daily OROS MPH associated with better compliance than immediate-release MPH and less need for school-time medication administration. The paper also reports better persistence with therapy and fewer treatment disruptions, but does not provide a single effect size across studies.
finding.measure: Medication adherence, persistence with therapy, school-time dosing burden

paper_profiles.title: The effect of intelligent monitoring of physical exercise on executive function in children with ADHD
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether different physical activity interventions can improve executive function and motor performance in children with ADHD, motivated by the limitations and side effects of medication and the need for non-drug treatments. The authors compare a specific skill training program (EG1) with a lower-demand exercise program (EG2) and a control group over 12 weeks, while also using smart monitoring devices to track participation and progress.

Participants were children aged 7-10 years diagnosed with ADHD and randomly assigned to one of the three groups (EG1 n=13, EG2 n=14, CG n=16). The intervention occurred twice weekly for 20 minutes per session. EG1 emphasized complex coordination activities such as catching, throwing, balancing, acrobatics, juggling, and slacklining; EG2 used more general sports activities such as swimming, relay races, wrestling, climbing, gymnastics, and track and field.

The main findings suggest that the more targeted, complex skill-training intervention produced the strongest benefits. EG1 showed significant short-term gains in catching/aiming performance and significant long-term improvements in working memory measures, including digit span and letter-number sequencing, while balance and manual dexterity improved less consistently and often did not reach significance. The paper concludes that targeted physical activity may be a promising non-pharmacological approach for children with ADHD, but also notes limitations such as the small sample size, the short intervention window for complex motor skills, and the lack of differentiation by ADHD subtype.

finding.finding_summary: The intervention primarily targeted executive functioning related to self-regulation and cognitive control in children with ADHD. The strongest effects were in the specific skill-training group (EG1), which showed significant improvements in working memory and related task performance over 12 weeks, while the lower-demand exercise and control groups changed less. The paper frames these gains as relevant to learning, behavior management, and self-control, but it did not directly measure classroom engagement or behavior ratings.
finding.measure: Working memory tasks (digit span, letter-number sequencing, vocabulary fluency); catching and aiming task performance

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studied executive function components that fall within durable skills, especially working memory and task-related cognitive control. EG1 showed significant group × time improvements on digit span, letter-number sequencing, and vocabulary fluency after 12 weeks, whereas EG2 and CG showed smaller changes. Short-term effects were also significant for catching and aiming accuracy/speed, indicating improved attention to task demands and coordination.
finding.measure: Digit span, letter-number sequencing, vocabulary fluency, catching and aiming tasks, balance/manual dexterity tests

paper_profiles.title: Dual-task Coordination in Children and Adolescents with Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether children and adolescents with ADHD show deficits in dual-task coordination, a marker of executive functioning and working memory. The authors ask whether ADHD-related differences appear when tasks are performed on their individual ability levels, whether task difficulty changes performance differently for ADHD versus control groups, whether a paper-and-pencil dual-task method yields results comparable to a computerized version, and whether general motor ability or comorbid disorders explain performance differences.

The study compared 91 children and adolescents with ADHD to 91 age- and education-matched typically developing controls (ages 6-16) in Tbilisi, using computerized and paper-and-pencil dual-task paradigms combining digit span recall with motor tracking. ADHD subtypes (inattentive, hyperactive/impulsive, combined) and comorbid conduct disorder/oppositional defiant disorder were assessed; autism and major neurological/learning impairments were excluded. The authors also measured intelligence, handedness, and motor functioning (MABC-2) and manipulated task difficulty across easy, standard, and difficult levels.

Overall, the paper concludes that dual-task coordination is generally preserved in children and adolescents with ADHD and does not differ meaningfully from controls when tasks are individualized. Task difficulty did not disproportionately impair the ADHD group, and the paper-and-pencil version produced broadly comparable results to the computerized version, though test-retest reliability was only moderate. Some associations were found between computerized dual-task performance and balance/motor functioning in controls, and comorbidity and sex influenced certain computerized outcomes, but ADHD subtype effects were not robust. The paper therefore suggests that dual-task deficits are not a general hallmark of ADHD in this sample, and that motor and comorbidity factors explain only limited variance.

finding.finding_summary: The study directly tested dual-task coordination, a measure of executive functioning/working memory. Across 91 children with ADHD and 91 matched controls, dual-task performance was generally similar; the computerized motor tracking task showed a small group difference (F(1,179)=5.642, p<.018) and a borderline combined μ score difference (controls 101.51 vs ADHD 98.43), but the paper concludes there was no substantive ADHD dual-task deficit overall. No robust subtype-specific deficit was found.
finding.measure: Dual-task coordination / combined μ score from digit span plus motor tracking (computerized and paper-and-pencil versions)

finding.finding_summary: The paper-and-pencil dual-task method was intended to test whether a more practical format could substitute for the computerized version in educational/clinical settings. Results showed comparable performance patterns across formats and a significant correlation between computerized and paper-and-pencil μ scores (r=.26, p<.0001), but the paper-and-pencil version did not show meaningful ADHD-control differences or evidence of superior sensitivity; overall applicability was supported but not associated with measurable performance gains.
finding.measure: Agreement/comparability between computerized and paper-and-pencil dual-task performance; test-retest and cross-format μ-score correlations

paper_profiles.title: Teaching Physics in the first years of Elementary School to children with ADHD
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper describes a science-fair-based learning activity carried out with a small group of elementary-aged children diagnosed with ADHD at Colégio Pedro II in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. The authors frame the work around the need to support scientific literacy while also stimulating executive function skills such as time management, planning, organizing, and prioritizing tasks.

The intervention was not a controlled experiment but a practice report of a six-week project in which eight students aged 8–12 researched electricity and energy, built batteries and circuits, created a quiz board and a fabric robot, and presented their work at a school science fair. The setting was a Learning Laboratory (LL) that already served students with learning difficulties, including ADHD and learning disorders, through extra classes and hands-on activities.

The paper’s main conclusion is that the experience appeared successful: the authors observed students explaining their project confidently to the public, demonstrating understanding of energy transformation and engaging in discussions about sustainability and responsible energy use. They argue that hands-on, interest-driven science fair projects can make school more inclusive for children with ADHD and can provide opportunities to practice executive-function-related skills, though the paper does not provide quantitative outcome data or causal evidence.

finding.finding_summary: The authors report that, during the science fair presentation, the eight ADHD students (n=8) were able to explain how the electrical circuit quiz board worked and demonstrated a solid understanding of storing and changing energy from one form to another. This is presented as an observed positive educational outcome, but no standardized measure, effect size, or comparison group is reported.
finding.measure: Observed explanation of electrical circuits and understanding of energy transformation during science fair presentation

finding.finding_summary: The project was explicitly designed to stimulate ADHD students’ self-regulation and executive functioning, especially their ability to manage time, plan ahead, organize tasks, and prioritize work over a six-week preparation period. The paper reports observational evidence that students engaged in these behaviors during the project, but no quantitative pre-post measure is provided.
finding.measure: Observed executive-function-related behaviors (planning, organizing, prioritizing, time management) during project work

finding.finding_summary: The science fair process was used to cultivate durable skills such as planning, task prioritization, collaboration, and problem solving while building the project and preparing for public presentation. The authors describe the students as organizing materials, revising plans when experiments failed, and working through design decisions, but the evidence is qualitative and not measured with a formal instrument.
finding.measure: Observed planning, prioritization, collaboration, and problem-solving during science fair preparation

finding.finding_summary: The activity aimed to promote scientific literacy and broader understanding of sustainability and energy use, which the authors treat as an educational outcome beyond standard subject scores. They report that students debated responsible use of energy resources and could communicate key ideas at the fair, but there are no numeric learning gains or formal assessments.
finding.measure: Observed scientific literacy / understanding of sustainability and energy concepts

paper_profiles.title: Cognitive characteristics of intellectually gifted children with a diagnosis of ADHD
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether children who are both intellectually gifted and diagnosed with ADHD (“twice exceptional,” or 2e-ADHD) show a cognitive profile that is distinct from, or essentially an extreme version of, the broader ADHD population. The authors were motivated by concerns that gifted children may sometimes be misdiagnosed with ADHD because their attention problems can be mistaken for boredom or uneven performance, and by the need to understand whether giftedness changes the way ADHD appears cognitively.

The study analyzed WISC-IV data from 1,051 Italian children diagnosed with ADHD, including 82 children with a General Ability Index (GAI) of at least 125. The authors compared these 2e-ADHD children with average-IQ children with ADHD and with gifted children who had specific learning disorders (SLD), and they also used Monte Carlo simulation to estimate what gifted profiles should look like if 2e-ADHD children were simply the high end of the ADHD distribution. The key finding was that 2e-ADHD children were overrepresented relative to chance expectations and showed the same basic ADHD cognitive pattern as other children with ADHD: relatively strong verbal/perceptual reasoning but persistent weaknesses in working memory and processing speed. The profile of 2e-ADHD children also closely matched simulated expectations from the ADHD sample, supporting the view that they were appropriately diagnosed and that giftedness does not eliminate ADHD-related cognitive weaknesses.

The study further found that comorbid SLD did not substantially alter the cognitive profile within the 2e-ADHD group, and that age did not produce clear differences in the main profile. Overall, the paper argues for careful differential diagnosis in gifted children, but concludes that intellectually gifted children with ADHD generally show a recognizable ADHD-linked cognitive pattern rather than merely high ability with situational inattention.

finding.finding_summary: The paper is primarily a cognitive/diagnostic study, but it bears directly on academic functioning insofar as it examines intellectual profiles relevant to learning. Among 2e-ADHD children (n=82), the authors found strong verbal/perceptual reasoning but persistent weaknesses in working memory and processing speed, a pattern that can affect academic performance; however, the paper did not report direct academic achievement outcomes or intervention effects.
finding.measure: WISC-IV cognitive indexes related to learning (VCI, PRI, WMI, PSI, GAI, FSIQ)
finding.study_size: n=82 2e-ADHD; n=680 average ADHD; simulated comparison group

paper_profiles.title: Enhancing Primary Teacher Training through Academic Portfolios in Advanced Mathematics Courses
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether academic portfolios can improve the training of preservice primary mathematics teachers by bridging the gap between advanced mathematical theory and classroom practice. The authors argue that traditional assessment in mathematics teacher education overemphasizes rote performance and underemphasizes reflection, engagement, and transfer to teaching practice.

The intervention was the use of academic portfolios in two university-level courses, Algebra and Number Systems I and II, within a primary teacher education program at Pontificia Universidad Católica de Chile. The portfolio approach included a negotiated learning contract, explicit rubrics, reflective writing, revisions based on feedback, presentations or discussion tables, and ongoing formative assessment. The study followed 37 female preservice teachers in their ninth and tenth semesters across four cohorts from 2022 to 2024, using attendance records, CANVAS interaction data, grades, self-assessment surveys, peer evaluations, and reflective texts.

The findings suggest positive associations between portfolio implementation and several outcomes, including higher attendance, increased digital engagement, improved grades, stronger self-reported self-study and time management, and reduced mathematics anxiety. However, the authors repeatedly caution that the results are preliminary and correlational, with possible confounds such as cohort differences, post-pandemic return to in-person learning, and instructor experience. Overall, the paper concludes that academic portfolios are a promising pedagogical and assessment strategy in mathematics teacher education, but stronger causal evidence is needed.

finding.finding_summary: Teacher candidates in Algebra and Number Systems I and II showed higher average grades after portfolio implementation. In MAT2920, the mean grade rose from 4.43 in the prior semester to 5.89 when portfolios were introduced, and later to 6.44; in MAT2925, the mean grade increased from 5.52 to 5.80 and then to 6.44. The paper reports these as promising associations rather than causal effects, with no formal effect size reported.
finding.measure: Course grades in Algebra and Number Systems I and II (Chilean 1.0-7.0 grading scale)

finding.finding_summary: The portfolio approach was associated with stronger engagement and lower mathematics anxiety among preservice teachers. Attendance remained above 70%, no absences were recorded for portfolio-related activities, and 11 of 12 respondents (91.7%) said alternative assessments like portfolios helped mitigate mathematics anxiety. Self-assessment also indicated improvements in self-study for 85.7% of respondents and time organization for 100%.
finding.measure: Attendance records, self-assessment surveys, and end-of-semester mathematics anxiety self-report
finding.study_size: n=37 overall; n=12 for the anxiety survey section reported in results

finding.finding_summary: The study found that portfolios supported metacognition, reflection, and time management. Teacher candidates reported that the portfolio process helped them organize their learning, connect abstract mathematical ideas to teaching, and develop more systematic self-study habits; 100% reported improved time organization and the peer-evaluation component showed students could identify strengths and weaknesses in colleagues' work.
finding.measure: Self-assessment surveys, peer evaluations, and reflective portfolio paragraphs

finding.finding_summary: The portfolio process was associated with increased course participation and sustained interaction with course materials, suggesting more active use of instructional time and resources. Attendance stayed above 70%, no absences were recorded for assessed portfolio activities, and CANVAS logs averaged 185 page views per week. The paper also notes that portfolios required substantial student time investment, with 42.9% spending more than eight hours per week near deadlines, but this is framed as workload rather than efficiency gain.
finding.measure: Attendance records and CANVAS digital interaction logs

finding.finding_summary: The intervention improved teacher candidates' ability to connect advanced mathematical content to future teaching practice, which is the central pedagogical goal of the paper. Qualitative responses and instructor observations suggested that portfolios made students more active participants in their learning and helped them translate abstract algebraic concepts into classroom-relevant representations and explanations.
finding.measure: Reflective portfolio writing, instructor observations, and discussion-table participation

paper_profiles.title: Increased Coupling in the Saliency Network is the main cause/effect of Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates the brain functional connectivity correlates of ADHD in children and adolescents, with the goal of identifying altered circuits that may underlie the disorder and potentially inform diagnosis and therapy. The authors frame the work as a brain-wide association study (BWAS), analogous to a genome-wide association study, applied to resting-state fMRI data from the ADHD-200 Consortium and an additional Peking University sample.

The study compares 249 ADHD cases with 253 healthy controls across two datasets (PU and NYU), using ROI-based correlation and partial correlation analyses on 90 brain regions. The main finding is increased coupling between the anterior insula and anterior cingulate gyrus—components of the salience network—in ADHD, with other altered connections also reported. A voxel-based morphometry analysis did not show significant grey matter volume differences in the regions with altered connectivity, suggesting the functional connectivity changes were not simply driven by structural volume loss.

The authors conclude that the salience network may play a central role in ADHD pathophysiology, potentially affecting switching between default-mode and executive-control systems. They also note that the altered connectivity was most evident in left-hemisphere regions and that the connectivity findings were largely not explained by IQ, duration, or other correlates examined, although many correlations were weak. The paper is a neuroimaging study rather than an intervention or education study, and it does not test medication efficacy or classroom outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: A Network Theory Investigation into the Altered Resting State Functional Connectivity in Attention-Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether adults with ADHD show altered resting-state functional connectivity compared with healthy controls. The authors focus on whether graph/network methods applied to resting-state fMRI can identify abnormal connectivity patterns in default mode, dorsal attention, and related brain regions.

Using the UCLA Neuropsychiatric Phenomics Consortium/OpenfMRI dataset, the study analyzes resting-state fMRI from 40 adults with ADHD and 40 matched healthy controls. The authors preprocess the data in SPM12, then apply multiple connectivity approaches: random field theory-based seed-to-voxel analysis, functional network connectivity using spatial ICA, and network-based statistics on ROI-to-ROI matrices.

Across analyses, they report lower average connectivity in ADHD for the supramarginal gyrus and superior parietal lobule, and higher connectivity in the lateral occipital cortex and inferior temporal gyrus. Network-level analyses also show increased connectivity between medial prefrontal regions and temporal regions, alongside decreased connectivity between medial prefrontal cortex and intraparietal/superior parietal regions, suggesting atypical organization of default mode and dorsal attention networks in ADHD. The study is neuroimaging-focused and does not examine educational interventions, medication, or academic outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: GenAI Content Detection Task 2: AI vs. Human – Academic Essay Authenticity Challenge
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reports the first edition of the Academic Essay Authenticity Challenge, a shared task on detecting whether academic essays are human-written or generated by large language models. The core problem is academic authenticity in the era of generative AI: given an essay in English or Arabic, systems must classify it as AI-generated or human-authored. The paper is not an intervention study; rather, it documents dataset construction, task design, baseline modeling, participant submissions, and leaderboard results for the shared task.

To build the challenge, the authors assembled development and evaluation datasets from multiple human-authored essay sources and generated additional essays using several LLMs, including GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, Gemini 1.5, Phi-3.5, Llama-3.1-8B, and Claude 3.5. They used both freehand generation and paraphrasing of human essays to create challenging AI examples, and they anonymized collected human essays to protect privacy. The task was run in two phases on Codalab, with performance ranked by macro-F1. The final benchmark attracted substantial participation, with 56 registered teams, 25 English submissions, 21 Arabic submissions, and 7 system description papers.

The main conclusion is that modern detector systems can perform very strongly on this benchmark, especially when fine-tuned transformer models are combined with stylometric or linguistic features. Top systems achieved macro-F1 above 0.98 in both languages, and nearly all submitted systems beat the n-gram baseline, although a few English systems fell below baseline. The paper also notes important limitations, especially the relatively small size of the datasets and the need for larger, more challenging corpora to improve robustness and generalizability.

finding.finding_summary: The shared task shows that machine-generated vs. human-authored academic essay classification can be performed with very high accuracy on this benchmark. The best systems achieved macro-F1 scores above 0.98 in both English and Arabic, indicating strong performance on essay-text classification, which is directly related to academic writing analysis rather than student learning outcomes.
finding.measure: Macro-F1 on academic essay authenticity classification
finding.study_size: n=4,591 test/development corpus total described for Arabic and English; 56 registered teams, 46 official test submissions across both languages

paper_profiles.title: Utilizing RxNorm to Support Practical Computing Applications: Capturing Medication History in Live Electronic Health Records
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of capturing medication history accurately and efficiently in live electronic health records (EHRs). The author argues that standardized medication terminology, specifically RxNorm, can support direct-capture of medication data at the point of entry rather than relying on post-hoc mapping from legacy systems.

The approach described is an implementation study in a large, multi-state outpatient behavioral healthcare provider serving over 75,000 distinct patients annually across 130 sites. RxNorm data were extracted and restructured into specialized database tables to support autocomplete search, dosage selection, and rapid retrieval within the EHR intake module. The system was designed to balance flexibility, speed, data integrity, and medication coverage, with partial support from SNOMED CT for dose frequency terms.

The paper reports implementation outcomes rather than patient-level clinical effects. The restructured RxNorm system supported searchable information for 18,708 medications and over 42,000 common dose forms, with response times measured in milliseconds and generally imperceptible to users. Coverage against one year of legacy medication records was 93.2% (85,795/92,058 prescriptions), and the author concludes that RxNorm is suitable for practical EHR medication-history capture when appropriately adapted for high-volume clinical use.

finding.finding_summary: The restructured RxNorm implementation improved medication-entry efficiency by enabling autocomplete search, rapid dosage selection, and low-lag EHR interaction. The system supported 18,708 medications and over 42,000 common dose forms, with response times measured in milliseconds and generally imperceptible to users during testing.
finding.measure: Medication search response time, searchable medication coverage, and usability of direct-capture workflow
finding.study_size: n=1 implementation system; coverage assessed on 92,058 prescription records

finding.finding_summary: The study found that RxNorm could be successfully adapted for live EHR deployment in a large outpatient behavioral healthcare organization, supporting interoperability-oriented medication history capture across 130 clinical sites. Over a 12-month period, a simple name-match algorithm showed 93.2% coverage (85,795/92,058) against legacy medication data, suggesting substantial institutional feasibility for standardized medication terminology in production systems.
finding.measure: Medication coverage/match rate between RxNorm-derived list and legacy EHR medication data

paper_profiles.title: Predicting Injectable Medication Adherence via a Smart Sharps Bin and Machine Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of medication non-adherence and the need for better methods to predict when patients will take injectable medications on time. The authors argue that accurate adherence prediction can help healthcare providers target interventions more efficiently, especially for self-administered chronic therapies taken at home.

The study uses a connected Internet-of-Things device, the HealthBeacon Smart Sharps Bin, to passively record disposal of used injection needles as a proxy for adherence. The dataset includes 165,223 historic injection disposal records from 5,915 units over roughly three years, with model development on historical data and evaluation on a later unseen dataset. Several machine learning models were trained (Extra Trees, Random Forest, XGBoost, Gradient Boosting, and Multilayer Perceptron), and a majority-vote ensemble was proposed.

The primary focus is predicting whether the next scheduled injection will be taken within the medication administration window. The best reported testing performance was AUC = 0.86 and accuracy = 81.24%, with specificity improving from 62% to 83% after class rebalancing. The paper concludes that historical smart-bin data can identify patients at risk of non-adherence and may support targeted follow-up interventions, though it does not study educational outcomes or ADHD medication specifically.

finding.finding_summary: The paper shows that machine learning models trained on Smart Sharps Bin history can predict whether the next injection will be taken on time, supporting more efficient targeting of adherence interventions. On the unseen testing set, the best model achieved AUC = 0.86 and accuracy = 81.24% (21,631 correct predictions out of 26,624 drops after exclusions).
finding.measure: Predictive classification performance for on-time vs not-on-time medication disposal/adherence
finding.study_size: n=26,624 testing drops after exclusions; training data from 160,865 drops across 4,609 units

paper_profiles.title: Measuring Effects of Medication Adherence on Time-Varying Health Outcomes using Bayesian Dynamic Linear Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of estimating how time-varying medication adherence affects longitudinal health outcomes, arguing that standard analyses often reduce adherence to a single summary measure and therefore miss important within-person temporal variation. The authors develop a Bayesian dynamic linear model (DLM) framework that treats adherence as a time-varying covariate and allows baseline characteristics to be modeled separately from dynamic state processes.

The main empirical application is a cohort of adults with hypertension receiving anti-hypertensive medication in outpatient primary care clinics at Boston Medical Center. Using electronic pill-bottle monitoring (MEMS caps) and repeated blood-pressure measurements, the model estimates daily adherence effects while also controlling for demographics and comorbidities.
