The paper compares the DLM with non-dynamic adherence summaries (average adherence and dichotomized adherence) and finds that the dynamic model yields small but statistically significant daily blood-pressure reductions associated with adherence, along with clearer interpretation and slightly improved precision for some covariate estimates.

The study is methodological rather than an intervention trial: it does not test an educational or AI-based program, but instead proposes an analytic framework for health-outcome modeling with irregularly observed longitudinal data. The authors show how the latent process can be marginalized for efficient inference and how missing adherence values can be handled via simple imputation assumptions. Overall, the paper concludes that time-varying adherence modeling can better capture medication effects than static summaries and can support forecasting of health trajectories under different adherence patterns.

finding.finding_summary: The proposed Bayesian DLM improves modeling efficiency by marginalizing the latent state process, reducing the number of parameters that must be sampled directly and simplifying inference for longitudinal adherence data. The paper reports that this two-stage approach makes posterior simulation more tractable than standard dynamic-model updating when health outcomes are infrequently and irregularly observed, but it does not provide a formal computational benchmark or runtime effect size.
finding.measure: Computational tractability / inferential efficiency of Bayesian dynamic linear model estimation

paper_profiles.title: Identifying attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder through the electroencephalogram complexity
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether electroencephalogram (EEG) complexity, quantified with q-statistics, can distinguish children with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) from typical peers. The authors focus on neural complexity rather than an educational intervention, using EEG recordings collected while children performed the Posner Attention Network Test (ANT) and during a short resting pretask period.

The sample consisted of 38 boys aged 11–13 years, of whom 15 ADHD and 15 typical participants remained after exclusion based on the fitting criterion. Boys with pharmacological treatment or neurological/psychiatric comorbidities were excluded, so the study does not examine treatment effects, medication classes, adherence, dose timing, or academic outcomes. EEG inter-occurrence-time distributions were fit with a stretched q-exponential model to estimate subject-level parameters c and q, which were then compared across groups and conditions.

The main result was that ADHD boys showed higher q and c values than typical boys, with task condition producing higher complexity than pretask in both groups. The authors report statistically significant group differences for averaged parameters and suggest that the (c, q) space may serve as a promising biomarker for ADHD diagnosis. The work is methodological and diagnostic, not an intervention study, and its findings are limited to EEG-based discrimination in a small, homogeneous sample of boys.

paper_profiles.title: Child and adolescent psychiatry: challenges, solutions, opportunities, and future directions
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a critical review of major challenges, solutions, opportunities, and future directions in child and adolescent psychiatry. It does not test a single intervention; instead, it synthesizes literature on diagnosis, stigma, access to care, funding, workforce shortages, and evidence-based treatments, with emphasis on how mental disorders in childhood and adolescence affect educational and functional outcomes.

The authors discuss the evolution of the field and then survey several contemporary problems, including weak access to services, insufficient funding, shortage of specialists, and limited evidence for some pharmacological uses in youth. They also review evidence on stigma-reduction interventions, access-to-care strategies, and psychotherapy outcomes, highlighting that interventions such as social contact approaches can reduce stigma-related behaviors and that school-based access interventions have limited effects unless paired with targeted linkage to services.

Overall, the paper concludes that child and adolescent mental health care remains underprioritized and underfunded relative to need, especially in low- and middle-income countries. The authors argue for multi-level solutions spanning policy, workforce development, digital tools, and improved implementation of evidence-based care, rather than relying on individual treatment alone.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that child and adolescent mental health systems are underfunded, underprioritized, and constrained by workforce shortages, insurance limitations, and access barriers. It cites multiple descriptive statistics and reviews showing large gaps in service provision, but also notes that targeted policy and service models can improve access and workforce capacity.
finding.measure: Funding levels, workforce availability, treatment access, and service utilization metrics reported across reviewed studies

finding.finding_summary: The paper reviews evidence that interventions can improve stigma-related behaviors and help-seeking-related outcomes among children and young people. In a meta-analysis of 74 RCTs (ages 10-24), social contact interventions appeared more effective than educational or video-based approaches for changing stigma-related behaviors, though effects declined over longer follow-up.
finding.measure: Stigma-related behaviors, knowledge, attitudes, help-seeking attitudes/intentions/behaviors

finding.finding_summary: The paper summarizes evidence that certain service-delivery interventions can improve early access steps, engagement, and satisfaction, especially when targeted to at-risk children already identified by health systems. In a meta-analysis of 34 RCTs, universal school-based programs improved knowledge and attitudes but had minimal impact on help-seeking or action, whereas targeted engagement/reminder interventions were more effective.
finding.measure: Care access steps, treatment engagement, reminder response, satisfaction

paper_profiles.title: Classification of ADHD and Healthy Children Using Multi-Band and Spatial Features of EEG
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of distinguishing children with ADHD from healthy children using EEG-based machine learning methods. The authors argue that objective, non-invasive neurophysiological signals may support early ADHD diagnosis, and they test whether multi-band EEG features can separate the two groups with high accuracy.

The study uses a benchmark EEG dataset with 61 children diagnosed with ADHD and 60 healthy controls, all aged 7 to 12. EEG was recorded from 19 channels during a visual attention task, then filtered into delta, theta, alpha, beta, and gamma bands. From each band, the authors extracted power spectral density and spectral entropy features, normalized them, and classified participants using SVM and XGBoost. The best result was obtained with an SVM using an RBF kernel, which achieved 99.2% mean cross-validation accuracy (std. dev. 0.0079), outperforming XGBoost (96.92% accuracy).

finding.finding_summary: The paper is substantively about classifying ADHD versus healthy children from EEG during a visual attention task, which is relevant to identifying a neurodevelopmental condition associated with school functioning, but it does not directly measure academic achievement outcomes. The main empirical result is diagnostic/classification performance rather than student learning; the best model (SVM-RBF) achieved 99.2% mean cross-validation accuracy (std. dev. 0.0079) on 61 ADHD and 60 control children aged 7-12.
finding.measure: ADHD vs. healthy child classification accuracy from EEG features during a visual attention task

paper_profiles.title: Increased Coupling in the Saliency Network is the main cause/effect of Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder
paper_profiles.population: Children and adolescents (ages 7-18) with ADHD; comparison to typically developing controls
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks which brain functional connectivity circuits are most altered in attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), using resting-state fMRI and a whole-brain association approach. The authors argue that prior seed-based and ICA studies were too narrow, and instead apply a brain-wide association study (BWAS) to identify connectivity differences in the largest ADHD imaging samples available to them.

The analysis combines two ADHD-200 Consortium datasets (Peking University and New York University), totaling 249 ADHD participants and 253 controls aged 7-18 years. Functional connectivity was computed across 90 ROIs, with both pairwise correlations and partial correlations, and significant links were then validated across datasets; voxel-based morphometry was used to test whether the altered connections were accompanied by gray- or white-matter changes.

The main finding is increased coupling within the salience network, especially between the anterior insula and anterior cingulate gyrus in the left hemisphere. Several other connectivity differences were also reported, but only the salience-network link consistently survived meta-analytic pooling, semi-independent validation, and permutation/Bonferroni checks. Voxel-based morphometry found no significant gray matter volume differences in the regions showing altered connectivity, and the authors also report only weak correlations between the connectivity measures and other variables such as IQ and illness-related scores.

paper_profiles.title: SSRepL-ADHD: Adaptive Complex Representation Learning Framework for ADHD Detection from Visual Attention Tasks
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of automatically detecting ADHD in children from EEG signals collected during visual attention tasks. The authors argue that self-supervised representation learning and transfer learning can improve downstream ADHD classification, especially when data are limited or imbalanced.

The study evaluates three machine-learning approaches on a public EEG dataset of 120 children aged 7 to 12: a Random Forest classifier, a lightweight SSRepL-based DNN, and a proposed SSRepL-ADHD model combining LSTM and GRU layers. The EEG data came from a visual attention task and were preprocessed using normalization, filtering, label encoding, scaling, and SMOTE-based balancing before being split into train/test sets.

Results show that the proposed SSRepL-ADHD model achieved the best weighted performance, with 81.11% accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score, outperforming Random Forest (78.01%) and the lightweight DNN (73.67%). The paper concludes that transfer learning with recurrent layers can help classify ADHD from EEG patterns, though it also notes limitations related to class imbalance, feature selection, and the substantial training time required. The work is a technical classification study rather than an intervention study, and it does not evaluate educational outcomes or medication effects in classroom settings.

paper_profiles.title: Learning for Dose Allocation in Adaptive Clinical Trials with Safety Constraints
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 37th International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2020)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of how to allocate doses in phase I adaptive clinical trials when both efficacy and toxicity matter. The authors argue that common dose-finding methods in clinical research often focus only on toxicity or ignore explicit safety constraints, which can lead to inefficient or unsafe patient allocation.

They propose Safe Efﬁcacy Exploration Dose Allocation (SEEDA), an adaptive multi-armed-bandit-style algorithm that dynamically restricts allocation to doses that are estimated to satisfy a toxicity threshold while still exploring for efficacy. A second variant, SEEDA-Plateau, adds an increase-then-plateau assumption for efficacy, which is intended to match molecularly targeted agents whose benefit rises and then saturates with dose. The paper derives regret and safety-violation guarantees and evaluates the methods in simulations and on two real-world dose-response datasets.

The experiments show that SEEDA can identify efficacy-optimal safe doses with controlled safety violation, while SEEDA-Plateau further improves recommendation accuracy and sample efficiency when the efficacy curve has a unimodal/increase-then-plateau shape. Overall, the contribution is methodological for clinical trial design: it provides a theoretically grounded adaptive allocation strategy that better balances learning, efficacy, and safety than several standard baselines.

paper_profiles.title: Fast SAM 3D Body: Accelerating SAM 3D Body for Real-Time Full-Body Human Mesh Recovery
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (computer vision / human mesh recovery methods paper; no human participant population studied)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the latency bottleneck of SAM 3D Body (3DB), a state-of-the-art monocular 3D human mesh recovery system, and asks how to preserve reconstruction fidelity while making inference fast enough for real-time use. The authors argue that the main limitation is not model accuracy but the multi-stage execution pipeline: detection, sequential encoding of body and hands, iterative refinement, and iterative MHR-to-SMPL conversion.

To solve this, they introduce Fast SAM 3D Body, a training-free acceleration framework that restructures the inference pipeline without changing the underlying 3DB weights. Their approach combines decoupled spatial priors from a pose detector, static graph compilation, pruning of intermediate predictions and keypoint-prompted refinement, batched body/hand crop processing, and a lightweight feedforward MHR-to-SMPL projection module. They evaluate on standard human mesh recovery benchmarks (e.g., 3DPW, EMDB, RICH, Harmony4D, COCO, LSPET, FreiHAND) and report that the accelerated system maintains near-baseline reconstruction quality while achieving substantial speedups, including roughly 8–11× end-to-end throughput gains and over 10,000× faster MHR-to-SMPL conversion.

The paper also demonstrates a real-world vision-only teleoperation system for a humanoid robot, showing that the accelerated pipeline can support real-time control from a single RGB stream. Overall, the main conclusion is that holistic, training-free systems optimization can make high-fidelity full-body mesh recovery practical for latency-sensitive downstream applications without materially degrading reconstruction accuracy.

paper_profiles.title: Strategic reciprocity improves academic performance in public elementary school children
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether children’s cooperative relationships in the classroom are associated with later academic performance, and whether the association depends on the symmetry and perceived direction of friendship ties. The authors argue that students with higher GPAs may benefit more from their social networks because they cooperate more selectively with friends and receive more reciprocated cooperation.

To study this, the authors collected data from 946 students in 45 classrooms across 14 public elementary schools in Chile (grades 3-5). They measured peer relations using a non-anonymous, tablet-based dyadic cooperation game based on a modified Prisoner’s Dilemma, and complemented it with peer-nomination friendship surveys. They then related cooperation metrics such as sent cooperation, received cooperation, reciprocated cooperation, and PageRank-style social ranking to GPA, controlling for gender, attendance, guardian education, classroom effects, and prior GPA in regression and difference-in-differences specifications.

The main finding is that reciprocated cooperation is positively associated with future GPA. In the preferred model, a one-standard-deviation increase in reciprocated cooperation is associated with a 0.088 increase in future GPA, and the difference-in-differences estimate is 0.039 (p<0.01). The paper also finds that high-GPA students are more selective: they cooperate less with non-friends and receive more cooperation overall, while reciprocated cooperation is highest in mutual friendships and lowest in non-friendships. The authors interpret these patterns as evidence that strategic reciprocity in classroom networks may help children reap academic benefits from peer relationships.

finding.finding_summary: Reciprocated cooperation was positively associated with later GPA in a sample of 946 elementary students from 45 classrooms. In the preferred regression model controlling for prior GPA, attendance, gender, guardian education, and classroom effects, a one-standard-deviation increase in reciprocated cooperation was associated with a 0.088 increase in future GPA; the difference-in-differences estimate was 0.039 (p<0.01).
finding.measure: Future GPA
finding.study_size: n=946 (regression analysis on n=769; diff-in-diff analysis on n=1,676 observations across two periods)
finding.effect_size: 0.088 GPA units per 1 SD increase in reciprocated cooperation; diff-in-diff estimate=0.039

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly measures cooperative behavior, reciprocity, and friendship-sensitive social strategy in classroom interactions. Students, especially those with higher GPA, sent more cooperation to mutual and asymmetrical friends than to non-friends, suggesting more strategic and selective prosocial behavior in peer relationships.
finding.measure: Dyadic cooperation in a modified Prisoner’s Dilemma; reciprocated cooperation; sent cooperation; received cooperation

finding.finding_summary: The study’s central mechanism is strategic reciprocity and selective investment in classroom relationships, which reflects collaboration and social strategy. High-GPA students were more selective, cooperating less with non-friends and showing higher reciprocated cooperation in friendship ties, indicating more effective relationship management within the classroom network.
finding.measure: Friendship-category-specific sent cooperation and reciprocated cooperation

paper_profiles.title: A Network Theory Investigation into the Altered Resting State Functional Connectivity in Attention-Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether adults with attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) show altered resting-state brain functional connectivity compared with healthy controls. The authors use resting-state fMRI (RS-fMRI) and graph/network methods to compare connectivity patterns in a UCLA Consortium for Neuropsychiatric Phenomics/OpenfMRI dataset.

The study preprocesses RS-fMRI scans from 40 adults with ADHD and 40 healthy controls, then applies seed-based connectivity, random field theory, functional network connectivity (ICA-based), and network-based statistics. The main finding is that ADHD is associated with lower connectivity in the supramarginal gyrus and superior parietal lobule, and higher connectivity in the lateral occipital cortex and inferior temporal gyrus, with additional network differences involving medial prefrontal and intraparietal regions. The paper concludes that graph/network analysis can identify atypical resting-state organization in ADHD, but it does not study medication effects or school-based outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: Saliency in primary school ranking and its effect on academic achievements
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether students’ relative position in their primary-school class affects later academic outcomes, and whether that effect depends on whether rank is salient to students. The authors focus on the long-standing challenge of separating rank effects from underlying ability differences and peer composition effects.

To identify a more credible “visible” rank effect, the paper uses a unique Italian panel in which students receive teacher-assigned class grades that are reported to students and parents, alongside standardized test scores that are not disclosed to students. Rank is computed from both measures: a visible rank from class grades and an invisible rank from test scores. The invisible rank serves as a placebo, while the visible rank is intended to capture the saliency channel.

The sample includes several hundred thousand Italian public school students observed in grade 5, grade 8, and grade 10 across two cohorts, with rich administrative class-level data and a student questionnaire. The authors show that standard rank-estimation strategies can be biased and that their preferred specification must include student fixed effects and flexible interactions to pass placebo checks using prior grade-2 test scores.

The main conclusion is that visible class rank in primary school has a sizable positive association with later test performance: moving from the bottom to the top of the class is associated with gains of about 8.5 percentile points in middle school and 7.7 percentile points in high school, while the invisible rank has no robust effect once the preferred controls are included. The paper also finds that class quality matters much more than rank, that higher-ranked students are more likely to enter academically stronger high schools, and that the rank effect appears to operate through self-esteem, school perception, and interest in subjects rather than through demographic heterogeneity or class size.

finding.finding_summary: A higher visible class rank in grade 5 is associated with better later academic performance. In the preferred specification with student fixed effects and flexible controls, moving from the bottom to the top of class predicts a gain of 8.5 percentile points in grade 8 standardized test scores and 7.7 percentile points in grade 10 scores.
finding.measure: National standardized test percentile scores in grade 8 and grade 10 (Italian and math)
finding.study_size: n=387,614 total across the two selected cohorts (205,123 in 2018 cohort; 182,491 in 2019 cohort)
finding.effect_size: 8.5 percentile points (grade 8); 7.7 percentile points (grade 10) for top vs bottom visible rank

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that visible rank affects students’ perceptions and self-concept. Higher visible rank is associated with improved self-esteem, better perceived school recognition, and greater interest in the subjects studied, while the invisible rank remains near zero.
finding.measure: Student questionnaire Likert-scale responses on self-esteem, perceived recognition, and interest in school subjects

finding.finding_summary: The study shows that class rank changes students’ high-school choices: higher-ranked primary-school students self-select into high schools with higher average student achievement. The paper also compares rank effects with class-quality effects and finds that a one-standard-deviation increase in class quality has about a six-fold larger effect than a one-standard-deviation increase in rank.
finding.measure: High-school choice and class value-added / class quality
finding.effect_size: Class quality effect is about 6x the rank effect; rank itself shifts later achievement by 8.5 and 7.7 percentile points from bottom to top
finding.std_deviation: 1 SD increase in class quality; 1 SD increase in rank

finding.finding_summary: The authors provide evidence consistent with rank influencing non-cognitive channels such as motivation and self-perception, which are durable skills. Higher visible rank increases students’ reported interests in the subjects studied, suggesting changes in motivation and engagement that may help explain later achievement gains.
finding.measure: Student questionnaire items on interest in subjects studied

paper_profiles.title: Structural Brain Asymmetries in Youths with Combined and Inattentive Presentations of Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder
paper_profiles.population: Youth (children/adolescents; ADHD-200 repository, mean ages approximately 8.5-12.9 years across sites)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether structural brain asymmetries differ across ADHD presentations, specifically inattentive (ADHD-I) and combined (ADHD-C), compared with typically developing youth. The authors focus on asymmetry indices derived from structural T1-weighted MRI across subcortical and cortical regions, using volume, surface area, and thickness metrics. Their goal is to characterize how diagnosis and age relate to hemispheric laterality in ADHD, addressing heterogeneity that may be obscured when ADHD is treated as a single category.

The study analyzed preprocessed ADHD-200 Repository scans from youth drawn from four sites, excluding medicated participants and those with unknown medication status, other psychiatric/neurological disorders, or poor-quality scans. The final sample included 413 participants: 64 ADHD-I, 51 ADHD-C, and 298 typically developing controls. The authors fit linear mixed-effects models with site as a random intercept and tested main effects of presentation and age as well as their interaction on asymmetry indices.

Results showed multiple presentation-specific asymmetry differences. Compared with controls, ADHD-I and ADHD-C differed in several volumetric and thickness regions, and age-related asymmetry trajectories also differed by presentation. In direct ADHD-I versus ADHD-C comparisons, significant differences appeared in the ventral diencephalon (volume), lateral orbitofrontal cortex (surface area), and caudal middle frontal cortex (thickness). The paper concludes that structural asymmetry patterns vary by ADHD presentation and age, supporting the idea that neurodevelopmental trajectories differ across ADHD subtypes. It does not study medication effects, academic achievement, or school outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: Autism spectrum disorder
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (review of autism spectrum disorder across the lifespan; includes children, adolescents, and adults)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a comprehensive review primer on autism spectrum disorder (ASD), covering epidemiology, etiology, neurobiology, diagnosis, screening, co-occurring conditions, management, and quality of life across the lifespan. It synthesizes existing research rather than reporting a single primary study, with emphasis on how ASD is identified, how it develops over time, and what is known about mechanisms and interventions.

The paper describes ASD as a heterogeneous neurodevelopmental disorder with strong genetic contributions and common co-occurring conditions, including ADHD, anxiety, and epilepsy. It reviews evidence from population studies, infant-sibling longitudinal cohorts, MRI/EEG studies, and intervention literature, concluding that early psychosocial interventions can improve specific child behaviors such as joint attention, language, and social engagement, but that long-term outcomes and optimal treatment pathways remain uncertain.

No single intervention or educational program is evaluated experimentally in this article. Instead, the authors summarize the current state of evidence and highlight limitations in methodology, replication, and generalizability, especially for screening tools, biomarkers, and intervention studies. The review stresses the need for better long-term studies and more inclusive research that addresses heterogeneity, family context, and outcomes across development.

finding.finding_summary: The review states that psychosocial interventions in children with ASD can improve language. It does not report a pooled effect size or a specific sample size because it synthesizes multiple prior studies rather than presenting new data.
finding.measure: Language outcomes in children receiving psychosocial interventions

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that psychosocial interventions in children with ASD can improve joint attention and social engagement, and may reduce symptom severity. These are presented as established benefits across prior intervention studies, but the primer does not provide a single aggregate effect size or a specific sample size.
finding.measure: Joint attention, social engagement, symptom severity

paper_profiles.title: The PRISMA statement for reporting systematic reviews and meta-analyses of studies that evaluate health care interventions: explanation and elaboration
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is the explanation-and-elaboration companion to the PRISMA reporting guideline for systematic reviews and meta-analyses of health care interventions. Its purpose is not to test an intervention, but to explain why each PRISMA checklist item exists and how authors should report systematic reviews transparently and completely.

The paper synthesizes methodological rationale, examples, and evidence about reporting practices, including title/abstract structure, eligibility criteria, information sources, search strategies, study selection, data extraction, and risk-of-bias assessment. It argues that poor reporting weakens the usefulness of systematic reviews for clinicians, policy makers, editors, and guideline developers, and it recommends a 27-item checklist plus flow diagram to improve clarity and reproducibility.

The intended audience is authors, reviewers, editors, and methodologists working on systematic reviews, largely in health care. The paper does not study a student- or school-based intervention and does not provide empirical outcome results about education or ADHD treatment; instead, it offers reporting guidance for systematic review methodology across health intervention topics.

paper_profiles.title: A systematic review and analysis of long-term outcomes in attention deficit hyperactivity disorder: effects of treatment and non-treatment
paper_profiles.population: K-12 and adults (longitudinal studies spanning childhood through adulthood; includes children, adolescents, and adults)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the long-term consequences of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and asks whether treatment changes those long-term outcomes. The authors systematically reviewed peer-reviewed primary studies published from 1980 to 2010, focusing only on outcomes measured at least 2 years later and excluding studies that measured only ADHD symptoms. The review included 351 studies and organized 636 outcome results into nine life-domain categories, including academic performance, antisocial behavior, social function, occupation, self-esteem, driving, services use, obesity, and drug use/addictive behavior.

The review compared untreated ADHD with non-ADHD controls and treated ADHD with untreated ADHD or pretreatment baselines. Across the evidence base, untreated ADHD was generally associated with poorer long-term outcomes in every domain, while treatment was usually associated with better long-term outcomes than no treatment. However, treatment often improved outcomes without fully normalizing them to the level of non-ADHD controls. Academic outcomes were among the more commonly studied domains, and the review notes that treatment was often beneficial for academic performance, though much of the evidence is observational and heterogeneous.

The paper is not a direct intervention trial; instead, it synthesizes long-term follow-up studies of pharmacological, non-pharmacological, and multimodal ADHD treatment. The authors conclude that treatment may reduce the negative life-course impact of ADHD, but more research is needed on which treatments improve which outcomes and whether short-term symptom relief translates into durable academic and functional gains. The review also highlights design differences, comparator choice, and regional diagnostic practices as important sources of variation in reported results.

finding.finding_summary: Across the review, academic outcomes were frequently better with ADHD treatment than with untreated ADHD, and several untreated longitudinal studies showed deterioration in reading-related outcomes over time. The paper specifically notes declines in reading scores in untreated ADHD and reports one included study in which stimulant treatment significantly improved reading scores and reduced grade retention, but most treated groups still did not fully normalize to non-ADHD controls.
finding.measure: Reading scores, grade retention, overall academic performance

finding.finding_summary: Academic math-related outcomes were also part of the long-term academic domain, and the review notes that untreated ADHD was associated with declines in math scores over long follow-up. In the synthesis, academic outcomes overall benefited from treatment in 71% of outcome results, indicating that numeracy-related school performance often improved relative to untreated ADHD even if not fully normalized.
finding.measure: Math scores, overall academic performance

finding.finding_summary: Academic outcomes were one of the main outcome groups in the review and were among the most frequently studied. Overall, 71% of academic outcome results were reported as benefiting from treatment compared with untreated ADHD, and untreated ADHD was consistently associated with poorer academic trajectories than non-ADHD controls. The paper specifically mentions outcomes such as achievement test scores, GPA, repeated grades, years of schooling, and degrees earned.
finding.measure: Achievement test scores, GPA, grade retention, years of schooling, degrees earned, overall academic performance

finding.finding_summary: Treatment was often associated with better social-emotional functioning, including self-esteem and social function, though improvements usually did not reach non-ADHD control levels. The review reports that 90% of self-esteem outcomes and 83% of social function outcomes benefited from treatment, while untreated ADHD was generally associated with poorer long-term social-emotional outcomes.
finding.measure: Self-esteem scales, peer rejection, social function measures

paper_profiles.title: European consensus statement on diagnosis and treatment of adult ADHD: The European Network Adult ADHD
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a European consensus statement focused on the diagnosis and treatment of adult attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). It addresses the problem that ADHD is often underrecognized and undertreated in adults across Europe, despite evidence that the disorder frequently persists from childhood into adulthood and is associated with broad functional impairment.

The authors synthesize evidence from reviews and randomized controlled trials, together with clinical expertise from an expert panel across 18 European countries. The statement reviews the adult clinical presentation of ADHD, diagnostic criteria and tools, differential diagnosis, comorbidity, and treatment options such as stimulants, atomoxetine, psychoeducation, cognitive behavioral therapy, coaching, and family-based supports.

The main conclusion is that adult ADHD is a real, impairing, lifelong condition that requires better recognition, proper diagnosis, and more consistent treatment. The paper argues that stimulant medications are the best-studied and most effective pharmacologic treatments, while psychosocial interventions may help but need stronger evidence before routine recommendation. It emphasizes that effective treatment can improve multiple domains of adult functioning, including professional and academic functioning, but the paper is not an empirical study of K-12 academic outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: Dual-task Coordination in Children and Adolescents with Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines whether children and adolescents with ADHD differ from typically developing peers in dual-task coordination, an executive-function skill involving simultaneous performance of a verbal memory task and a motor tracking task. The authors also ask whether task difficulty, ADHD subtype, comorbid behavioral disorders, sex, and general motor functioning help explain any performance differences. The work is framed around working memory and executive control, with an emphasis on whether ADHD-specific deficits appear when task demands are matched to each child’s ability.

The study included 91 children/adolescents with ADHD and 91 age- and education-matched controls (ages 6-16). Participants completed computerized and paper-and-pencil dual-task paradigms combining serial digit recall with motor tracking, along with measures of IQ, ADHD symptoms, autism symptoms, comorbid disorders, and motor skills (MABC-2). The authors also manipulated task difficulty in a set of dual-task conditions to test whether ADHD participants were disproportionately affected by increased load.

Overall, the paper finds little evidence of a robust ADHD-specific deficit in dual-task coordination. On the computerized task, there were small group differences favoring controls, but the authors report that dual-task coordination was generally available in ADHD and not significantly different from controls on several metrics; paper-and-pencil results were similarly close between groups. General motor functioning and comorbidity were related to performance in some analyses, especially in controls, but did not consistently explain dual-task performance in ADHD. The authors conclude that dual-task coordination is not substantially impaired in ADHD when tasks are individualized, and that task difficulty did not disproportionately worsen performance in the ADHD group.

finding.finding_summary: The central finding is that dual-task coordination, a measure of executive control / working memory coordination, was generally not significantly worse in children and adolescents with ADHD than in matched controls when tasks were individualized. On the computerized version, there was a small group difference on motor tracking (F(1,179)=5.642, p<.018; η2=.031) and a near-significant difference on the combined μ score (controls 101.51 vs ADHD 98.43; one-tailed t(179)=1.847, p<.066), but the authors interpret the overall pattern as showing preserved dual-task coordination in ADHD.
finding.measure: Computerized and paper-and-pencil dual-task performance (serial digit recall plus motor tracking), including percentage change scores and combined μ score
finding.effect_size: η2=.031 for computerized motor tracking group effect; μ score difference small and not clearly reported as a standardized effect size
finding.std_deviation: Computerized μ: controls SD=10.34, ADHD SD=12.01; computerized motor tracking accuracy: controls SD=8.45, ADHD SD=9.13

finding.finding_summary: The paper is not an academic achievement study, but it does assess school-relevant cognitive performance and reports that the paper-and-pencil dual-task method may be applicable in educational settings. Performance on the paper-and-pencil version did not significantly differ between ADHD and controls, suggesting limited evidence that this classroom-adjacent task format is affected by ADHD status. The authors present the method as feasible for educational/clinical settings rather than demonstrating an academic achievement impact.
finding.measure: Paper-and-pencil dual-task performance used as an educationally relevant cognitive task
finding.std_deviation: Paper-and-pencil μ: controls SD=9.97, ADHD SD=13.02

finding.finding_summary: The study includes ADHD symptoms, comorbidity, and sex-related analyses rather than direct social-emotional outcomes, but it does show that comorbid disorders were associated with worse computerized motor-tracking performance in some ADHD subgroups. For example, groups with comorbidity performed worse than those without comorbidity on computerized single and dual motor tasks (e.g., U=11 and U=13, both exact p<.001 in hyperactive/impulsive ADHD), yet comorbidity did not consistently affect paper-and-pencil outcomes or the broader dual-task μ score.
finding.measure: Computerized motor tracking and dual-task performance by comorbidity status (ODD/CD)
finding.study_size: n=182 total; subgroup counts vary by comorbidity and subtype
finding.std_deviation: e.g., comorbidity vs no-comorbidity motor task SDs reported as 6.12 vs 9.99 and 7.92 vs 6.84 in one subtype comparison

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly evaluates whether the paper-and-pencil dual-task can serve as a practical substitute for the computerized version, which is an operational/administrative concern. The authors report moderate test-retest reliability for both formats (computerized μ r=.36; paper-and-pencil μ r=.37) and significant correlations between formats (r=.26 overall), but no significant group differences on the paper-and-pencil version and no strong evidence that one format meaningfully outperforms the other operationally.
finding.measure: Test-retest reliability and correspondence between computerized and paper-and-pencil dual-task formats
finding.effect_size: r=.26 between computerized and paper-and-pencil μ scores; test-retest r=.36 computerized, r=.37 paper-and-pencil

paper_profiles.title: Increased Coupling in the Saliency Network is the main cause/effect of Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder
paper_profiles.population: Children and adolescents (ages 7-18) with ADHD and typically developing controls
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates the functional brain circuitry underlying attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) using resting-state fMRI data and a brain-wide association study (BWAS) framework. The authors argue that prior seed-based and ICA approaches are biased or too local, and instead use a whole-brain, network-level method to identify altered functional connectivity links in ADHD.

The study combines data from the ADHD-200 consortium, focusing on two large cohorts: Peking University (PU) and New York University (NYU). Across 249 children and adolescents with ADHD and 253 healthy controls, the strongest and most reproducible difference was increased coupling within the salience network, especially between the anterior insula and anterior cingulate gyrus in the left hemisphere. Several other connectivity differences were identified, but most did not survive cross-dataset validation as strongly as the salience-network finding.

The authors also performed voxel-based morphometry and found no significant grey matter volume reductions in the regions showing altered connectivity, suggesting that the connectivity findings were not simply driven by structural volume differences. They report a weak correlation between one interhemispheric temporal-lobe connection and IQ in patients, but overall correlations with clinical variables were weak. The paper concludes that altered salience-network coupling may be a central feature of ADHD and may relate to switching between default-mode and executive-control networks.

paper_profiles.title: Classifying attention deficit hyperactivity disorder in children with non-linearities in actigraphy
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether wrist actigraphy can provide objective features that help classify attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) in children, and whether those features can also separate ADHD subtypes from autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and typical controls. The authors frame the work as a diagnostic-support problem rather than a treatment study, focusing on which activity-derived measures are most informative for distinguishing groups.

The approach used continuous 7-day wrist actigraphy in 29 boys aged about 10 years, divided into control, ADHD combined type, ADHD hyperactive-impulsive type, and ASD groups. From the raw activity records, the study extracted 47 features spanning sleep timing, mean and variance of activity, activity increments, return-map properties, Hurst/DFA scaling, activity/rest duration distributions, excursion-shape descriptors, nonlinear forecasting measures, and Lempel-Ziv complexity. These features were entered into supervised machine-learning classifiers with cross-validation to estimate diagnostic performance.

The strongest result was that some actigraphy features differentiated children better than chance: the best 4-feature nearest-neighbor model achieved 46.5% accuracy in the 4-class task and 69.4% accuracy in the binary ADHD-vs-control task. A single feature, skewness of the averaged ZCM activity shape, was the most informative feature on its own, while several nonlinear and sleep-related measures also contributed. The authors conclude that actigraphy may be a useful low-cost adjunct for ADHD assessment and subtype differentiation, but the study is limited by a small all-male sample, no inattentive subtype, and no medication use during recording.

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates whether actigraphy can function as a diagnostic-support tool for ADHD classification in a clinical/school-age child setting. In the best binary task, a nearest-neighbor model achieved 69.4 ± 1.6% accuracy with 78.0 ± 2.2% sensitivity and 60.8 ± 2.6% specificity, suggesting potential utility as an adjunct assessment method rather than a standalone diagnostic instrument.
finding.measure: Cross-validated diagnostic classification accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity using actigraphy-derived features

finding.finding_summary: The authors argue that actigraphy is inexpensive, causes only minor discomfort, and could be a practical add-on test that helps clinicians differentiate ADHD from control and other neurodevelopmental groups. Diagnostic performance was modest but above chance in several classification settings, including 46.5 ± 1.1% accuracy for the 4-class task and 69.4 ± 1.6% accuracy for the binary ADHD-vs-control task.
finding.measure: Cross-validated machine-learning classification performance from wearable actigraphy data
finding.std_deviation: ±1.1% accuracy in 4-class task; ±1.6% accuracy in binary task

finding.finding_summary: The study does not directly measure social-emotional outcomes, but it focuses on behavioral hyperactivity/impulsivity, sleep, and motor activity patterns that are closely related to self-regulation. Some features, especially ZCM shape skewness and nonlinear forecasting measures, separated ADHD groups from controls better than chance, whereas several other features such as nocturnal mean and standard deviation were among the least informative.
finding.measure: Actigraphy-derived behavioral activity features used for ADHD subtype classification

paper_profiles.title: Impact of EEG biofeedback on event-related potentials (ERPs) in attention-deficit hyperactivity (ADHD) children
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether EEG biofeedback (neurofeedback) changes event-related potential (ERP) measures in children with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). The authors focus on whether neurofeedback alters the later ERP component P300/P3, which they interpret as reflecting attention allocation, action selection, and decision making, and whether it affects earlier sensory components such as N1.

The study prospectively followed 39 children with ADHD combined subtype, ages 10-12, all without pharmacological treatment. Sixteen children received 30 neurofeedback sessions over 6 weeks, while 23 children served as an untreated comparison group. ERP recordings and omission/commission error rates were assessed before and after the intervention, with repeated-measures ANOVA and nonparametric tests used to compare groups and time points.

The main finding is that neurofeedback was associated with improved later-stage ERP and task-performance outcomes. Treated children showed significant increases in P3 amplitude and decreases in P3 latency, along with fewer omission and commission errors, compared with untreated children. The authors conclude that neurofeedback may improve cognitive processes related to attention and decision making in children with ADHD, although earlier ERP components such as N1 were less consistently affected and the design is not randomized.

finding.finding_summary: Neurofeedback was associated with better cognitive control during an auditory oddball task, reflected in significantly improved P3 parameters. In the treated group (n=16), P3 latency decreased from 465.94 ms to 417.31 ms and P3 amplitude increased from 6.87 to 9.81, while the untreated group (n=23) showed smaller changes; the group × condition interaction for P3 latency was significant, F(1,37)=22.698, p<.0001, partial eta squared=.38.
finding.measure: Auditory ERP P3 latency and amplitude during an oddball task
finding.effect_size: partial eta squared=.38 (latency), partial eta squared=.543 (amplitude)
finding.std_deviation: latency P3 treated pre SD=33.73, post SD=22.51; amplitude P3 treated pre SD=2.03, post SD=1.87

finding.finding_summary: The intervention also improved behavioral indicators linked to self-regulation and attention during task performance. In the treated group (n=16), omission errors decreased from 5.13 to 2.38 and commission errors decreased from 4.5 to 0.88 after neurofeedback; both were significantly better than the untreated group (n=23), with large group × condition effects for omission and commission errors (partial eta squared=.344 and .503, respectively).
finding.measure: Omission and commission errors on the auditory oddball task
finding.effect_size: partial eta squared=.344 (omission errors), partial eta squared=.503 (commission errors)
finding.std_deviation: omission errors treated pre SD=1.59, post SD=.89; commission errors treated pre SD=2.31, post SD=.89

paper_profiles.title: The Effectiveness of a Virtual Reality-Based Training Program for Improving Body Awareness in Children with Attention Deficit and Hyperactivity Disorder
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether a virtual reality (VR)-based training program can improve body awareness in young children diagnosed with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). The authors frame body awareness as a foundational psychomotor skill related to spatial positioning, body-part identification, and motor expression, arguing that deficits in this area may contribute to later difficulties in movement, self-regulation, and school participation.

Using a two-group quasi-experimental design, the study recruited 10 children aged 4 to 7 years from an early intervention center in Alexandria, Egypt. Participants were screened for ADHD using the Conners Rating Scale and for cognitive eligibility with the Stanford-Binet (IQ 90-110), then assigned to an experimental group (n=5) and a control group (n=5). The experimental group received a structured VR intervention over 10 weeks (36 sessions), while outcomes were measured with a researcher-developed Body Awareness Scale covering body parts identification, body position in space, and motor expressions.

The results showed significant pre-post gains for the experimental group on all body awareness subscales and the total score, with improvements maintained at one-month follow-up (no significant decline from post-test). The paper concludes that immersive VR may be an engaging and effective way to address psychomotor deficits in early childhood ADHD, though the authors note substantial limitations including the very small sample and narrow age range. The study does not evaluate academic achievement directly, but it suggests potential downstream relevance for learning through improved motor and spatial functioning.

finding.finding_summary: The VR intervention significantly improved body awareness-related psychomotor functioning in children with ADHD (n=5 experimental), with gains sustained at one-month follow-up. The paper reports statistically significant pre-post improvements on body parts identification, body position in space, and motor expressions (p<0.05), and no significant post-test to follow-up decline (p>0.05).
finding.measure: Researcher-developed Body Awareness Scale (33 items: body parts identification, body position in space, motor expressions, total body awareness)

paper_profiles.title: Structural brain asymmetries in youths with combined and inattentive presentations of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether structural brain asymmetries differ across attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) presentations, specifically inattentive (ADHD-I) and combined (ADHD-C), compared with typically developing (TD) youths. The authors address a gap in the neuroimaging literature by focusing on hemispheric asymmetry rather than only absolute brain volume or thickness differences, and by testing whether age moderates these patterns across presentations.

Using preprocessed T1-weighted MRI data from the ADHD-200 repository, the study analyzed asymmetry indices for 13 subcortical and 33 cortical regions across volume, surface area, and thickness. The sample included youths with ADHD-I (n=64), ADHD-C (n=51), and TD controls (n=298), with scans drawn from four sites. A linear mixed-effects model with site as a random intercept was used to compare presentation groups and age interactions.

The study reports multiple significant asymmetry differences between ADHD groups and TD youths, as well as between ADHD-I and ADHD-C. Notable findings include presentation-specific differences in orbitofrontal, temporal, cingulate, and ventral diencephalon regions, along with age-related shifts in asymmetry direction. The authors conclude that structural asymmetry patterns vary by ADHD presentation and age, and suggest these differences may relate to distinct neurodevelopmental trajectories and previously reported functional network differences.

finding.finding_summary: This paper does not measure academic achievement or school performance outcomes. It is a neuroimaging study of structural brain asymmetry in ADHD presentations, so there is no direct evidence about academic outcomes such as literacy, numeracy, or grades.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: The academic wanderer: structure of collaboration network and relation with research performance
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper studies how scientists’ collaboration networks relate to their research performance and mobility over the course of their careers. The authors ask whether productivity, impact, and academic migration patterns are associated with the size and structure of co-authorship ego networks, drawing on social-brain/Dunbar-style theories about cognitive limits in maintaining relationships.

Using Scopus data for 81,500 scholars (geo-referenced publications, co-authorship histories, affiliations, and h-index/publication counts), the paper reconstructs each researcher’s collaboration ego network and clusters collaborators into five layers of tie strength. It then correlates layer sizes with productivity, impact, and mobility features such as number of affiliations, domestic vs. international migration, and distance traveled. The main conclusion is that stronger performers tend to have larger collaboration networks, especially in outer layers, but the association weakens for inner circles, consistent with a capacity-bound effect.

The mobility analysis suggests that international and domestic migration play different roles: international migrants tend to grow collaboration networks earlier in their careers, while domestic migrants appear to exploit collaboration ties more effectively for impact. Overall, the study argues that high mobility does not necessarily translate into better scholarly performance, and that collaboration networks in science exhibit layered, cognitively constrained structures similar to those observed in social networks.

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds a clear positive association between productivity/impact and the size of collaboration ego-network layers, especially in the outer circles. Across 81,500 researchers, Pearson correlations between number of publications and layer size ranged from r=0.26 in the innermost circle (C1) to r=0.80 in the outermost circle (C5); correlations with h-index ranged from r=0.28 to r=0.68. This is interpreted as evidence that more productive researchers maintain larger collaboration networks, but with a capacity-bound effect that makes inner-circle expansion much harder.
finding.measure: Co-authorship ego-network layer size correlated with number of publications and h-index
finding.effect_size: r=0.26 to r=0.80 (publications); r=0.28 to r=0.68 (h-index)

finding.finding_summary: The paper shows that academic mobility patterns are associated with differences in collaboration-network growth and performance, but not uniformly in a positive way. International migrants tend to have slightly stronger associations between collaboration circle size and productivity, while domestic migrants show stronger associations between collaboration circle size and impact; the authors conclude that high mobility does not necessarily produce better academic performance or larger collaboration networks.
finding.measure: Correlation of mobility status and number of institution changes with co-authorship ego-network layer size; migration category (international vs domestic)
finding.effect_size: r=0.24 to r=0.68 for number of institution changes across layers; exact migrant-type subgroup effect sizes not_reported

paper_profiles.title: A Network Theory Investigation into the Altered Resting State Functional Connectivity in Attention-Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether adults with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) show altered resting-state functional connectivity compared with healthy controls. The authors use resting-state fMRI and graph/network methods to compare connectivity patterns in a publicly available dataset, focusing on differences in brain network organization rather than on any educational intervention or academic outcome.

The study analyzes 40 adults with ADHD and 40 healthy controls from the UCLA Consortium for Neuropsychiatric Phenomics / OpenfMRI dataset. After preprocessing and denoising the fMRI scans, the authors apply three connectivity approaches: random field theory-based seed analysis, functional network connectivity using independent component analysis, and network-based statistic. Across methods, they report reduced connectivity in ADHD in regions including the supramarginal gyrus, superior parietal lobule, and intraparietal sulcus, alongside increased connectivity in regions including the lateral occipital cortex, inferior temporal gyrus, and medial prefrontal cortex.

The main conclusion is that adults with ADHD exhibit atypical resting-state connectivity in both default mode and dorsal attention network regions, consistent with altered network organization. The paper is descriptive and neuroimaging-focused; it does not test an educational intervention, medication, or academic performance outcome. As such, it provides background evidence on ADHD-related brain connectivity differences rather than direct evidence about educational effectiveness.

paper_profiles.title: Techniques for supercharging academic writing with generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This Comment argues that generalist large language models can improve the quality and efficiency of academic writing and provides a conceptual and practical framework for using them responsibly. Rather than testing an intervention experimentally, the paper synthesizes the author’s perspective on how LLMs can support researchers through brainstorming, outlining, drafting, editing, and feedback across the writing process.

The paper distinguishes between short-term goals, such as greater writing productivity, better prose quality, and enhanced creativity, and long-term goals, such as learning through interactive feedback and repeated use. It proposes a writer–AI collaborative model with two stages: an AI-inspired stage for idea generation and structuring, and an AI-assisted stage for iterative drafting and editing. It also categorizes assistance into five levels, ranging from basic proofreading to evaluation and feedback.

The article emphasizes that generative AI should be used as a tool for cognitive offloading and imaginative stimulation, but with human oversight, fact-checking, attribution, and attention to journal policies. It cautions against overdependence, hallucinations, privacy risks, copyright ambiguity, and ethical issues around authorship and disclosure. Overall, the paper concludes that LLMs can meaningfully ease communication bottlenecks in scholarly writing, but only if used prudently and transparently.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that generative AI can improve writing productivity and efficiency by offloading mechanical and compositional tasks such as spelling, grammar, paraphrasing, summarization, outlining, and drafting. No empirical effect size is reported because this is a conceptual Comment rather than an intervention study, but the central claim is that LLMs can make academic writing faster and reduce cognitive burden.
finding.measure: Writing productivity, drafting/editing efficiency, and time savings (conceptual, not empirically measured in the paper)

finding.finding_summary: The paper contends that LLM use can support learning-by-doing through iterative feedback, helping writers improve their writing skills, recognize and correct mistakes, and deepen understanding of language. This is presented as a theoretical educational benefit rather than a measured outcome, with no sample size or effect size reported.
finding.measure: Writing skill development, reflective revision, and metacognitive engagement (conceptual)

paper_profiles.title: Microsoft Academic Automatic Document Searches: Accuracy for Journal Articles and Suitability for Citation Analysis
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether Microsoft Academic can be used reliably for large-scale document searches and citation analysis. The central question is not about education or student outcomes, but about bibliometric methods: how accurately Microsoft Academic can identify journal articles when queried by title, author, journal, and year, and whether the resulting citation counts are comparable to Scopus.

The study samples 126,312 Scopus-indexed journal articles published in 2012 across 323 subfields. It tests several query strategies, showing that title-only searches followed by filtering out mismatches perform best for both DOI-bearing and non-DOI articles. Average recall is about 89.6% for DOI-based matching and 89.1% for metadata-based matching, with precision around 93.8% and 93.3% respectively for title-only searches. The paper also finds high Spearman correlations between Microsoft Academic and Scopus citation counts across fields (mean rho=0.948), suggesting the two sources are largely interchangeable for citation analysis of articles from this period.

The paper’s main conclusion is that Microsoft Academic can support practical citation analysis of journal articles if users search by title and filter false matches, but that coverage varies by language and journal-level indexing, especially for non-English or dual-language titles. It also cautions that national comparisons may be biased because retrieval rates differ across countries and languages. The work is methodological and scientometric in nature, with no intervention, educational population, or learning outcome analysis.

paper_profiles.title: PaperCard for Reporting Machine Assistance in Academic Writing
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a governance and transparency problem in academic writing: how to document and evaluate the use of machine assistance, especially generative AI systems such as ChatGPT, in the production of scholarly manuscripts. The authors argue that rapid advances in large language models have blurred the boundary between human and machine contribution, raising questions about authorship, accountability, fairness, copyright, and transparency.

Rather than testing an educational intervention or measuring learning outcomes, the paper proposes a reporting framework called PaperCard. PaperCard is intended to help authors disclose whether AI was used, what kind of assistance it provided (e.g., idea generation, outlining, drafting, editing, proofreading), what risks were considered, and which models/prompts were used. The paper situates this framework in the context of recent debates and policies in academia and publishing, and it includes a sample PaperCard for the manuscript itself showing how ChatGPT was used to generate and edit portions of the paper.

The paper is conceptual and normative, not empirical. Its main contribution is a taxonomy and reporting template for machine assistance in academic writing, along with discussion of ethical and legal challenges and suggestions for how institutions, publishers, and reviewers might use such a framework to improve transparency and accountability.

finding.finding_summary: The paper proposes PaperCard as a transparency and governance framework for documenting AI use in academic writing. It argues that standardized disclosure of whether AI was used, which model/version was used, and at what stage of writing it was used could improve accountability and reviewer interpretation, but it also notes possible burdens, reviewer bias, and implementation challenges. No empirical effect size is reported because the paper is conceptual rather than outcome-tested.
finding.measure: Policy and governance framework for AI disclosure in academic writing

paper_profiles.title: Automatic Diagnosis of Schizophrenia and Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder in rs-fMRI Modality using Convolutional Autoencoder Model and Interval Type-2 Fuzzy Regression
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses automated diagnosis of schizophrenia (SZ) and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) from resting-state fMRI (rs-fMRI) data. The authors propose a computer-aided diagnosis pipeline that preprocesses rs-fMRI scans, converts them into 118×118 functional connectivity matrices, extracts features using a convolutional autoencoder (CNN-AE), and classifies subjects with several machine learning and fuzzy-logic models.

The study uses the UCLA rs-fMRI dataset, containing healthy controls, SZ patients, and ADHD patients, and compares conventional classifiers (DT, MLP, KNN, SVM, RF), ANFIS variants, and interval type-2 fuzzy regression (IT2FR) variants. The best reported result is IT2FR-GWO with 72.71% accuracy. The paper concludes that the proposed CNN-AE plus IT2FR-GWO approach outperforms the compared classifiers on this dataset and may be useful as a computer-aided diagnostic tool, but it is a method-development study rather than a clinical intervention study.

Because the work is based on retrospective neuroimaging data and classifier benchmarking, it does not evaluate educational interventions or student outcomes. The ADHD-related discussion includes general statements about childhood ADHD and medication, but no academic outcomes, comparator-specific treatment effects, or medication-class evidence are empirically tested in this paper.

paper_profiles.title: Exposía: Academic Writing Assessment of Exposés and Peer Feedback
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces Exposía, a new public dataset for studying academic writing and peer feedback in higher education. The dataset links draft and revised research project exposés with instructor and peer feedback, including inline comments, free-text reviews, and fine-grained instructor assessment scores for both the writing and the feedback itself.

The work is centered on a Bachelor-level Computer Science course, "Introduction to Scientific Work," offered in winter term 2024. Students wrote research exposés on computer science / AI topics, reviewed peers’ drafts, received feedback from instructors, revised their exposés, and had both drafts and reviews graded on detailed rubrics. The authors use the dataset to benchmark several open-weight LLMs on criterion-based scoring of exposés and reviews, finding that combined prompting works best and that model agreement is strongest on lower-expertise criteria and weaker on content-heavy, domain-specific criteria.

The main empirical contribution is descriptive rather than causal: the paper reports that final exposés improve relative to drafts, especially on content-related rubrics such as Approach, Motivation, Language/Quality, and Methodology. It also shows that human agreement is moderate overall and that LLMs can approximate human scoring on some criteria, though they exhibit systematic generosity and struggle more on expert-level dimensions. The paper argues that these models are best viewed as decision-support tools rather than replacements for human grading.

finding.finding_summary: Final exposés improved relative to drafts after feedback. Across 55 exposés, average rubric scores increased most for Approach, Motivation, Language/Quality, and Methodology; the paper also reports average length growth from 528 to 649 words, suggesting substantive revision. No single global effect size is reported, but the pattern is consistently positive across the draft-to-final comparison.
finding.measure: Criterion-based exposé rubric scores and draft-to-final word count

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that combined prompting is more effective and more computationally efficient than single-criterion prompting for automated scoring of exposés and reviews. This supports lower-cost classroom deployment of LLM-based scoring, although the paper does not report a numerical efficiency effect size.
finding.measure: LLM scoring performance and computational efficiency under single-criterion vs combined prompts

paper_profiles.title: What is essential is visible to the eye: Saliency in primary school ranking and its effect on academic achievements
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether a student’s rank within a primary school class affects later academic achievement, and whether the effect depends on whether that rank is visible to students. The authors argue that prior rank studies may be biased because rank derived from standardized test scores is not the same as the rank students actually observe, which is based on teacher grades.

Using panel data on several hundred thousand Italian public school students, the paper compares two rankings in grade 5: a visible rank based on teacher-assigned grades and an invisible rank based on standardized test scores. The authors show that the visible rank has a sizable positive effect on later standardized test performance, while the invisible rank becomes small and insignificant after stronger controls are added. Their preferred specification suggests that moving from bottom to top of the class rank distribution in primary school raises later standardized test performance by about 8.5 percentile points in middle school and 7.7 percentile points in high school.

The study also examines heterogeneity and mechanisms. It finds little evidence that the rank effect differs by gender, immigrant status, socio-economic status, class size, or ability, but it does find that higher visible rank improves self-esteem, perceived peer recognition, and interest in school subjects, and it influences later school sorting into higher-achieving high schools. The authors conclude that saliency matters: students respond to the rank they can see, and standard invisible-rank approaches likely understate the true effect of class rank on achievement.

finding.finding_summary: Higher visible class rank in grade 5 predicts stronger later academic performance. In the preferred specification with student fixed effects and flexible controls, ranking at the top of class rather than the bottom increases later national standardized test performance by 8.5 percentile points in grade 8 and 7.7 percentile points in grade 10 (roughly 37,000 national rank positions).
finding.measure: National standardized test percentiles in Italian and math (grade 8 and grade 10)
finding.study_size: n=387,614 combined across two cohorts after sample restrictions

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that a higher visible rank improves students’ self-esteem, perceived recognition by peers, and attitudes toward school subjects. These results come from the 2018 student questionnaire and are interpreted as evidence that visible rank changes perceptions and motivation, which may help explain later academic gains.
finding.measure: Student questionnaire responses on self-esteem, perceived peer recognition, and interest in subjects (6-point Likert scales)

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that using invisible standardized-test-based rank understates the true effect of rank because it does not match what students actually observe. It also shows that students with higher visible rank self-select into high schools with higher average student achievement, indicating that rank can affect subsequent educational sorting and institutional pathways.
finding.measure: High school choice/sorting into tracks and schools with higher average student achievement

paper_profiles.title: Teaching Physics in the first years of Elementary School to children with ADHD
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper describes a science fair project conducted at Colégio Pedro II in Rio de Janeiro with a small group of elementary school students diagnosed with ADHD. The authors frame the work as an inclusive learning experience intended both to introduce basic physics/scientific literacy concepts and to support executive functioning skills such as planning, organizing, and prioritizing tasks.

The activity was organized as a six-week project in a Learning Laboratory and physics lab with eight students ages 8–12. Students chose and revised experiments, researched electricity and energy, built materials such as batteries and a circuit quiz board, and presented the work at a school science fair. The paper emphasizes hands-on, STS-oriented learning and describes the process narratively rather than as a controlled study.

The main conclusion is that the students were able to explain their projects confidently to the public and showed solid understanding of energy storage and transformation. The authors interpret the experience as successful for promoting scientific literacy, curiosity, and engagement, while also helping students practice self-management and time organization. However, the paper does not report quantitative outcome data, comparison groups, or formal measures of learning gains, so its evidence is descriptive and anecdotal.

finding.finding_summary: In a six-week science fair project with eight ADHD students ages 8–12, the authors report that students could clearly and confidently explain how the electric circuit quiz board worked and showed a solid understanding of energy storage and transformation. The paper presents this as evidence of improved scientific literacy and conceptual understanding, but it is observational and does not include pre/post testing or effect sizes.
finding.measure: Oral explanations at the science fair; informal observation of understanding of energy conservation and electrical circuits

finding.finding_summary: The intervention was explicitly designed to stimulate executive function, especially students’ ability to manage time, plan future tasks, organize activities, and prioritize work. The authors report that organizing the six-week science fair project gave students repeated practice with planning and task management, but they provide no standardized measure of executive function or durable skills.
finding.measure: Observed participation in planning, organizing, and prioritizing science-fair tasks

finding.finding_summary: The paper describes the students as interested, engaged, and able to present their work to visitors with confidence during the science fair. The authors interpret the experience as positive for curiosity and self-regulation, but the evidence is narrative and based on informal classroom observation rather than a validated engagement or self-regulation measure.
finding.measure: Observed engagement, confidence, and participation during project work and public presentation

paper_profiles.title: VLM@school – Evaluation of AI image understanding on German middle school knowledge
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents VLM@school, a new benchmark for evaluating vision-language models (VLMs) on German middle-school knowledge. The authors argue that existing multimodal benchmarks are overly English-centric, often multiple-choice based, and sometimes allow success from text-only cues rather than true image understanding. To address this, they created a dataset of 486 images and 2,038 open-ended questions spanning nine school subjects, with some questions embedded in the image and additional adversarial items designed to be unanswerable from the image alone.

The paper evaluates 13 open-weight VLMs on the benchmark using an LLM-as-a-judge / panel-of-LLMs scoring setup. Models were tested on open-ended answers, and the study compares performance across domains, model families, and adversarial versus non-adversarial questions. Overall accuracy is modest: the best model reaches 43.26% overall, while adversarial-question accuracy is much lower, topping out around 32.83% and often far lower. The results suggest that current VLMs still struggle with combining visual interpretation, subject knowledge, and robust refusal behavior in semantically tricky cases.

The study is set in German middle-school curriculum content and is aimed at benchmarking AI systems rather than measuring student outcomes. It concludes that middle-school-level multimodal tasks are sufficiently challenging to stress-test modern VLMs, especially in non-English settings. The authors also show that leaderboard performance on public benchmarks does not necessarily transfer to this more realistic, open-ended German dataset, and they propose future work such as English translations and chain-of-thought style reasoning evaluations.

finding.finding_summary: The benchmark spans nine middle-school subject domains and directly evaluates VLM performance on subject-specific knowledge tasks using 2,038 open-ended questions on 486 images. Performance was highly variable by domain: the best model reached 54% in history/religion but only about 31% in music and 34% in math, with overall accuracy capped below 45% (best model 43.26%).
finding.measure: Open-ended accuracy on German middle-school benchmark questions across arts, biology, geography, history, math, music, physics, religion, and sports

finding.finding_summary: Math was one of the most difficult domains. The best model reached 34.09% on math questions, and the paper reports that models were often better at calculating than at correctly counting or identifying geometric features needed to set up the calculation (e.g., identifying sides, corners, hypotenuse, or coordinates).
finding.measure: Accuracy on open-ended math questions involving geometry, counting, and simple calculations

finding.finding_summary: Science-related performance was uneven.
