In physics, the best model reached 47.65% overall, but explanatory questions and causal reasoning from diagrams were frequently answered incorrectly; in biology, the best model reached 48.53% overall and struggled with labeling technical terms in illustrations. The paper emphasizes that models often handled recognition better than explanation.
finding.measure: Accuracy on physics and biology questions requiring diagram interpretation, labeling, and causal explanation
finding.study_size: n=234 physics questions; n=169 biology questions

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not study reading or writing instruction outcomes, but it does include open-ended question answering in German and discusses the impact of language and textual context on model performance. There are no direct literacy learning results for students, so this is only a tangential outcome area.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: Democratizing Signal Processing and Machine Learning: Math Learning Equity for Elementary and Middle School Students
paper_profiles.venue: Submitted to IEEE Signal Processing Magazine
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This article argues that strong early mathematics preparation is essential for later success in signal processing, machine learning, and STEM more broadly, and that inequities in elementary math learning can compound over time. The authors frame the problem as one of systemic barriers to early arithmetic fluency, including uneven school resources, family access, teacher quality, and low expectations.

Rather than presenting a formal experiment, the paper describes and reflects on three out-of-school math support programs run by the authors and collaborators: CyMath at Iowa State, Algebra by 7th Grade at Purdue, and Math Motivators from the Actuarial Foundation. These programs provide tutoring, mentoring, adaptive software support (e.g. ALEKS), parent engagement, and STEM enrichment for students in grades roughly 3–8, especially those from underrepresented or disadvantaged backgrounds.

The paper also offers practice-based lessons learned from operating these programs, including the importance of strong school partnerships, consistent mentor retention, parent awareness, sufficient math practice, and hybrid/online access. It reports a few illustrative student test-score gains and notes that some participants who completed full grade levels in ALEKS showed associated gains on state assessments, but the article is primarily a perspective and program description rather than a rigorous outcome study. Its main conclusion is that early, sustained, and well-supported math intervention can help close learning gaps and broaden access to later STEM opportunities.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports illustrative improvements in elementary/middle school math performance across several tutoring programs, but these are descriptive rather than experimentally identified. For CyMath, the authors describe individual student percentile gains on MAP/iReady (e.g., one student moved from the 40th percentile in Sept. 2023 to the 85th in May 2024 and the 92nd in Jan. 2025), while for Ab7G they cite prior work noting significant growth in mathematics proficiency among students who completed a full grade level in ALEKS each year (n=20) and a correlation with proficiency on Indiana ILEARN outcomes.
finding.measure: Standardized math test percentiles (MAP, iReady) and mathematics proficiency on ALEKS/ILEARN

paper_profiles.title: Schools as a Safety-net: The Impact of School Closures and Reopenings on Rates of Reporting of Violence Against Children
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether school closures during the COVID-19 pandemic disrupted schools’ role as a reporting channel for violence against children. The authors ask whether formal reports of intra-family violence, sexual abuse, and rape against children fell when schools closed, and whether reporting recovered as schools gradually reopened.

Using administrative data for all municipalities in Chile from 2019 through 2021, the study combines police crime reports, school closure/reopening records, attendance data, and municipal COVID/lockdown measures. The analysis uses two-way fixed effects regressions and counterfactual projections to compare reporting during closure and reopening periods against pre-closure baselines.

The findings show sharp declines in reported violence immediately after nationwide school closure in March 2020, followed by only partial and slow recovery after reopening. Estimated declines at closure are substantial across outcomes, including roughly -1.6 reports per 100,000 children per week for intra-family violence, -0.95 for sexual abuse, and about -0.10 for rape in baseline specifications. Counterfactual analyses suggest thousands of reports were potentially 'missing' during closure and reopening periods, and that school closures accounted for a large share of the observed under-reporting. The paper concludes that schools function as a social safety net and that reduced in-person attendance weakens detection and reporting of child maltreatment.

finding.finding_summary: School closures sharply reduced the institutional reporting of violence against children in Chile, and reopening only partially restored reporting. In baseline two-way fixed effects models, closure was associated with declines of about 1.6 reports per 100,000 children per week for intra-family violence, 0.95 for sexual abuse, and about 0.10 for rape, with reopening effects smaller in magnitude and often still below baseline.
finding.measure: Formal criminal reports of violence against children (intra-family violence, sexual abuse, rape) per 100,000 children by municipality-week
finding.study_size: n=54,214 municipality-week observations for intra-family violence; n=53,179 municipality-week observations for sexual abuse and rape

finding.finding_summary: The school reporting channel became less effective during closures and recovered slowly after reopening, implying reduced institutional efficiency in identifying and channeling child abuse cases. Counterfactual projections estimate 1,533 missing intra-family violence reports, 1,223 missing sexual abuse reports, and 155 missing rape reports during closure alone, with school closure explaining a substantial share of total under-reporting.
finding.measure: Estimated number of missing reports relative to counterfactual projections based on pre-pandemic trends; reporting rates per 100,000 children
finding.confidence_interval: 95% CI for missing reports: DV 1,002–2,083; sexual abuse 941–1,509; rape 70–246

paper_profiles.title: Automatic Classification of the Complexity of Nonfiction Texts in Portuguese for Early School Years
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of automatically estimating the reading complexity of Portuguese nonfiction texts for early school years. The authors motivate the work by noting that Brazilian elementary students often struggle with reading and that teachers need better tools to match texts to students’ grade levels. The goal is to support text selection for classroom use and avoid giving students texts that are too easy or too difficult.

The paper develops a manually annotated corpus of Portuguese informational texts labeled into five grade-level complexity bands (mapped to 3rd through 7th grades) and trains machine-learning classifiers to predict text complexity. The authors compare a small set of language-independent readability features against a larger feature set combining lexical, syntactic, textual, punctuation, sentiment, and named-entity features. Using SVM classification, they report about 52% accuracy with simple statistics, 56% with 108 features on the initial balanced sample, and 52% accuracy on the expanded annotated corpus of 1,456 texts; collapsing adjacent levels improves accuracy to 65% and 63%, and combining to three classes reaches 74% accuracy. The main conclusion is that fine-grained five-level classification is difficult because of substantial overlap between adjacent grades, but coarser groupings are more tractable and align better with curriculum cycles.

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studies automatic classification of nonfiction texts by reading complexity to support reading instruction. On a balanced sample of 971 texts, an SVM using 10 language-independent features reached 52% accuracy (±14), and a larger 108-feature set reached 56% accuracy (±13); with the full corpus of 1,456 texts, 5-class accuracy was 52% (±15), improving to 74% when reduced to 3 classes. These results suggest the approach is useful for matching texts to grade-level reading demands, but fine-grained discrimination among adjacent levels remains limited.
finding.measure: Text complexity / grade-level classification accuracy for reading materials

paper_profiles.title: Elementary School Students’ and Teachers’ Perceptions Towards Creative Mathematical Writing with Generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates how elementary school students and teachers perceive creative mathematical writing supported by generative AI. The authors are interested in both the educational benefits and the challenges of using a GenAI-powered learning platform for math story creation, especially as students work with AI to generate, revise, and improve story-based math problems.

The study was conducted in six fifth-grade classrooms across two U.S. schools with 79 students and six teachers. The intervention followed a three-step structure: Ask, Represent, and Transform. Students first analyzed math stories, then visually represented solutions, and finally used GPT-4 and DALL·E 3 to co-create culturally relevant mathematical stories, which they evaluated with a checklist.

Using interviews, open-ended survey responses, and classroom observations, the researchers conducted thematic analysis and identified six themes. Reported benefits included fostering creativity, improving mathematical understanding, promoting AI literacy, and enhancing affective factors such as interest, curiosity, and ownership. Reported challenges included weak critical evaluation of AI output, difficulty generating coherent stories, AI systems being too perfect, lack of pedagogical feedback, reduced autonomy, weak social connection, and limited communication options.

Overall, the paper concludes that GenAI can support elementary students’ mathematical creativity and understanding, but its educational value depends on careful instructional and system design. The authors emphasize that GenAI should function as a collaborator with intentional room for student revision, feedback, and interaction rather than as a fully autonomous content generator.

finding.finding_summary: Students and teachers reported that GenAI-supported creative mathematical writing helped students understand math problems, represent mathematical ideas, and uncover misconceptions, suggesting positive effects on mathematical understanding. However, students also sometimes struggled to generate coherent math stories and align them with the AI system, indicating challenges in mathematical problem formulation.
finding.measure: Qualitative interview themes, open-ended survey responses, and classroom observation notes about mathematical understanding, problem representation, and misconception detection
finding.study_size: n=79 students; n=6 teachers (interviews with n=10 students in focus groups)

finding.finding_summary: The paper found that GenAI-supported creative mathematical writing fostered students’ creative writing processes, including divergent thinking, originality, and revising AI-generated drafts into coherent stories. At the same time, some students lacked critical evaluation skills and difficulty formulating coherent written stories, which limited writing quality and independent composition.
finding.measure: Qualitative interview themes and open-ended survey responses about story writing, revising, and evaluating AI-generated text
finding.study_size: n=79 students; n=6 teachers (interviews with n=10 students in focus groups)

finding.finding_summary: Students and teachers described increased interest, curiosity, and enjoyment in math learning when students collaborated with GenAI on culturally relevant story creation. The study also reports a stronger sense of ownership and responsibility for learning because students became authors of their own math stories.
finding.measure: Qualitative interview themes, open-ended survey responses, and classroom observation notes about interest, curiosity, enjoyment, and ownership
finding.study_size: n=79 students; n=6 teachers (interviews with n=10 students in focus groups)

finding.finding_summary: The study reports gains in AI literacy and prompt engineering, with students learning to make more specific requests and revise prompts through trial and error. It also describes flexible thinking and evaluation of AI strengths and weaknesses as important outcomes of the activity.
finding.measure: Qualitative interview themes and classroom observations regarding prompt engineering, evaluating AI outputs, and flexible thinking
finding.study_size: n=79 students; n=6 teachers (interviews with n=10 students in focus groups)

paper_profiles.title: Quadratic Forms and Automorphic Forms
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a set of graduate lecture notes surveying the theory of quadratic forms over fields and rings, with an emphasis on the local-global arithmetic of quadratic forms and their connections to modular and automorphic forms. It introduces core definitions, classification results over local fields, lattice theory, genus and class theory, neighboring lattices, theta functions, and theta lifts.

The notes are expository rather than empirical: they do not study an intervention, sample, or outcome in education, and they do not concern AI in education research. Instead, they develop mathematical background and explain classical theorems such as Hasse–Minkowski, Jordan decomposition, and modular transformation properties of theta series. The paper’s purpose is pedagogical and theoretical, aimed at graduate students in mathematics.

No educational population is studied, and there are no intervention effects or empirical findings relevant to K-12 academic or socio-emotional outcomes. Accordingly, there are no outcome assignments for the requested education research taxonomy.

paper_profiles.title: Labor Market Outcomes and Early Schooling: Evidence from School Entry Policies Using Exact Date of Birth
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether earlier school entry, induced by birthdate-based school entry rules, causally affects later educational attainment and labor market outcomes. The authors focus on Brazil, where primary school entry eligibility depended on a cutoff date, and they use exact date of birth to create exogenous variation in years of schooling.

Using Brazilian National Sample Household Survey (PNAD) data, especially a 2014 supplement with retrospective information on where respondents lived at age 15, the authors implement a fuzzy regression discontinuity design around the March 31 entry cutoff. They examine several samples of young adults, including those who were living in urban areas or state capitals at age 15, and use the discontinuity in schooling as an instrument for labor market outcomes.

The main conclusion is that being born just before the cutoff increases schooling and college completion, and that additional schooling raises labor income. In their preferred sample, one more year of schooling increases labor income by about 25.8%, while holding a college degree is associated with an even larger income premium of about 201%. They find little evidence that the cutoff affects employment or labor supply, and robustness checks suggest no strong manipulation of birthdates or parental education around the threshold.

finding.finding_summary: Children born just before the March 31 school-entry cutoff accumulated more schooling in adulthood than those born just after the cutoff. In the preferred urban-at-age-15 sample, the fuzzy RD first stage implies an increase of 0.77 years of study (significant at 5%); in the state-capital-at-15 sample the increase was 1.12 years (significant at 10%).
finding.measure: Years of study / years of formal education

finding.finding_summary: Being born just before the cutoff also increased the probability of holding a college degree in adulthood. In the sample of respondents who lived in an urban area at age 15, the estimated discontinuity was 9.6 percentage points (significant at 5%), corresponding to a sizable increase in tertiary completion around the threshold.
finding.measure: Probability of holding a college degree

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates a school-entry policy rule as an institutionally generated source of exogenous variation and concludes that the March 31 cutoff meaningfully changes educational trajectories. Robustness checks show no evidence of meaningful manipulation of the running variable or systematic discontinuities in parent education, supporting the institutional relevance of the entry rule as a policy instrument.
finding.measure: Discontinuity in school entry / policy cutoff effects

paper_profiles.title: Causal Sets: Discrete Gravity
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a set of lecture notes reviewing the causal set approach to quantum gravity. It asks whether spacetime might be fundamentally discrete and whether its continuum geometry can emerge from a locally finite partial order equipped with a causal relation.

The paper develops the kinematics of causal sets, including how continuum spacetime geometry can be approximately recovered from order plus counting (e.g., dimension estimators, longest-chain proper-time estimators, sprinkling, and coarse-graining). It then reviews candidate dynamics, especially classical sequential growth models constrained by discrete general covariance and Bell causality, and discusses phenomenological implications such as cosmological-constant fluctuations and black-hole horizon entropy via links crossing horizons.

The intended audience is the quantum-gravity research community rather than an education or schooling population. The paper is theoretical and expository, drawing on prior results and open conjectures; it does not present an intervention study or an empirical study of educational outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: The quality of life of children with attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder: a systematic review
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper systematically reviews published research on quality of life (QoL) in children and adolescents with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). The authors ask three questions: how ADHD affects QoL, how symptoms and impairment relate to QoL, and whether ADHD treatment improves QoL.

The review searched multiple databases from 1988 to April 2008 and included 36 empirical articles, most of them cross-sectional or case-control studies, plus several treatment studies. Across studies, parent ratings showed robust and fairly large QoL deficits for children with ADHD, especially in psychosocial, family, achievement, and self-evaluation domains, while physical functioning was usually less affected. Child self-reports were less consistently negative than parent reports, with some studies finding no difference from controls and others finding lower QoL depending on the measure used.

The review also found that higher ADHD symptom severity, greater impairment, and comorbid conditions were associated with worse QoL. Treatment studies, mostly involving atomoxetine or methylphenidate, generally showed improvements in QoL alongside symptom improvement. The authors conclude that ADHD substantially compromises QoL and recommend including QoL outcomes more routinely in future treatment research.

finding.finding_summary: ADHD was consistently associated with poorer parent-reported academic functioning and achievement-related QoL. In the review, parent ratings on the CHIP-CE and CHQ showed large deficits in achievement/school-related domains, often about 1.5–2.0 SD below norms; for example, in the ADORE sample (about n=1,500), academic achievement/threats to achievement were among the most impaired subdomains.
finding.measure: QoL subscales related to academic achievement/school functioning (e.g. CHIP-CE achievement, CHQ role/school functioning)
finding.study_size: multiple studies; largest observational sample n≈1,500
finding.effect_size: approximately 1.5–2.0 SD below norms in several studies

finding.finding_summary: This was the central outcome of the review: ADHD was associated with robust reductions in quality of life across psychosocial, emotional, self-esteem, family, and peer domains. Parent ratings typically showed large deficits relative to controls/norms, often around 1.5–2.0 SD below norms; child self-reports were less consistently negative but still often showed impaired psychosocial QoL (e.g. PedsQL, CHQ, YQOL-R).
finding.measure: Generic QoL scales capturing psychosocial, emotional, self-esteem, family, peer, and school functioning (CHQ, PedsQL, CHIP-CE, KINDL, YQOL-R, DUX-25, TACQOL)
finding.study_size: 36 studies in total; several large samples including n=1,478 and n≈1,500
finding.effect_size: approximately 1.5–2.0 SD below norms in parent-report studies; individual studies reported moderate correlations (e.g. r=-0.21 to -0.60) with symptom severity

finding.finding_summary: The review included evidence that ADHD-related QoL deficits extended into domains overlapping with self-regulation and functioning, such as resilience, autonomy, cognitive functioning, and social problem solving. These domains were especially impaired in parent-report CHIP-CE and related measures, although the paper does not isolate durable skills as a separate construct.
finding.measure: QoL domains overlapping with resilience, autonomy, cognitive functioning, and social problem solving
finding.study_size: multiple studies; e.g. n=1,477 to n=1,500 in CHIP-CE samples
finding.effect_size: approximately 1.5–2.0 SD below norms in several parent-report studies

finding.finding_summary: Several studies reviewed showed that ADHD was associated with lower functioning on school/role performance and everyday task completion, including homework and general activity limitations. These are not teacher workload outcomes, but they do reflect reduced day-to-day efficiency and functioning; treatment studies reported that symptom improvement predicted better psychosocial QoL and school functioning.
finding.measure: CHQ role limitations, CHIP-CE academic performance and usual activities, QoL items about school/home functioning
finding.study_size: multiple studies; treatment samples ranged from n=51 to n=912

paper_profiles.title: Females with ADHD: An expert consensus statement taking a lifespan approach providing guidance for the identification and treatment of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder in girls and women
paper_profiles.population: Girls and women across the lifespan
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the under-recognition and under-referral of females with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), arguing that girls and women often present differently from boys and men and may be missed because their symptoms are less overt, more internalized, or masked by compensatory strategies. The authors aim to improve identification, assessment, treatment, and multi-agency support for females with ADHD across development, from childhood through adulthood.

The paper is an expert consensus statement developed by the United Kingdom ADHD Partnership. Experts from multiple disciplines met in London in 2018 to review selected literature and share professional experience, then discussed presentation, referral triggers, assessment methods, pharmacological treatment, non-pharmacological interventions, and liaison with schools and other agencies. The report emphasizes that inattentive symptoms, emotional dysregulation, internalizing comorbidities, and functional impairments may be more prominent or more easily missed in females, and it recommends lifespan-sensitive assessment and treatment approaches.

The consensus concludes that ADHD medication and psychological interventions are expected to improve long-term outcomes for girls and women, but that clinical practice should be sex-sensitive in how symptoms are assessed and how response is monitored. It recommends collateral information, careful developmental history, attention to transitions such as puberty and school changes, and individualized treatment targets such as emotional regulation and academic participation rather than relying only on conventional rating scales. Because this is a consensus/guidance paper rather than an empirical study, it does not provide new effect estimates or primary outcome data.

paper_profiles.title: Basic psychological need theory: Advancements, critical themes, and future directions
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This editorial review synthesizes two decades of research on Basic Psychological Need Theory (BPNT) within Self-Determination Theory. The paper asks how psychological needs such as autonomy, competence, and relatedness should be defined, how need frustration differs from simple lack of need satisfaction, whether additional needs should be added to the theory, and what the implications are for motivation, adjustment, and well-being.

Rather than testing a single intervention, the article reviews a broad literature of empirical studies and special-issue contributions across domains including education, work, exercise, relationships, health, and culture. It argues that basic psychological need satisfaction is essential for flourishing, while need frustration predicts maladjustment, distress, and compensatory behaviors. The authors emphasize that the field has moved toward stronger measurement of need frustration and toward more nuanced questions about universality, contextual support, and possible new need candidates such as novelty, morality, and beneficence.

Because this is a conceptual/editorial synthesis, its main contribution is theoretical: it clarifies criteria for identifying basic needs, summarizes evidence for the “dark side” of need frustration, and outlines future directions for research. It is not an empirical study of students’ academic outcomes, and it does not report a new intervention effect. The paper is relevant to education research mainly as a framework for understanding motivation, engagement, and adjustment in school and other settings.

finding.finding_summary: The paper synthesizes evidence that satisfaction of autonomy, competence, and relatedness supports motivation, adjustment, and well-being, while need frustration predicts amotivation, disengagement, stress, depressive symptoms, anxiety, and other forms of ill-being. Across the reviewed literature, need frustration is described as a distinct predictor beyond low need satisfaction, but this article itself reports no new effect sizes or sample-specific estimates.
finding.measure: Need satisfaction / need frustration scales; motivation, engagement, well-being, distress, and ill-being outcomes from reviewed studies

finding.finding_summary: The review links basic psychological need satisfaction to higher-order self-regulatory and adaptive functioning processes, including internalization, identity consolidation, and proactive coping. These outcomes are discussed as downstream effects of need support across the reviewed literature, but the paper does not present a new study or pooled estimate.
finding.measure: Internalization, identity development, proactive coping, and related adaptive functioning measures from reviewed studies

paper_profiles.title: ADHD: Current Concepts and Treatments in Children and Adolescents
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a narrative review of attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) in children and adolescents, covering current diagnostic concepts, epidemiology, comorbidity, neuropsychology, neurophysiology, neuroimaging, genetics, and treatment. It does not test a new intervention or compare treatment groups; instead, it synthesizes existing research and clinical guidelines to explain how ADHD is defined, assessed, and managed.

The review emphasizes that ADHD remains a heterogeneous, behaviorally defined neurodevelopmental disorder without a single objective biomarker. It discusses multiple dimensions of the condition, including overlapping constructs such as sluggish cognitive tempo and emotional dysregulation, the dimensional versus categorical nature of ADHD, and the complexity of differential diagnosis and comorbidity in children and adolescents.

In treatment, the paper summarizes multimodal care, including psychoeducation, parent training, school-based supports, behavioral interventions, and pharmacological approaches such as methylphenidate as first-line medication in Europe. The overall conclusion is that ADHD diagnosis and treatment require specialist expertise and individualized, multimodal management; while neurobiological and treatment-response findings are informative at the group level, they are not yet sufficiently robust for routine biomarker-based diagnosis or precision treatment in individual patients.

paper_profiles.title: Evidence-based Kernels: Fundamental Units of Behavioral Influence
paper_profiles.venue: Clinical Child and Family Psychology Review
paper_profiles.population: Not population-specific; primarily children and adolescents in educational, family, and prevention contexts
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper argues for a new conceptual framework for prevention and intervention called “evidence-based kernels”: indivisible, behavior-influence procedures that have each been shown in experimental studies to reliably change behavior. The authors contrast kernels with full intervention programs, arguing that kernels may help explain the active ingredients of effective programs and could make behavior-change practices easier to disseminate, adapt, and combine.

The paper is primarily a conceptual and theoretical review rather than a report of a single empirical study. It organizes 52 example kernels into a taxonomy based on whether they work through consequences, antecedents, relational framing, or physiological processes. Examples include timeout, praise, response cost, peer tutoring, self-monitoring, structured play, omega-3 supplementation, and nasal breathing, with citations to prior experimental work supporting each. The paper’s main conclusion is that identifying and cataloging kernels could improve the efficiency, portability, and practical use of behavior-change science in schools, families, and other applied settings.

Although the article discusses educational examples and cites studies involving classroom behavior, academic engagement, ADHD-related behavior, and peer interactions, it does not itself test an intervention or estimate effects. Instead, it synthesizes prior evidence to propose a taxonomy and a research agenda for building a database of effective behavioral “building blocks.”

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not present new academic outcome data, but it cites prior experimental work showing that several kernels can improve academic engagement, accuracy, achievement, and retention. Examples include response cards, choral responding, peer tutoring, self-monitoring, and paragraph shrinking; however, no pooled effect sizes, sample sizes, or confidence intervals are reported for these academic outcomes in this paper.
finding.measure: Academic engagement, academic achievement, accuracy, retention, reading responses

finding.finding_summary: The paper centrally focuses on kernels that influence behavior, self-regulation, cooperation, compliance, aggression, and ADHD-like symptoms. It cites multiple prior studies indicating positive effects of kernels such as timeout, self-monitoring, response cost, structured play, and aerobic play on disruptive behavior, aggression, compliance, and ADHD symptoms, but the article itself does not provide a single consolidated effect estimate.
finding.measure: Disruptive behavior, aggression, compliance, self-regulation, ADHD symptoms, engagement

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses kernels that can improve broader self-management and interaction skills such as cooperation, problem solving in groups, and adherence to routines. Evidence is cited for peer tutoring, cooperative structured play, self-monitoring, and correspondence training, but the paper does not report a quantitative synthesis of durable-skill outcomes.
finding.measure: Collaboration, self-monitoring, cooperation, rule-governed behavior

paper_profiles.title: Media Use and ADHD-Related Behaviors in Children and Adolescents: A Meta-Analysis
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether children’s and adolescents’ use of screen media is associated with ADHD-related behaviors, and whether the association differs by media type, media content, age, sex, and measurement approach. The authors synthesize 45 empirical studies published up to September 2013, covering cross-sectional, longitudinal, and experimental designs, and examine television viewing, video game playing, violent content, fast-paced content, and overall media use.

The meta-analysis focuses on ADHD-related behaviors rather than educational outcomes: attention problems, hyperactivity, impulsivity, and composite ADHD measures among children and adolescents under 18. The authors report a small but significant overall association between media use and composite ADHD-related behaviors (r=.12, 95% CI [.09, .14], k=43), a larger association for attention problems (r=.32, 95% CI [.11, .50], k=7), and a small association for impulsivity (r=.11, 95% CI [.00, .22], k=7). Hyperactivity could not be meta-analyzed because only one study measured it separately, and moderator analyses suggested stronger associations in studies with more boys and with unstandardized measures, but not for media type or media content.

The paper concludes that the evidence supports a modest positive relationship between media use and ADHD-related behaviors, while also emphasizing major limitations in the literature, including conceptual overlap among outcome measures, too few studies on fast-paced media, limited longitudinal evidence, and insufficient tests of transactional effects and differential susceptibility. The authors argue for more theory-driven, better-specified future studies rather than treating media exposure as a single uniform input.

finding.finding_summary: Across 43 independent effect sizes, media use was positively associated with composite ADHD-related behaviors in children and adolescents. The pooled correlation was small but significant (r=.12, 95% CI [.09, .14]), indicating that greater screen media use was associated with more attention problems/hyperactivity/impulsivity on composite measures.
finding.measure: Composite ADHD-related behavior measures (attention problems, hyperactivity, impulsivity)
finding.study_size: k=43 studies; over 155,000 participants across the full meta-analysis

finding.finding_summary: For attention problems specifically, the meta-analysis found a moderate positive association with media use. The pooled correlation was r=.32 (95% CI [.11, .50]) across 7 independent effect sizes, suggesting that greater media use was associated with more attention difficulties.
finding.measure: Attention problems

finding.finding_summary: For impulsivity, the meta-analysis found a small but significant positive association with media use. The pooled correlation was r=.11 (95% CI [.00, .22]) across 7 independent effect sizes; the authors note this effect was smaller than the attention-problems association and should be interpreted cautiously because of the small number of studies.
finding.measure: Impulsivity

paper_profiles.title: A Review of Heterogeneity in Attention Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This review examines why attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is so heterogeneous across children and across the lifespan. Rather than testing a single intervention, the paper synthesizes research on etiological risk factors, clinical subtypes, neurocognitive deficits, and neurobiological mechanisms that may explain why children with ADHD present differently and respond differently to treatment.

The authors summarize evidence on genetic, prenatal/perinatal, psychosocial, and environmental contributors to ADHD, as well as variability in symptom profiles, comorbidities, and developmental trajectories. They also review theoretical models of ADHD pathology, including cognitive/motivational impairment models, the cognitive-energetic model, and a neurodevelopmental model, arguing that no single model fully accounts for the disorder.

A major conclusion is that ADHD is not a unitary condition but a collection of biologically and clinically diverse subgroups. The paper emphasizes that this heterogeneity likely contributes to inconsistent findings across studies and variable treatment response. The authors recommend future research on more homogeneous subgroups and integrated multi-level approaches to better understand mechanisms and tailor interventions.

finding.finding_summary: The review concludes that ADHD is associated with heterogeneous impairments in self-regulation, emotional regulation, and behavior across children, but these deficits are not uniform across individuals. It notes that responses to treatment and the severity of symptoms vary widely, and that self-regulation deficits are central to some theoretical accounts (e.g., Barkley’s model) but not sufficient to explain ADHD as a whole.
finding.measure: Behavioral inhibition, self-regulation, emotional regulation, ADHD symptom profiles, response inhibition tasks

paper_profiles.title: Audiovisual Speech-In-Noise (SIN) Performance of Young Adults with ADHD
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the Symposium on Eye Tracking Research and Applications (ETRA '20 Short Papers)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This pilot study examines whether young adults with ADHD differ from age-matched neurotypical controls in an audiovisual speech-in-noise task. The authors were interested in whether background noise changes speech perception performance and eye-movement behavior when listeners can also see the speaker’s face, especially because ADHD is often associated with weaker inhibitory control and working memory capacity.

Five young adults with a prior ADHD diagnosis and six neurotypical young adults (ages 18–30) completed the QuickSIN sentence-repetition task while their eye movements were recorded with a Tobii eye tracker. The task presented six signal-to-noise ratios (25 dB to 0 dB) with visual speech cues, and the authors analyzed keyword-repetition accuracy, fixation counts on facial areas of interest, gaze-transition entropy, and pupillary activity as a proxy for cognitive load. Participants with ADHD were asked to remain medication-free for 12 hours before participation.

The main behavioral result was that overall QuickSIN performance did not differ by group, but a significant group difference emerged at 15 dB SNR, where NT participants recalled slightly more keywords on average than participants with ADHD (4.9 vs. 4.7 keywords). Eye-tracking results suggested different visual attention patterns: ADHD participants fixated more on the left eye region, while NT participants tended to fixate more on the right eye or mouth depending on listening condition. The authors conclude that audiovisual cues may support speech-in-noise perception similarly across groups in easy and difficult conditions, but that medium difficulty (15 dB SNR) may reveal group differences in cognitive load and performance.

finding.finding_summary: This pilot study directly measured audiovisual speech-in-noise performance using keyword repetition in QuickSIN sentences. Overall performance did not differ between ADHD and neurotypical groups (F(1,9)=1.97, p>0.05), but at 15 dB SNR there was a significant group difference (p<0.05), with ADHD participants recalling 4.7 keywords on average and neurotypical participants recalling 4.9 keywords on average.
finding.measure: QuickSIN sentence keyword-repetition accuracy across six SNR levels

finding.finding_summary: The paper treats pupil-based index of pupillary activity (IPA) as an indicator of cognitive load during listening. IPA showed no overall main effect of group or SNR, but there was a significant group-by-SNR interaction (F(5,45)=3.265, p<0.02), with a significant difference at 15 dB SNR (p<0.04) at the sentence level, suggesting condition-specific differences in effort or cognitive load.
finding.measure: Index of pupillary activity (IPA) during audiovisual QuickSIN listening

paper_profiles.title: Challenges in the Differential Classification of Individual Diagnoses from Co-Occurring Autism and ADHD Using Survey Data
paper_profiles.population: Children aged 0-17 years (population-based survey; elementary school children included but not limited to them)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of distinguishing autism, ADHD, co-occurring autism+ADHD, and no diagnosis using population survey data rather than clinician-administered diagnostic tools. The authors ask whether a small set of parent-reported behavioral items from the National Survey of Children’s Health (NSCH) can support machine-learning-based differential classification and feature selection for these neurodevelopmental conditions.

The study uses NSCH data from 2016-2022 (filtered dataset n=270,978) and trains logistic regression, decision tree, and random forest models on behavioral and sociodemographic features. Three tasks are evaluated: identifying any neurodevelopmental condition vs none, autism or ADHD vs none, and a 4-way classification of autism only, ADHD only, both, and none. The authors also apply sequential forward feature selection to identify the most informative behavioral items and compare performance using grouped features versus a combined set with kNN imputation for missing values.

The main conclusion is that the models perform reasonably well for broad binary screening but much worse for the fine-grained differential task of separating autism from ADHD and co-occurrence. The combined feature set yields strong binary performance (e.g., accuracy 93.8%, sensitivity 93.6%, specificity 94.04% for any neurodevelopmental condition vs none; accuracy 93.5%, sensitivity 92.3%, specificity 94.7% for autism/ADHD vs none), but 4-way classification remains only moderate (about 68% accuracy) with substantial confusion between autism and ADHD. The authors conclude that parent-reported behavioral questionnaires can support preliminary screening, but they are not yet robust enough for clinical-grade differential diagnosis, especially given missing data, recall bias, underdiagnosis, and demographic imbalance in the survey sample.

finding.finding_summary: The paper primarily evaluates whether parent-reported behavioral items related to social interaction, attention regulation, emotion regulation, and adaptive behavior can distinguish autism, ADHD, both, and none. The best 4-way model achieved only moderate performance (about 68% accuracy), with repeated confusion between autism and ADHD, while broader binary tasks performed much better (93.8% accuracy for any neurodevelopmental condition vs none; 93.5% accuracy for autism/ADHD vs none).
finding.measure: Machine-learning classification performance on parent-reported behavioral questionnaire items from NSCH, including attention, friendship, emotion regulation, and social interaction features

finding.finding_summary: The study proposes a scalable screening approach using publicly available survey data to support clinical decision support and early identification of neurodevelopmental delays. However, the authors emphasize that the approach is not yet clinically robust for differential diagnosis and that external validation, demographic representativeness, and clinically annotated datasets are still needed.
finding.measure: Classification accuracy and feature selection for potential screening/decision-support utility

paper_profiles.title: Challenges, Strengths, and Strategies of Software Engineers with ADHD: A Case Study
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates how adults with ADHD experience software engineering work, focusing on the challenges they face, the strengths they perceive, and the coping strategies they use. The authors note that prior ADHD-in-workplace research is general and does not sufficiently address software engineering contexts, which involve rapid pace, constant collaboration, frequent context switching, and task estimation.

To address this gap, the authors conducted an exploratory single-case qualitative study using 19 semi-structured interviews with software engineering professionals with ADHD, plus four follow-up interviews with experienced managers to discuss implications. Participants worked across roles such as software developer, QA engineer, engineering manager, security analyst, and founder, and were located in Europe, South America, North America, and Asia. The analysis used in vivo coding, iterative category building, member checking, and triangulation across interviewees.

The paper reports recurring challenges in task organization, deadlines and estimation, sustaining attention, memory, meeting participation, communication, and emotional/physical health. It also identifies strengths such as creativity, puzzle-solving, broad interests, systems thinking, and occasional hyperfocus. The main practical conclusion is that many participants use medication, externalizing tools (to-do lists, notes, calendars), help from others, work-mode adjustments, and clearer company processes to manage ADHD-related difficulties, and the authors argue that some agile practices and workplace accommodations may better support these professionals.

finding.finding_summary: The study primarily examines how ADHD affects work performance and day-to-day productivity in software engineering. Nineteen interviews found recurring operational challenges including task organization, deadline management, estimation, maintaining focus, context switching, and consistent performance; participants also reported coping strategies such as medication, to-do lists, calendars, and work-environment adjustments. No effect size was reported because the study is qualitative.
finding.measure: Interview-reported work productivity, task efficiency, deadline management, estimation, focus, and consistency in software engineering tasks

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively focuses on durable skills including time management, planning, collaboration, communication, and metacognitive/self-awareness strategies. Interviewees described difficulty with planning, time estimation, communication with colleagues, and aligning with neurotypical coworkers, but also reported strategies like self-awareness, clear communication, and help-seeking that support these skills. No quantitative effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Interview-reported planning, time management, communication, collaboration, and self-awareness in software engineering work

finding.finding_summary: The study reports substantial social-emotional challenges and supports, including anxiety, fear of negative emotions, rejection sensitivity, impostor syndrome, and general emotional regulation difficulties. At the same time, participants described self-awareness, therapy, medication, and adapting over time as helpful strategies; the paper also notes strengths like mentoring others and increased focus. No quantitative effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Interview-reported emotional regulation, anxiety, stigma, rejection sensitivity, and coping/self-awareness strategies

finding.finding_summary: The paper draws implications for software engineering workplaces and company practices, arguing that organizational policies, manager education, flexible work arrangements, clearer meeting structures, and ADHD coaching could improve inclusion and functioning for employees with ADHD. These are presented as qualitative, practice-oriented recommendations rather than measured institutional effects. No quantitative effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Interview-reported implications for workplace policies, management practices, and organizational accommodations

paper_profiles.title: Misty Forest VR: Turning Real ADHD Attention Patterns into Shared Momentum for Youth Collaboration
paper_profiles.venue: Extended Abstracts of the 2026 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI EA '26)
paper_profiles.population: Adolescents and young adults (ages 10–24); mixed ADHD and non-ADHD participants
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how ADHD is understood and experienced in collaborative settings, especially in cultural contexts where ADHD-related behaviors are moralized and stigmatized. The authors argue that many existing ADHD interventions focus on individual symptom management, leaving unexplored how ADHD and non-ADHD peers can build shared understanding and coordinate effectively.

To address this gap, the paper presents Misty Forest, a two-player virtual reality collaborative game co-designed with Chinese adolescents with ADHD, clinicians, and educators. The game uses asymmetric roles: an ADHD player can trigger short burst phases of high-speed progress, while a non-ADHD partner provides support by stabilizing the environment, reducing distractions, and marking routes. The design intentionally translates attentional fluctuation, time blindness, and coordination mismatch into gameplay mechanics that require mutual adaptation rather than compensation.

The authors evaluated the system in a controlled mixed-methods study with 60 participants (30 with clinically diagnosed ADHD and 30 without ADHD), ages 10–24, across three conditions: mixed ADHD–non-ADHD dyads, same-group dyads, and individual play. Results suggest that mixed-pair collaboration improved task completion, increased self-acceptance among ADHD participants, improved tolerance and understanding among non-ADHD participants, and enhanced ADHD knowledge for both groups. The paper concludes that culturally grounded, reciprocal collaboration designs can promote empathy, agency, and inclusion in neurodiverse interaction.

finding.finding_summary: In a controlled pre–post study with 60 participants (n=60; 30 ADHD, 30 non-ADHD), ADHD participants in the mixed-dyad condition showed the largest increase in self-acceptance, from M=7.1 to M=12.2. The paper reports a significant time × group interaction, F(2,54)=26.64, p<.001, indicating that role-based collaborative play improved ADHD participants’ self-perception relative to same-group and individual-play controls.
finding.measure: ADHD self-acceptance / self-perception scale

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studies collaboration and coordination in mixed ADHD–non-ADHD dyads. Mixed pairs achieved 10/10 task completion, compared with 8/20 in same-group collaboration and 1/20 in individual play, suggesting that the asymmetric VR mechanics improved teamwork, coordination, and mutual adaptation during task completion.
finding.measure: Task completion outcome / collaborative performance

finding.finding_summary: Non-ADHD participants in mixed dyads showed the largest gains in tolerance toward ADHD, with a significant between-group comparison reported as F(2,27)=17.68, p<.001. Interview data indicate an attribution shift away from moralized judgments (e.g., 'lazy') toward more contextualized interpretations of ADHD behavior.
finding.measure: Self-determination / tolerance scale (SDS)

finding.finding_summary: The intervention improved ADHD knowledge for both ADHD and non-ADHD participants. In the experimental mixed-pair group, pre–post gains were significant for ADHD participants, t(9)=-9.00, p<.001, and non-ADHD participants, t(9)=-8.51, p<.001, exceeding the learning outcomes in the control conditions.
finding.measure: ADHD knowledge questionnaire

paper_profiles.title: Preliminary Results of a Scoping Review on Assistive Technologies for Adults with ADHD
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of Workshop: AT@WORK: Intelligent Assistive Technologies for Enabling Workplace Inclusion (ASSETS ’25)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents preliminary results from a scoping review of technology-based approaches intended to support adults with ADHD. The authors motivate the review by noting that ADHD research and design work has historically focused on children, while adults face distinct challenges in education, work, and daily functioning that may not be adequately addressed by existing interventions. They aimed to systematically map the state of the art in assistive technologies for adults with ADHD using PRISMA-ScR methods.

The review searched ACM Digital Library, IEEE Xplore, and Scopus, returning 3,538 records, of which 46 papers were included after abstract and full-text screening. The included papers were categorized into psychotherapy and psychoeducation, cognitive training, assistive tools, behavioral interventions, passive agents, and virtual environments. The paper is primarily descriptive rather than evaluative: it reports that most technologies take a therapeutic or intervention-oriented perspective, that mobile apps and PC-based tools are common, and that usability/user-centered design are relatively underused in many categories.

Overall, the authors conclude that there is growing research attention to ADHD technology for adults, but the field remains dominated by deficit-oriented approaches such as psychoeducation and cognitive training. They argue for more participatory, user-centered, and context-sensitive design, especially for adult users, and identify this as an important gap for future work. Because this paper is a scoping review and does not synthesize intervention effect sizes, it does not provide direct causal evidence about academic outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: An ADHD Diagnostic Interface Based on EEG Spectrograms and Deep Learning Techniques
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of ADHD diagnosis in children, arguing that current behavior-based approaches can lead to misdiagnosis and gender bias. The authors propose an EEG-based diagnostic pipeline that converts children’s EEG recordings into spectrograms and classifies ADHD vs. control status using a ResNet-18 convolutional neural network.

The study uses a publicly available EEG dataset of 121 children aged 7–12 (61 with ADHD, 60 controls) who completed a visual attention task. The model is trained on spectrogram representations of the EEG signals and evaluated with 5-fold cross-validation. The reported classification performance is high (accuracy 0.90; F1-score 0.90), and feature extraction suggests that frontopolar, parietal, and occipital channels are most informative for ADHD classification.

The paper’s second contribution is a proposed three-part digital screening interface based on the identified brain regions, intended for use in school settings and paired with commercial EEG headsets. The authors argue that such a system could support earlier and more accessible ADHD screening, though the paper does not test deployment in schools or evaluate downstream educational outcomes. Overall, the work is a proof-of-concept diagnostic/ screening study rather than an intervention study on learning or behavior.

paper_profiles.title: Investigating Current State-of-The-Art Applications of Supportive Technologies for Individuals with ADHD
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents a systematic literature review of assistive and supportive technologies for individuals with ADHD, with a focus on human-computer interaction research published in ACM Digital Library between 2007 and 2017. The review asks what challenges and ages of users are represented, what methods are used to involve users in the design process, what technologies are developed, and what design frameworks or protocols have been proposed.

The review includes 27 papers and synthesizes them across themes such as attention deficit, executive functioning, learning deficit, sleep disorder, sensory processing disorder, stress release, and mixed challenges. It finds that children are the most frequently studied population, especially in home and school contexts, and that participatory design, prototyping, and user testing are common methods. The paper concludes that the field is still emerging, that design frameworks and protocols are a major focus, and that there are notable gaps in coverage for some ADHD-related challenges and populations such as teachers.

Because this is a review of assistive technologies rather than a study of medication effects, it does not provide evidence about confounding by indication, selective reporting, or robustness of academic effects of ADHD medication in elementary school children. Its value for the retrieval question is primarily contextual: it describes the broader ADHD technology landscape and highlights a need for standardized measures and careful reporting in studies involving children with ADHD.

finding.finding_summary: Across the reviewed literature, supportive technologies were commonly reported to improve attention, stress, sleep routines, and self-regulation-related outcomes for children and adults with ADHD. Examples include MOBERO reducing parent frustration and improving child sleep habits (n=11 families, 13 children), ChillFish showing positive calming effects, and other systems supporting attention monitoring or routine adherence; however, the paper does not pool effect sizes across studies.
finding.measure: Child sleep habits, parent frustration, attention/self-regulation indicators, and stress-related biofeedback or interview outcomes
finding.study_size: n=27 papers reviewed; individual study sizes varied (e.g., n=11 families/13 children; n=12 children; n=10 adults)

finding.finding_summary: The review reports that several technologies were designed to support executive functioning and related durable skills such as time management, planning, and task persistence. Examples include TangiPlan and Takt for morning routines and time management, and several design-guideline papers emphasizing external cues and structured supports; the evidence is narrative and study-specific rather than synthesized quantitatively.
finding.measure: Executive functioning tasks, morning routine completion, time-management support, and related usability/evaluation outcomes
finding.study_size: n=27 papers reviewed; individual study sizes varied (e.g., n=3 children, n=15 children, n=13 adults)

finding.finding_summary: Only one included study directly addressed academic mathematics outcomes: Kang et al. (2007) used visual cues to support geometry learning for 2nd- to 4th-grade students with and without ADHD. The review reports that additional visual cues were more helpful than low-level visual cues for learning difficult geometry terminology and perimeter calculations, but provides no effect size.
finding.measure: Geometry learning performance, including terminology and perimeter calculations

finding.finding_summary: The review identifies a small set of educational technologies aimed at learning-related outcomes beyond literacy and numeracy, including persuasive or game-based tools intended to support problem solving, attention in learning tasks, and academic engagement. The strongest direct academic example is the geometry-learning study, while other papers mainly target classroom attention and learning support rather than subject-matter achievement.
finding.measure: Learning task performance and educational engagement in classroom/school contexts

paper_profiles.title: Lifespan associations of resting-state brain functional networks with ADHD symptoms
paper_profiles.population: Children and adults with ADHD and healthy controls (ages 7-50 years)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how resting-state brain functional network organization changes across the lifespan in attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), and whether those network features relate differently to hyperactivity and inattention. The authors focus on hierarchical segregation and integration in functional connectivity (FC) networks, using a nested-spectral partition (NSP) method designed to capture multiscale network organization rather than only single-level modularity.

The study combines resting-state fMRI from 97 ADHD patients and 97 age- and sex-matched healthy controls spanning ages 7-50 years. Data were drawn from multiple sites, harmonized, and analyzed with FC networks parcellated into 100 regions. The authors examined age-related trajectories of global and regional network segregation/integration, compared ADHD vs control groups, and tested whether functional systems predict symptom severity after controlling for age, sex, and motion.

The main finding is that healthy controls showed a linear association between age and brain network organization, whereas ADHD participants showed a quadratic lifespan pattern, with integration rising and then falling after about age 30. ADHD-related abnormalities were concentrated in local regions, especially within the default mode and control systems in the full sample, with children and adults showing partly different regional patterns. The limbic system was the strongest predictor of hyperactivity, while the salient attention system was the strongest predictor of inattention, suggesting partially distinct neural bases for these symptom dimensions across the lifespan. Because the work is cross-sectional and correlational, it does not test medication effects or causal pathways, but it does identify age-related network signatures associated with ADHD symptoms.

finding.finding_summary: Resting-state network measures were associated with ADHD symptom severity, a core self-regulation outcome. Across all ADHD patients (n=97), hyperactivity was best predicted by limbic-system heterogeneity/integration (e.g., HIn of the limbic system, β=-0.276, p=0.020), and inattention was best predicted by salient attention-system heterogeneity (e.g., CVSe, β=0.233, p=0.047). These are correlational associations, not intervention effects, and the paper reports symptom prediction rather than behavioral change.
finding.measure: ADHD Rating Scale hyperactivity/impulsivity and inattention scores linked to resting-state FC network metrics
finding.study_size: n=97 ADHD patients; hyperactivity analysis also included healthy children n=26

paper_profiles.title: How Easterners and Westerners perceive ADHD differently
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how ADHD is understood differently in Western and Eastern contexts, with a focus on why qualitative work on ADHD strengths is more common in Europe and North America than in East and Southeast Asia. The author frames ADHD as a neurodivergent condition that can be associated with strengths such as creativity, hyperfocus, resilience, and rapid thinking, and contrasts this with deficit-oriented and highly stigmatized views that are still prominent in many Asian settings.

Rather than testing an intervention, the paper is a narrative/qualitative review that compares three prior qualitative studies of adults with ADHD: Schippers et al. (2022), Sedgwick et al. (2018), and Crook and McDowall (2023). It discusses how sample recruitment, sample size, and interview methods shape the kinds of strengths identified, and it highlights trade-offs between breadth, depth, and generalizability. The paper argues that the available Western studies provide evidence of positive self-reported traits and career strengths, but that most Asian contexts still emphasize diagnosis, stigma, and treatment rather than strengths-based perspectives.

The paper further attributes cross-cultural differences to colonial-era schooling, the interaction between Western biomedical models and local cultural values, and postcolonial economic pressures in places such as Hong Kong, Singapore, and Malaysia. The main conclusion is that culturally sensitive ADHD research and support are needed in Asia, especially studies that capture lived experience and strengths rather than only pathology. The paper also calls for more qualitative research on self-reported career strengths and positive traits among people with ADHD in Asian settings.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that colonial schooling systems, biomedical importation, and postcolonial economic pressures collectively shape how ADHD is understood and handled in Hong Kong, Singapore, and Malaysia. These institutional factors are presented as producing stigma, diagnostic delay, and reduced access to strengths-based support, while also making diagnostic tools and clinical knowledge more available.
finding.measure: Comparative qualitative discussion of cultural, educational, and institutional factors shaping ADHD perception and support

paper_profiles.title: The quality of life of children with attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder: a systematic review
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper systematically reviews the published literature on quality of life (QoL) in children and adolescents with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). The authors ask three questions: how ADHD affects QoL, how ADHD symptoms and functional impairment relate to QoL, and whether ADHD treatment improves QoL.

The review searched multiple databases from 1988 to April 2008 and identified 36 relevant studies, including case-control, cross-sectional, longitudinal, and treatment studies. Most studies used generic QoL measures such as the CHQ, PedsQL, and CHIP-CE, with parents as the primary raters. The review concludes that ADHD is associated with substantial QoL impairment, especially in psychosocial, family, achievement, and self-evaluation domains, while physical health domains are less consistently affected.

The paper also finds that symptom severity, impairment, and comorbidity are related to poorer QoL, and that there is emerging evidence that effective ADHD treatment improves QoL. The authors emphasize that children often rate their own QoL less negatively than parents do, and they recommend routine inclusion of QoL outcomes in future treatment studies.

finding.finding_summary: ADHD was consistently associated with poorer achievement-related quality of life, especially in school/academic functioning and threats to achievement. Across multiple parent-report studies using the CHIP-CE and related measures, children with ADHD scored about 1.5-2.0 SD below norms on academic-achievement-related domains, indicating robust impairment.
finding.measure: Quality-of-life domains related to academic achievement, school functioning, and threats to achievement (e.g., CHIP-CE achievement, academic performance subscales)
finding.study_size: multiple studies; large sample studies included n=1,500 in ADORE and n=1,478 medication-naive children

finding.finding_summary: The review found robust negative effects of ADHD on psychosocial quality of life, including behavior, emotional health, self-esteem, family activities, peer relations, and social functioning. Parent-rated impairments were large, often around 1.5-2.0 SD below norms, and were seen across several measures (CHQ, PedsQL, CHIP-CE, KINDL).
finding.measure: Psychosocial quality-of-life domains including behavior, emotional functioning, self-esteem, peer relations, family activities, and psychosocial summary scores
finding.study_size: multiple studies; examples include n=308, n=921, n=1,500, and n=1,478 across individual studies
finding.effect_size: approximately -1.5 to -2.0 SD below norms; several subscale effect sizes reported as clinically meaningful

finding.finding_summary: ADHD was associated with poorer social and self-related functioning, including relationships, self-concept, and coping-related aspects of QoL. Children and adolescents with ADHD reported poorer scores on domains such as self, relationships, and social problem solving, though the effect was less consistent in self-report than in parent report.
finding.measure: Self and relationship domains on YQOL-R; social problem solving and related CHIP-CE domains
finding.study_size: multiple studies; examples include n=55 ADHD on YQOL-R and n=1,500 in ADORE

finding.finding_summary: The review includes evidence that ADHD is associated with poorer functioning in daily activities and routine task performance, such as homework, school participation, and general activity limitations. These effects were reflected mainly in parent-rated QoL domains like role-emotional/behavioral, family activities, and usual activities rather than direct measures of productivity.
finding.measure: Role limitations, family activities, usual activities, homework-related items, and related QoL functioning domains
finding.study_size: multiple studies; examples include n=308, n=297, n=921

paper_profiles.title: ADHD: Current Concepts and Treatments in Children and Adolescents
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This review paper synthesizes contemporary evidence on attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) in children and adolescents, with a broad focus on diagnostic concepts, neurobiological findings, comorbidity, assessment, and treatment. It addresses the ongoing challenge of ADHD diagnosis and management in the absence of objective biomarkers, and it discusses how ADHD is defined in DSM-5 and ICD-10/11, how it overlaps with related constructs such as sluggish cognitive tempo and emotion dysregulation, and why ADHD should be understood as heterogeneous rather than a single uniform condition.

The treatment section reviews multimodal care, including psychoeducation, parent training, school-based interventions, behavioral approaches, and pharmacological treatment. For medication, it emphasizes that treatment should be initiated and monitored by experienced clinicians, that methylphenidate is first-line in Europe for school-age children, and that medication decisions should follow careful assessment of medical history, cardiovascular risk, and functional impairment. The article does not test a specific intervention itself; instead, it summarizes the evidence base and current guideline recommendations for children and adolescents across clinical settings.

Overall, the authors conclude that ADHD is highly heterogeneous at behavioral, cognitive, neurophysiological, and neuroimaging levels, which limits the utility of single biomarkers for diagnosis or treatment personalization. They also conclude that multimodal treatment is recommended, but that evidence for specific neurobiological markers or individualized prediction tools remains insufficient for routine clinical use.

paper_profiles.title: European clinical guidelines for Tourette syndrome and other tic disorders. Part II: pharmacological treatment
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a European clinical guideline on the pharmacological treatment of Tourette syndrome (TS) and other tic disorders. It was written by the ESSTS Guidelines Group after a broad literature search and discussion of available evidence, with the goal of summarizing medication options for clinicians and highlighting where the evidence is strong versus weak.

The paper is not a single empirical study; it synthesizes prior Cochrane reviews and a large body of trials, open-label studies, retrospective reviews, and case reports on antipsychotics, alpha-2 adrenergic agonists, atomoxetine, and other agents. The authors conclude that although several drugs can reduce tic severity, rigorous randomized evidence is limited, sample sizes are often small, and many findings are constrained by adverse effects, short follow-up, and confounding by the waxing and waning natural course of tics.

For children and adolescents, the guideline especially notes the frequent comorbidity of TS with ADHD and OCD and emphasizes that treatment choices should be based on the most impairing condition, not tics alone. It also warns that evidence is insufficient to make firm recommendations for many agents, and that apparent treatment benefits must be interpreted cautiously because natural symptom fluctuation can mimic medication response. Overall, the paper is a consensus guideline grounded in evidence review rather than an original effectiveness trial.

finding.finding_summary: The guideline discusses academic functioning mainly as a potential consequence of tic suppression and comorbid ADHD rather than as a directly tested educational outcome. It notes that children may expend mental energy suppressing tics in the classroom, reducing attention to schoolwork and interfering with academic performance, but this is presented as background rationale rather than an empirically estimated effect.
finding.measure: academic performance / classroom attention (descriptive discussion)

paper_profiles.title: A Review of Heterogeneity in Attention Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This review examines why attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is such a heterogeneous condition and how that heterogeneity affects research on etiology, symptom profiles, neurocognitive impairments, and biological mechanisms. The paper is not an intervention study; instead, it synthesizes literature on genetic, environmental, developmental, and neurobiological contributors to ADHD and discusses why findings across studies are often inconsistent.

The review argues that ADHD arises from multiple small-effect genetic and environmental risk factors that interact across development, producing diverse clinical presentations, comorbidities, and trajectories. It also reviews competing models of ADHD pathology, including cognitive/motivational impairment models, the cognitive-energetic model, and neurodevelopmental models, concluding that each explains only part of the disorder. The authors emphasize that heterogeneity and sample bias help explain inconsistent findings in genetics and neuroimaging, and they call for more work on biologically homogeneous subgroups to support more tailored interventions. Because the paper is a broad narrative review rather than an empirical treatment study, it does not provide new outcome effects on academic or school performance.

finding.finding_summary: The review synthesizes evidence that ADHD is associated with heterogeneous deficits in self-regulation, emotional regulation, and related behavioral functioning, but these impairments vary substantially across individuals and presentations. For example, meta-analytic and behavioral studies cited in the paper report that only a subset of individuals show deficits on key executive-function measures, and treatment responses are widely variable across patients.
finding.measure: Self-regulation, emotional regulation, executive function, response inhibition, and related behavioral profiles

finding.finding_summary: The paper reviews heterogeneous neurocognitive impairments in executive function, working memory, sustained attention, planning, and response inhibition, noting that these are common but neither necessary nor sufficient for ADHD. It cites a meta-analysis of 83 studies and reports that only about 50%–60% of individuals with ADHD were impaired on the most sensitive executive-function measures, underscoring mixed and variable findings across studies.
finding.measure: Executive function, working memory, sustained attention/vigilance, planning, and response inhibition
finding.study_size: n=83 studies (meta-analysis cited); individual samples not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The review states that ADHD is associated with educational failure and that symptoms negatively affect educational outcomes, but this is presented as background synthesis rather than a new estimate. The paper does not report a single pooled academic effect size; instead, it summarizes prior work linking ADHD with poorer school functioning and learning-related difficulties.
finding.measure: Educational outcomes / school functioning

paper_profiles.title: ADHD: Current Concepts and Treatments in Children and Adolescents
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This review synthesizes current conceptual, neurobiological, diagnostic, and treatment literature on attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) in children and adolescents. It is not an intervention trial; instead, it provides an overview of ADHD definitions, comorbidity, differential diagnosis, neuropsychological and neurophysiological findings, brain imaging and genetics, and evidence-based treatment approaches.

The treatment section reviews multimodal care, including psychoeducation, parent training, school-based supports, and pharmacological treatment. The paper emphasizes that ADHD is heterogeneous, that objective biomarkers are not ready for routine diagnosis or treatment personalization, and that assessment and treatment should be individualized and guided by specialist clinical expertise.

Regarding medication, the review states that stimulant treatment can normalize some functional brain activation patterns and may improve ADHD symptoms, while also noting that evidence for biomarker-guided prediction of medication response remains insufficient. It also distinguishes age-specific recommendations, including nonpharmacological first-line strategies for preschool children and medication use for school-age children only when impairment persists after environmental modifications.

finding.finding_summary: The review reports that stimulant medication studies have shown some normalization of dysfunctional activation patterns in critical dorsolateral frontostriatal and orbitofrontostriatal regions along with improvements in ADHD symptoms. However, it does not provide a pooled effect size or a single study estimate in this section, so the mechanism evidence is qualitative rather than quantitative.
finding.measure: ADHD symptoms and neuroimaging activation patterns

paper_profiles.title: A Review of Heterogeneity in Attention Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This review examines why attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is so heterogeneous in its causes, clinical presentation, developmental course, neurocognitive profile, and neurobiological substrates. Rather than testing a single intervention, the paper synthesizes evidence from genetic, environmental, neuroimaging, neuropsychological, and developmental studies to explain why children with ADHD differ so widely in symptoms, comorbidities, and outcomes.

A major theme is that ADHD is not a unitary condition: multiple small-effect genetic and environmental risk factors, along with their interactions, likely produce different developmental pathways. The review highlights heterogeneity in symptom profiles, treatment response, and brain/behavioral markers, and argues that existing categorical diagnostic approaches are limited for explaining these differences.

In relation to treatment, the paper notes that stimulant medications such as methylphenidate and amphetamines can reduce symptoms for many individuals, but responses vary considerably across patients in dosage needs, tolerability, and adverse effects.
