To address these issues, the paper describes three out-of-school math support programs: CyMath at Iowa State, Algebra by 7th Grade at Purdue, and Math Motivators run by the Actuarial Foundation. The programs provide tutoring/mentoring, adaptive software such as ALEKS, parent engagement, STEM enrichment, and hybrid or in-person support for grades 3-8 (and in some cases up to grade 12), with an emphasis on students from underrepresented or disadvantaged backgrounds.

The paper is not an experimental evaluation, but it includes descriptive implementation details and a few anecdotal or program-reported indicators of student progress. The main conclusions are that early and sustained math support, parent awareness, sufficient practice, and school-university partnerships may help students close foundational gaps before they become harder to remediate in later grades and college.

finding.finding_summary: The paper describes program-reported gains in math performance across several tutoring initiatives, but these are not derived from a controlled study. For CyMath, the authors report individual percentile increases on school standardized tests (e.g., one student from the 40th to 85th percentile, then 92nd; another from 20th to 38th to 60th), and for Ab7G they cite prior program work showing significant growth in mathematics proficiency among students who completed a full grade level in ALEKS each year (n=20), associated with proficiency or higher on Indiana’s ILEARN.
finding.measure: Standardized test percentiles (MAP, iReady); ALEKS mastery/progress; ILEARN proficiency

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that the programs build student self-efficacy, motivation, and persistence through mentorship, recognition of goals, parent encouragement, and fun-lab activities. However, these claims are descriptive and implementation-oriented rather than based on a formal measurement of social-emotional outcomes.
finding.measure: Program descriptions of self-efficacy, motivation, and persistence supports

finding.finding_summary: The article suggests that the programs support durable skills such as time management, collaboration, and self-regulation by pairing students with tutors, setting daily ALEKS goals, and structuring sessions around sustained practice before game time. No formal outcome assessment is reported, so this is an implementation claim rather than an evaluated effect.
finding.measure: Program design features targeting collaboration, time-on-task, and goal completion

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s central contribution is a description of university- and community-based tutoring partnerships intended to widen access to early math support and reduce inequities. It reports scaling and implementation details such as CyMath’s expansion across modes and schools and Ab7G’s growth to 208 participants by 2024, but does not evaluate institutional outcomes with a comparison design.
finding.measure: Program scale, partnership development, recruitment/retention, and access to tutoring

paper_profiles.title: Vocalnayno: Designing a Game-Based Intervention to Support Reading Development in Primary Schools
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 6th European Conference on Games-Based Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper explores whether a game-based reading activity can be integrated into primary school practice to support reading development and, importantly, provide teachers and teaching assistants with more useful assessment information than traditional paper-based records. The author frames the problem as one of inefficiency and limited diagnostic value in existing volunteer- and assistant-supported reading sessions, where feedback is often slow, fragmented, and difficult for teachers to use.

To address this, the paper proposes and prototypes "Vocalnayno," a game in which pupils read letters, phonics, numbers, and words aloud to power in-game actions. The system is intended to record oral reading performance in a database accessible to parents and teachers, while also flagging immediate concerns and helping assistants tailor support. The work uses an action-research-inspired, participatory design process with informal feedback from teaching assistants, parents, and children at a local primary school.

The paper does not report a classroom deployment or formal evaluation of learning outcomes. A small pilot with the author and one primary school pupil found that the platform's built-in voice recognition was not sufficiently accurate for the intended use, leading the author to suggest that a tailored speech-recognition approach might improve performance. Overall, the paper is best understood as a design-and-conceptualization study focused on feasibility, stakeholder acceptance, and assessment support rather than demonstrated academic impact.

finding.finding_summary: The paper is about supporting reading development, but it reports no classroom deployment or formal outcome evaluation of literacy gains. A tiny pilot with the author and one primary school pupil only revealed that the prototype's voice-recognition was not accurate enough for the system to function as intended, so there are no measured reading improvements to report.
finding.measure: reading/phonics aloud accuracy captured by the prototype
finding.study_size: n=2 (author and one primary school pupil)

finding.finding_summary: The proposed system is designed to make assessment and communication of pupil reading progress more efficient for teaching assistants, parents, and teachers by replacing paper-based records with a database-accessible game. The paper argues that this could provide quicker feedback, automatically flag concerns, and reduce the burden of managing multiple record sources, but these are design claims rather than tested effects.
finding.measure: assessment/feedback workflow, teacher-accessible progress records, proposed helper support features

paper_profiles.title: Altered Oscillatory Brain Networks During Emotional Face Processing in ADHD: An eLORETA–fICA Study
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether children, adolescents, and adults with ADHD show altered large-scale oscillatory brain-network activity during inhibitory control and emotional face-processing tasks. The authors focus on two parallel Go/NoGo paradigms: a non-emotional Visual Continuous Performance Test (VCPT) and an Emotional Continuous Performance Test (ECPT) using facial expressions. Using EEG source localization (eLORETA) combined with functional independent component analysis (fICA), they extracted ten stable cortical networks and tested group, task, and condition effects while controlling for age and sex.

The sample included 272 participants from a multicenter Swiss ADHD project (ADHD n=102; controls n=170), ages 6–60, and all participants were unmedicated on the testing day. The study found statistically reliable but small ADHD-related differences in several networks, especially a gamma-dominant inferior temporal component (IC3) that showed stronger NoGo-related activation in ADHD, plus weaker NoGo-selective effects in other components. Behavioral performance followed the expected ADHD pattern: slower reaction times, greater variability, and more commission and omission errors, with emotional trials producing larger deficits.

Overall, the authors conclude that ADHD is associated with subtle alterations in temporal, frontal, and parietal oscillatory networks during inhibitory processing, but these neural effects are modest and highly overlapping between groups. They argue that the results support a dimensional view of ADHD neurobiology rather than a categorical one, and that network-level EEG markers have limited discriminative power at the group level.

finding.finding_summary: ADHD participants showed worse performance on emotional and non-emotional inhibitory control tasks, including slower reaction times, greater reaction-time variability, and more commission and omission errors. The emotional ECPT amplified these deficits, with significant Group × Task interactions for reaction time, RT variability, and omission errors, indicating that emotional context disproportionately worsened performance in ADHD.
finding.measure: Reaction time, reaction-time variability, commission errors, omission errors on VCPT and ECPT
finding.effect_size: RT mean group ges=.05; RTvar group ges=.15; commission group ges=.03; omission group ges=.12

finding.finding_summary: The study provides evidence of impaired inhibitory control and response regulation in ADHD during Go/NoGo tasks, as reflected in behavioral errors and slower, more variable responding. These findings map most directly onto self-regulation and executive control rather than academic achievement, and they were especially pronounced under emotional conditions.
finding.measure: Go/NoGo task performance (inhibitory control), reaction-time variability, commission/omission errors

paper_profiles.title: Data Augmentation for Children’s Speech Recognition: The “Ethiopian” System for the SLT 2021 Children Speech Recognition Challenge
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of children’s speech recognition, focusing on the common mismatch between adult-heavy training data and child speech at evaluation time. The authors ask whether a range of data augmentation methods can improve automatic speech recognition (ASR) performance on the SLT 2021 Children Speech Recognition Challenge, where evaluation consists of Mandarin child reading and conversational speech.

The proposed approach combines several augmentation strategies, including pitch perturbation, speed perturbation, tempo perturbation, volume perturbation, reverberation, and spectral augmentation. The authors test these methods in two ASR toolkits: Kaldi chain models for ablation studies and ESPnet end-to-end Conformer models for the final submission. They compare tokenizer choices, feature settings, language-model rescoring, and multiple augmentation combinations, reporting character error rate (CER) on development and evaluation sets.

The population/context is children aged roughly 4-11 years old in Mandarin speech recognition, using the CSRC datasets (child reading and conversational speech) plus adult speech for augmentation. The main conclusion is that data augmentation consistently improves recognition robustness and lowers CER, especially when augmentation is tailored to child speech and combined with stronger language modeling. The final ESPnet system achieved 18.82% CER on Track 1 and 16.48% CER on Track 2 evaluation sets, with the best Kaldi post-challenge configuration reaching 13.61% CER on the dev set.

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studies children’s speech recognition performance, using character error rate (CER) as the outcome measure. Across the Kaldi experiments, data augmentation and related system improvements reduced average CER from 16.28% in the baseline to 13.61% in the best post-challenge configuration (Exp12), and the final ESPnet submission achieved 18.82% CER on Track 1 and 16.48% CER on Track 2. These results indicate improved speech recognition accuracy for child speech, with the strongest gains coming from augmentation plus rescoring/model refinements.
finding.measure: Character error rate (CER) on child reading and conversational speech recognition tasks

paper_profiles.title: Attitudes of Children with Autism towards Robots: An Exploratory Study
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This exploratory study examines whether children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) have positive attitudes toward robots and whether those attitudes, along with autism-related social impairments, are associated with how children interact with a robot versus a person. The authors frame robots as potentially useful because they are predictable and rule-based, which may align with characteristics often present in ASD.

The study used a convenience sample of 10 boys with ASD ages 6 to 14 years old (M=10.20, SD=2.64). Children completed attitude cards about robots, the Social Responsiveness Scale-2 (SRS-2), and a brief interaction comparison involving QTrobot and an equivalent interaction with a person. The main behavioral measures were gaze patterns, imitation, and repetitive/stereotyped behaviors.

Results suggested that children generally held positive attitudes toward robots and often preferred interacting with a robot over a person. More positive robot attitudes were associated with longer gazes toward the robot, while greater social impairments were associated with more repetitive/stereotyped behaviors and, for some subscales, less favorable robot-person interaction patterns. The authors conclude that these are preliminary correlational findings from a very small sample, useful mainly for identifying subgroups of children with ASD who might respond differently to robot-based interventions.

finding.finding_summary: In a small correlational study of 10 boys with ASD (ages 6-14), children reported generally positive attitudes toward robots and often preferred robots over people for interaction. Positive robot attitudes were associated with longer gaze durations toward QTrobot, while greater autism-related social impairments were linked to more repetitive/stereotyped behaviors and less favorable robot-person interaction patterns.
finding.measure: Attitude cards toward robots; gaze duration, gazes per minute, imitation, repetitive and stereotyped behaviors during QTrobot vs person interaction; SRS-2 social impairment scores

paper_profiles.title: Efficacy of behavioral classroom programs in primary school. A meta-analysis focusing on randomized controlled trials
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This meta-analysis examined whether behavioral classroom programs reduce disruptive behavior and improve on-task behavior among primary school children. The authors focused specifically on randomized controlled trials, because earlier reviews had included designs more vulnerable to bias and therefore potentially inflated effects.

The review synthesized 19 RCTs (N = 18,074) of behavioral classroom programs, including universal classroom management programs and more intensive multimodal programs that still contained a classroom behavioral component. The included studies covered children in kindergarten through elementary school, with samples spanning community, at-risk, and clinical groups, and outcomes were primarily teacher-rated disruptive behavior, teacher-rated ADHD and ODD/CD symptoms, classroom-observed disruptive behavior, and classroom-observed on-task behavior.

Results showed small but significant beneficial effects on teacher-rated disruptive behavior (d = -0.20, 95% CI [-0.29, -0.10]) and on classroom-observed on-task behavior (d = 0.39, 95% CI [0.21, 0.57]). Teacher-rated ADHD symptoms (d = -0.19) and ODD/CD symptoms (d = -0.15) also improved, with effects appearing similar across clinical, at-risk, and community samples. Effects were not moderated by age or gender, but shorter interventions tended to be more effective than longer ones. Overall, the paper concludes that behavioral classroom programs produce small, reliable benefits for disruptive behavior and engagement in primary school classrooms.

finding.finding_summary: Behavioral classroom programs produced a small but significant improvement in classroom on-task behavior among primary school children. Across 6 RCTs (N = 1,658), the pooled effect was d = 0.39 (95% CI [0.21, 0.57]), indicating better academic engagement/time on task in the intervention condition than in control conditions.
finding.measure: Classroom-observed on-task behavior / academic engagement time (AET)

finding.finding_summary: Teacher-rated disruptive behavior declined significantly following behavioral classroom programs. Across 17 studies (N = 18,074), the meta-analytic effect was d = -0.20 (95% CI [-0.29, -0.10]), a small reduction in disruptive classroom behavior relative to no treatment or treatment as usual. A sensitivity analysis excluding studies with baseline group differences still found a significant effect (14 studies, d = -0.15, p = 0.001).
finding.measure: Teacher-rated disruptive behavior

finding.finding_summary: Teacher-rated ADHD symptoms improved modestly with behavioral classroom programs. In 9 studies (N = 13,313), the pooled effect was d = -0.19 (95% CI [-0.35, -0.02]), indicating fewer ADHD symptoms in intervention classrooms. The authors also report similar beneficial effects across samples, with no clear moderation by age, gender, or severity.
finding.measure: Teacher-rated ADHD symptoms

finding.finding_summary: Teacher-rated ODD/CD symptoms also showed a small beneficial effect. Across 10 studies (N = 16,743), the pooled effect was d = -0.15 (95% CI [-0.23, -0.06]), suggesting reduced oppositional/conduct symptoms in the treatment group compared with controls.
finding.measure: Teacher-rated ODD/CD symptoms

paper_profiles.title: ADHD symptoms and learning behaviors in children with ASD without intellectual disability. A mediation analysis of executive functions
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how ADHD symptoms relate to classroom learning behaviors in children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) without intellectual disability, and whether executive functioning (EF) explains part of that relationship. The authors focus on learning behaviors that matter for classroom success, including motivation/competence, attitude toward learning, persistence on task, and strategy/flexibility, rather than on grades or test scores.

The study included 89 children ages 7 to 11 from schools in the Valencian Community, Spain: 52 children with ASD and 37 typically developing (TD) peers matched on age and IQ. Teachers rated executive functioning and learning behaviors, while parents and teachers reported ADHD symptoms. Children with ASD showed significantly higher ADHD symptoms and significantly poorer learning behaviors than TD peers. When ADHD symptoms were added as a covariate, the group differences in learning behaviors were no longer significant, suggesting that ADHD symptoms explain a substantial portion of the gap.

Within the ASD group, ADHD symptoms were negatively associated with learning behaviors and positively associated with executive function difficulties. Mediation analyses showed that the behavioral regulation index and metacognitive index of EF significantly mediated the links between ADHD symptoms and learning behaviors, especially attitude toward learning, persistence, and strategy/flexibility. The authors conclude that EF-related self-regulation and metacognition are key pathways through which ADHD symptoms affect classroom readiness and engagement in children with ASD, and they suggest that interventions should target executive functioning and learning behaviors in school settings.

finding.finding_summary: Children with ASD showed significantly poorer learning behaviors than TD peers on teacher ratings of motivation/competence, attitude toward learning, persistence on task, and strategy/flexibility. In the ASD group, ADHD symptoms were negatively associated with these learning behaviors, and the learning behavior differences between ASD and TD were no longer significant after adding ADHD symptoms as a covariate, indicating that ADHD symptoms account for substantial variance in classroom engagement-related behaviors.
finding.measure: Teacher-rated Learning Behavior Scale (Motivation/Competence, Attitude toward learning, Persistence/attention, Strategy/Flexibility; total LBS)
finding.effect_size: partial eta squared values for group differences ranged from .25 to .33; total LBS η2p=.27

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly tested metacognitive and behavioral regulation executive functions as mediators of the relation between ADHD symptoms and learning behaviors in children with ASD. Metacognition significantly mediated the association between ADHD symptoms and attitude toward learning and persistence, while behavioral regulation significantly mediated the association with strategy/flexibility; one path showed partial mediation. These findings suggest that executive functioning is a key mechanism linking ADHD symptoms to students’ ability to manage tasks, persist, and adapt strategies.
finding.measure: Teacher-rated BRIEF Behavioral Regulation Index (BRI) and Metacognitive Index (MI); mediation of ADHD symptoms predicting learning behaviors
finding.confidence_interval: Indirect effects: MI for attitude [.004, .211]; MI for persistence [.003, .225]; BRI and MI together for persistence [.026, .232]; BRI for strategy [-.450, -.128]; BRI and MI together for strategy [-.471, -.059]

paper_profiles.title: One-year trajectory analysis for ADHD symptoms and its associated factors in community-based children and adolescents in Taiwan
paper_profiles.venue: Child and Adolescent Psychiatry and Mental Health
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This prospective school-based study examined how ADHD-related symptoms change over one year in a community sample of Taiwanese children and adolescents. The authors were interested in whether inattention, hyperactivity-impulsivity, and oppositional-defiance symptoms cluster into distinct developmental trajectories, and which baseline child, family, and school factors distinguish those trajectories.

A total of 1,281 students in grades 3, 5, and 8 from Northern Taiwan were followed across four quarterly waves. Parents rated ADHD-related symptoms using the Chinese SNAP-IV, while students and parents provided baseline information on behavioral/emotional difficulties, family support, and school/home adjustment. Group-based trajectory modeling identified three symptom-severity trajectories for each domain: Low, Intermediate, and High. The High-trajectory groups were relatively small (6.9% to 12.5%) and were characterized by more externalizing problems, poorer school and home functioning, fewer prosocial behaviors, and less perceived family support.

Across symptom domains, poor school function and low prosocial behavior were the most consistent predictors of membership in the High trajectory. The authors conclude that these baseline correlates may help identify children at risk for more severe ADHD symptom patterns in school settings, although the study did not test an intervention or medication effect. The work is primarily descriptive and correlational, contributing evidence about developmental symptom trajectories rather than treatment outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: This study focused centrally on ADHD-related behavioral symptom trajectories and associated psychosocial functioning. In a prospective community sample of 1,281 students, three trajectories were identified for inattention, hyperactivity-impulsivity, and oppositional-defiance over 1 year; the High trajectories were associated with more externalizing problems, fewer prosocial behaviors, poorer school function, more home behavior problems, and less family support. The paper reports associations and trajectory group differences rather than intervention effects; no causal effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Parent-rated SNAP-IV ADHD symptom trajectories; student-rated SDQ prosocial and externalizing subscales; parent-rated SAICA school/home function; family APGAR

paper_profiles.title: Oligoantigenic Diet Improves Children’s ADHD Rating Scale Scores Reliably in Added Video-Rating
paper_profiles.extended_summary: This paper examines whether an oligoantigenic diet (OD)—a highly restricted elimination diet often discussed in ADHD treatment—reduces ADHD symptoms in children, and whether blinded video-based ratings reproduce the same symptom changes as non-blinded clinician ratings. The specific methodological question is about reliability: can external blinded raters, using pseudonymized videos of ADHD Rating Scale IV (ARS) interviews, agree with the study clinician’s ratings after the dietary intervention?

finding.finding_summary: In this uncontrolled open-label dietary intervention (n=10; complete video data for n=8), ADHD symptoms improved substantially after 4 weeks of oligoantigenic diet. The clinician-rated ARS total score decreased from 24.60±8.82 at T1 to 12.90±7.68 at T2 (F(1,9)=28.21, p<.001), with significant reductions on both inattention and hyperactivity/impulsivity subscales (p=.004 for each).
finding.measure: ADHD Rating Scale IV (total, inattention, hyperactivity/impulsivity)

finding.finding_summary: Blinded external raters reproduced the symptom improvement seen by the non-blinded clinician, supporting that the apparent reduction in ADHD symptoms was not limited to unblinded observation. In the complete-video subset (n=8), the blinded raters also showed significant pre-post improvement in ARS total scores (rater 1: F=17.19, p=.004; rater 2: F=24.5, p=.002; rater 3: F=16.2, p=.005), with very high agreement with the clinician (ICC=.996-.997; Pearson r=.992-.994).
finding.measure: Blinded video-rated ADHD Rating Scale IV total score; inter-rater reliability (ICC, Pearson r, Spearman rho)
finding.study_size: n=8 for pre-post video subset; n=33 video ratings for reliability
finding.effect_size: estimated Cohen's d=1.42 to 1.75 across blinded raters
finding.confidence_interval: ICC 95% CI reported as [.991,.998] to [.993,.998] depending on rater; Pearson r 95% CI [.984,.997] to [.988,.997]

finding.finding_summary: Parent-rated secondary behavior measures also improved after the diet. On the DISYPS-II FBB-ADHD (n=7), total ADHD symptoms dropped from 1.76±0.42 to 0.70±0.56 (F=41.56, p<.001), with significant improvements on inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity. Parent-rated ACS and CBCL/4-18 scores likewise showed significant reductions in restlessness/impulsivity, emotional lability, externalizing problems, internalizing problems, anxious/depressed symptoms, delinquent behavior, and aggressive behavior.
finding.measure: DISYPS-II FBB-ADHD, ACS, and CBCL/4-18 parent ratings
finding.study_size: n=7 to n=10 depending on measure
finding.effect_size: estimated Cohen's d=0.77 to 2.44 across subscales
finding.std_deviation: varies by scale; e.g., DISYPS-II total SD 0.42 to 0.56; CBCL total SD 5.19 to 5.50

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s main implementation finding is that blinded video-rating can reliably substitute for live non-blinded clinician rating in this context. Inter-rater agreement was extremely high across 33 videos (ICC=.996-.997; Spearman rho=.984-.989), suggesting that video-based assessment is a feasible way to reduce bias while preserving measurement consistency in small clinical ADHD diet studies.
finding.measure: Inter-rater reliability of video-rated ARS assessments (ICC, Pearson correlation, Spearman rho)

paper_profiles.title: Dual-task Coordination in Children and Adolescents with Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This case-control study examines whether children and adolescents with ADHD differ from typically developing peers on dual-task coordination, a working-memory/executive-function skill that requires simultaneously performing a verbal memory task and a motor tracking task. The authors also ask whether dual-task performance in ADHD varies by subtype (inattentive, hyperactive/impulsive, combined), by task difficulty, by administration format (computerized vs. paper-and-pencil), and by potential confounds such as general motor ability, comorbid disruptive disorders, sex, and age/education/IQ matching.

The sample included 91 children and adolescents with ADHD and 91 matched healthy controls ages 6-16. Participants completed computerized and paper-and-pencil versions of a dual-task paradigm, plus standardized measures of intelligence, ADHD symptoms, autism symptoms, disruptive behavior, and motor skills (MABC-2). Parents of ADHD participants were asked to withhold psychostimulants for 24 hours before testing, but the paper does not test medication effects as an outcome.

Overall, the study reports that dual-task coordination was broadly preserved in ADHD: children with ADHD did not differ significantly from controls on most dual-task measures, and task difficulty did not disproportionately impair ADHD performance. The paper-and-pencil version produced similar results to the computerized version, suggesting it may be suitable for educational or clinical settings. The study found some associations between computerized dual-task performance and general motor/balance ability in controls, but not in ADHD, and comorbidity and ADHD subtype generally did not explain dual-task outcomes. A small number of sex- and comorbidity-related effects appeared in exploratory analyses, but the central conclusion was that dual-task functioning is not markedly impaired in this ADHD sample.

finding.finding_summary: The primary outcome was dual-task coordination, an executive-function/working-memory skill. In the main computerized analysis, ADHD and control groups were not significantly different on List Memory performance (type of task effect only; no group effect) and the combined μ score difference was not significant (controls M=101.51, SD=10.34; ADHD M=98.43, SD=12.01; one-tailed t(179)=1.847, p<.066). On the paper-and-pencil version, neither the dual-task scores nor the μ score differed significantly between groups.
finding.measure: Dual-task coordination / executive functioning measured by computerized and paper-and-pencil dual-task performance (List Memory Task + motor tracking) and combined μ score
finding.std_deviation: Computerized μ: controls SD=10.34, ADHD SD=12.01; Paper-and-pencil μ: controls SD=9.97, ADHD SD=13.02

finding.finding_summary: The study tested whether the paper-and-pencil dual-task could substitute for the computerized version in a more practical educational/clinical format. Correlation between computerized and paper-and-pencil μ scores was modest but significant (r=.26, p<.0001), and test-retest reliability was moderate for both formats (computerized μ r=.36 overall; paper-and-pencil μ r=.37 overall). However, no significant mean differences were found between formats in either controls or ADHD, supporting functional equivalence rather than superior efficiency.
finding.measure: Agreement/reliability of computerized vs. paper-and-pencil dual-task format; correlation of μ scores; test-retest reliability
finding.effect_size: r=.26 between formats; test-retest r=.36 computerized and r=.37 paper-and-pencil

finding.finding_summary: The study directly examined whether increasing task difficulty disproportionately harmed ADHD performance. Across the various difficulty manipulations, ADHD and control groups generally showed the expected main effects of difficulty, but no robust group-by-difficulty interaction was found. The authors conclude that increased task demand did not disproportionately affect children and adolescents with ADHD compared with matched controls.
finding.measure: Dual-task performance under manipulated difficulty levels (tracking speed at .5x, 1.0x, 1.5x; digit span-2, span, span+2)

finding.finding_summary: The paper tested whether dual-task functioning in ADHD varied by subtype. Across analyses, ADHD type generally did not significantly predict computerized or paper-and-pencil dual-task μ scores, and no consistent subtype differences emerged in dual-task coordination. Some exploratory interactions involving comorbidity and sex were reported, but subtype itself was not a clear determinant of performance.
finding.measure: Computerized and paper-and-pencil dual-task μ scores by ADHD subtype (inattentive, hyperactive/impulsive, combined)
finding.study_size: n=91 ADHD total; subtype counts reported as inattentive n=21, hyperactive/impulsive n=22, combined n=48

finding.finding_summary: The study included comorbid conduct disorder/oppositional defiant disorder and asked whether these factors explained dual-task deficits. The authors report that dual-task functioning in ADHD was not defined by comorbidity factors overall, although some exploratory analyses suggested lower computerized motor performance among comorbid subgroups. The main conclusion was that comorbidity did not account for the central dual-task findings.
finding.measure: Dual-task performance by comorbidity status (CD/ODD vs. no comorbidity)
finding.study_size: n=91 ADHD total; comorbidity subgroup analyses within ADHD

paper_profiles.title: Classifying attention deficit hyperactivity disorder in children with non-linearities in actigraphy
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether actigraphy-derived movement features can help classify ADHD in children, and whether nonlinear features of motor activity are more informative than simple summary statistics. The authors analyze a week of wrist actigraphy from 29 boys aged about 10 years, divided into control, ADHD combined type, ADHD hyperactive-impulsive type, and autism spectrum disorder (ASD) groups, and compute 47 features from sleep timing, activity intensity, activity increments, return maps, Hurst exponents, duration distributions, excursion shapes, nonlinear forecasting, and Lempel-Ziv complexity.

The study uses supervised machine-learning classifiers with cross-validation to compare diagnostic performance across binary and multiclass tasks. The best-performing model was a nearest-neighbors classifier using four features, achieving 69.4% accuracy in ADHD vs control classification and 46.5% accuracy in a four-class task (control, ASD, c-ADHD, hi-ADHD), with the most informative single feature being skewness of the ZCM activity shape. The paper concludes that actigraphy is inexpensive and low-burden and may be a useful adjunctive test for ADHD differential diagnosis, especially for distinguishing ADHD subtypes, but the evidence is limited by the small male-only sample and lack of the inattentive subtype.

finding.finding_summary: The paper shows that wearable actigraphy plus machine-learning feature extraction can support automated ADHD screening/classification with modest accuracy. The best nearest-neighbors classifier using 4 features achieved 69.4 ± 1.6% accuracy for binary ADHD vs control classification and 46.5 ± 1.1% accuracy for a 4-class task (control, ASD, c-ADHD, hi-ADHD), suggesting potential utility as an inexpensive add-on diagnostic tool rather than a standalone test.
finding.measure: Cross-validated diagnostic classification accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity from actigraphy-derived features

finding.finding_summary: The authors argue that actigraphy could be incorporated into clinical diagnostic workflows to improve differential diagnosis of ADHD subtypes and reduce ambiguity in assessment. However, this is a methodological demonstration rather than an implementation study, so the institutional impact is suggested by the authors' interpretation rather than directly measured.
finding.measure: Feasibility and classification performance of actigraphy as an adjunct diagnostic test

paper_profiles.title: Classification of ADHD and Healthy Children Using Multi-Band and Spatial Features of EEG
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of accurately distinguishing children with ADHD from healthy controls using non-invasive EEG signals. The authors motivate the work as a support for early diagnosis and assessment of ADHD, noting that conventional diagnosis is challenging and that EEG may capture relevant neural differences in attention-related brain activity.

The study uses a benchmark EEG dataset containing 61 children with ADHD and 60 healthy controls, all aged 7 to 12, recorded on a 19-channel 10-20 montage during a visual attention task. The children with ADHD had been on Ritalin for up to six months, but the paper does not compare medicated versus unmedicated subgroups or analyze medication effects; medication status is only part of the sample description. The EEG was preprocessed with bandpass filtering and decomposed into delta, theta, alpha, beta, and gamma bands. From each band, the authors extracted power spectral density and spectral entropy features, then trained SVM and XGBoost classifiers.

The main finding is that SVM with an RBF kernel achieved the best reported performance, with 99.2% mean cross-validation accuracy (std. dev. 0.0079), precision of 0.98, recall of 0.99, and F1-score of 0.99. XGBoost performed slightly worse at 96.92% accuracy. The paper concludes that multi-band EEG features combined with machine learning can classify ADHD versus healthy children with very high accuracy, suggesting potential utility as a non-invasive diagnostic aid. It does not evaluate educational interventions, learning outcomes, or implementation outcomes in schools.

finding.finding_summary: The paper studies ADHD-related attention differences using EEG during a visual attention task, but it does not directly measure social-emotional or self-regulation outcomes. It uses classification accuracy as a proxy for distinguishing ADHD from healthy children, with the best model (SVM-RBF) reaching 99.2% mean cross-validation accuracy (std. dev. 0.0079) on n=121 children (61 ADHD, 60 controls).
finding.measure: EEG-based ADHD vs. healthy child classification during a visual attention task

paper_profiles.title: Excessive Screen Time is Associated with Mental Health Problems and ADHD in US Children and Adolescents: Physical Activity and Sleep as Parallel Mediators
paper_profiles.population: Children and adolescents aged 6-17 years; K-12 relevant subgroup includes ages 6-10 years
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines whether excessive screen time is associated with children’s mental health problems and ADHD, and whether physical activity and sleep-related behaviors help explain those associations. The authors used nationally representative data from the US National Survey of Children’s Health (2020-2021) and analyzed 50,231 children and adolescents aged 6-17 years.

The exposure was daily screen time, categorized as light (<2 hours), moderate (2-3 hours), and heavy (≥4 hours). Outcomes were parent-reported current anxiety, depression, behavior/conduct problems, and ADHD. The study used adjusted logistic regression, exact mediation methods, and structural equation modeling to test whether physical activity, short sleep duration, and irregular bedtime mediated the screen time-outcome relationships.

Heavy screen time (≥4 hours/day) was positively associated with all four outcomes after adjustment, including ADHD (aOR=1.17, 95% CI 1.05-1.30) and depression (aOR=1.45, 95% CI 1.32-1.58). The mediation analyses suggested that physical activity was the strongest mediator, with irregular bedtime also contributing meaningfully, while short sleep duration had a smaller role. In the parallel mediation models, the three mediators jointly explained substantial portions of the associations, including 52.04% for ADHD. Multi-group analyses indicated that mediation patterns varied by age, with physical activity and bedtime regularity especially important in older children and adolescents.

finding.finding_summary: Heavy daily screen time (≥4 hours/day) was associated with higher odds of ADHD in a nationally representative sample of US children and adolescents aged 6-17 years (n=50,231). In the adjusted logistic regression model, the odds ratio for ADHD was 1.17 (95% CI 1.05-1.30) relative to light screen time (<2 hours/day).
finding.measure: Parent-reported current ADHD diagnosis/status

paper_profiles.title: Identifying Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder through the Electroencephalogram Complexity
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether a complexity metric derived from EEG signals can distinguish boys with ADHD from typically developing peers, and whether the metric relates to DSM-IV-TR symptom severity. The authors frame the work as a methodological study: they apply q-statistics from nonextensive statistical mechanics to EEG recordings collected during a resting pretask period and during the Posner Attention Network Test (ANT).

The sample included 19 typical boys and 19 boys diagnosed with ADHD, with analyses ultimately reported on 15 boys per group after an exclusion criterion based on the fitted parameter c. EEG signals were filtered, inter-occurrence times of amplitudes crossing a threshold were modeled with a stretched q-exponential, and individual (c, q) values were estimated for each subject and condition. The authors report that ADHD boys had higher q and c values than typical boys, especially in the task condition, and that the (c, q) space formed non-overlapping clusters that separated ADHD from typical participants in the task condition.

The paper further reports that q and c showed little or no monotonic relationship with DSM inattention scores overall, though q during the pretask condition showed a moderate positive correlation with inattention (r = 0.55). The authors conclude that q-statistics may be a promising biomarker for ADHD classification and that EEG complexity appears higher in the ADHD group under these experimental conditions. However, they also caution that the clinical meaning of the q differences remains uncertain and that larger studies are needed.

finding.finding_summary: The study directly examines attention-related functioning in children with ADHD using the Posner Attention Network Test and EEG-derived complexity metrics. ADHD boys showed higher complexity than typical boys, and the task condition separated the groups well in (c, q)-space; however, the paper does not test a behavioral intervention or school-based outcome, so the finding is about diagnostic/physiological differentiation rather than improvement in self-regulation itself.
finding.measure: EEG-derived complexity parameters (c, q) during resting pretask and the Attention Network Test; DSM-IV-TR inattention and hyperactivity/impulsivity symptom counts
finding.study_size: n=30 analyzed (15 typical, 15 ADHD); originally 38 recruited
finding.std_deviation: reported for group means in Table 1, but not consistently for effect estimates

finding.finding_summary: The paper focuses on attentional control and sustained attention as measured by the Attention Network Test, which is a durable cognitive skill relevant to executive functioning. ADHD participants differed from typical peers in EEG complexity and the task condition produced stronger group separation, but the paper does not provide a direct behavioral effect size for task performance outcomes in this article.
finding.measure: Attention Network Test performance context plus EEG complexity parameters; diagnostic clustering in (c, q)-space
finding.std_deviation: reported for parameter means in Table 1, but no task-performance SDs emphasized

paper_profiles.title: Impact of EEG biofeedback on event-related potentials (ERPs) in attention-deficit hyperactivity (ADHD) children.
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines whether EEG biofeedback (neurofeedback) changes event-related potential (ERP) measures in children with ADHD. The authors focus on whether treatment affects early ERP components (N1) and later cognitive components, especially P3, which they frame as reflecting attention, selection of action, and decision making.

The sample consisted of 39 unmedicated children with combined-type ADHD, ages 10-12. Sixteen children received neurofeedback over 6 weeks (30 sessions), while 23 similar children did not receive treatment. The study used auditory oddball ERP testing before and after the treatment interval, and also measured omission and commission errors as behavioral indices of attention/impulsivity.

Results showed that neurofeedback was associated with significant improvement in later ERP components, especially shorter P3 latency and higher P3 amplitude, while effects on the earlier N1 component were absent or weaker. The treated group also showed significantly fewer omission and commission errors after treatment than the untreated group. The authors conclude that neurofeedback may improve the cognitive processes involved in attention and decision making in children with ADHD, with effects evident in P3-related measures and task performance.

finding.finding_summary: EEG biofeedback was associated with improved attention-related task performance and fewer impulsivity errors in children with ADHD. In the treated group (n=16), omission errors fell from 5.13 (SD=1.59) to 2.38 (SD=0.89) and commission errors fell from 4.5 (SD=2.31) to 0.88 (SD=0.89), with significant group-by-condition effects in ANOVA (omission: F(1,37)=19.421, partial eta squared=.344; commission: F(1,37)=37.515, partial eta squared=.503).
finding.measure: Omission errors and commission errors on auditory oddball task
finding.study_size: n=39 total; treated n=16, untreated n=23
finding.effect_size: partial eta squared=.344 (omission); partial eta squared=.503 (commission)
finding.std_deviation: treated omission SD=1.59 pre, 0.89 post; treated commission SD=2.31 pre, 0.89 post

finding.finding_summary: The intervention improved ERP markers linked by the authors to executive control, especially later cognitive processing. In the treated group, P3 latency decreased from 465.94 ms (SD=33.73) to 417.31 ms (SD=22.51), and P3 amplitude increased from 6.87 (SD=2.03) to 9.81 (SD=1.87), both with significant treatment effects (latency: F(1,37)=22.698, partial eta squared=.38; amplitude: F(1,37)=44.044, partial eta squared=.543).
finding.measure: Auditory ERP P3 latency and amplitude
finding.study_size: n=39 total; treated n=16, untreated n=23
finding.effect_size: partial eta squared=.38 (P3 latency); partial eta squared=.543 (P3 amplitude)
finding.std_deviation: treated P3 latency SD=33.73 pre, 22.51 post; treated P3 amplitude SD=2.03 pre, 1.87 post

paper_profiles.title: Cognitive characteristics of intellectually gifted children with a diagnosis of ADHD
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether intellectually gifted children with ADHD (twice-exceptional, or 2e-ADHD) show a cognitive profile that is distinct from other children with ADHD, and whether their profile suggests misdiagnosis or a genuine ADHD presentation. The authors focus on WISC-IV-based intelligence indices, especially on the contrast between general reasoning abilities (VCI, PRI, GAI) and the weaker working memory and processing speed components often seen in ADHD.

The study used archival clinical data from Italian clinicians and analyzed 1,051 children diagnosed with ADHD, of whom 82 met the giftedness criterion (GAI  125). The authors compared these children with an average-IQ ADHD group, with gifted children with SLD, and with simulated profiles based on the full ADHD distribution and normative data. They also examined whether the 2e-ADHD group differed by sex, ADHD subtype, and comorbid SLD.

The main finding is that gifted children with ADHD were overrepresented relative to what would be expected from a normal intelligence distribution, and their cognitive profile closely matched the typical ADHD pattern of strong reasoning combined with weaknesses in working memory and processing speed. The gifted ADHD group looked more similar to gifted children with SLD than to typically developing gifted children, and no meaningful cognitive differences emerged between 2e-ADHD children with and without SLD. The simulation analysis showed that the observed 2e-ADHD profile closely followed what would be expected from the broader ADHD sample, supporting the view that these cases are genuine ADHD presentations rather than misdiagnoses.

finding.finding_summary: The paper did not directly measure academic achievement outcomes, but it did assess clinically relevant cognitive abilities that are closely tied to learning performance. In the 2e-ADHD group (n=82), giftedness was associated with much higher reasoning scores (GAI=130.24, VCI=127.15, PRI=126.05) but only modest gains in working memory and processing speed (WMI=97.37, PSI=95.88), suggesting a mixed profile with likely educational strengths and weaknesses.
finding.measure: WISC-IV cognitive indices and subtests relevant to learning (VCI, PRI, WMI, PSI, GAI; subtests including Digit Span, Letter-Number Sequencing, Coding, Symbol Search)
finding.std_deviation: WMI SD=11.54; PSI SD=15.24; GAI SD=5.58

paper_profiles.title: The effect of intelligent monitoring of physical exercise on executive function in children with ADHD
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether structured physical activity can improve executive function and motor performance in children with ADHD, with a particular emphasis on comparing two exercise programs and tracking participation via smart monitoring devices. The motivation is that medication is common for ADHD but can have side effects, so the authors investigate a non-pharmacological alternative focused on exercise-based intervention.

The study randomly assigned children aged 7-10 with DSM-IV-diagnosed ADHD and no current medication or systematic behavioral intervention to one of two 12-week exercise programs or a control group. EG1 received specific skill training emphasizing catching, throwing, balance, acrobatics, juggling, and other coordination-heavy tasks; EG2 received lower-demand but more varied exercise activities such as swimming, gymnastics, climbing, track and field, and relay races; the control group continued usual activities. Working memory was measured with digit span, letter-number sequencing, vocabulary fluency, and Corsi tasks, and motor coordination was measured with the KTK test.

Results indicated that the specific skill training group (EG1) showed the clearest benefits. Short-term improvements were significant for catching/aiming tasks, with the paper reporting that 75% of children in EG1 improved versus 40% in EG2 and 30% in controls. Over the 12-week period, EG1 also showed significant gains in working memory, including digit span and letter-number sequencing, while EG2 and the control group improved less and often not significantly. The authors conclude that targeted, coordination-heavy physical activity may be more effective than general exercise for improving working memory and certain motor skills in children with ADHD, though balance and manual dexterity may require longer interventions and inhibitory control was not directly tested.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that structured physical activity may improve self-regulation-related functions in children with ADHD, particularly working memory and task engagement during motor training. In the short term, EG1 showed significant gains in catching and aiming, and over 12 weeks it showed significant improvement in working memory tasks; however, direct measures of broader social-emotional outcomes (e.g., behavior ratings, motivation, or anxiety) were not reported in the extracted results.
finding.measure: Working memory tasks and motor task performance used as proxies for self-regulation/executive functioning

finding.finding_summary: The central outcome studied is executive function, especially working memory and aspects of task switching/coordination. EG1 (n=13) showed significant improvement in digit span, letter-number sequencing, and vocabulary fluency over 12 weeks, while EG2 (n=14) and controls (n=16) showed smaller or non-significant gains; the paper also reports a 15% improvement in working memory (p<0.05) in EG1.
finding.measure: Digit span, letter-number sequencing, vocabulary fluency, Corsi square tapping, and motor coordination tasks

paper_profiles.title: VACO: a Multi-perspective Development of a Therapeutic and Motivational Virtual Robotic Agent for Concentration for children with ADHD
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents VACO, a participatory development project for a virtual robotic agent designed to support concentration training for children with ADHD. The central question is whether a digitally delivered, motivational, attention-sensitive system can translate elements of an established intensive ADHD camp intervention into a child-facing software tool, while also incorporating the perspectives of parents, clinicians, and children.

The work includes three linked sub-studies. First, an online survey of 517 parents in Germany examined willingness to use attention-support software during homeschooling, expected benefits, and concerns; about one-third said they would use it, and willingness was higher among more-stressed parents. Second, clinicians and developers refined a prototype by mapping elements of the ADHD camp to the virtual agent, especially immediate verbal feedback and a response-cost token system. Third, a feasibility/usability test with 10 children and adolescents found strong usability (SUS M=78.89, SD=11.93), with mixed reactions to fairness, feedback frequency, and the agent’s appearance. The authors conclude that AI-supported attention training is promising for ADHD, but that it must be individualized, usable, and developed through close collaboration among stakeholders.

finding.finding_summary: In the parent survey, 165 of 504 respondents (32.7%) said they would use the software, and willingness was higher among parents with higher stress levels (X²(4)=34.43, p<.001, V=0.15). In the child usability test (n=10), the system was rated usable (SUS M=78.89, SD=11.93) and about half of participants found Flobi motivating, suggesting a generally positive motivational/engagement effect rather than a strong behavioral efficacy effect.
finding.measure: Parent willingness to use software; System Usability Scale (SUS); child ratings of motivational value

finding.finding_summary: The prototype was tested during five-minute math tasks intended to mimic the ADHD camp schoolwork condition. The system delivered immediate feedback during math problem solving, but the paper reports usability and acceptability rather than achievement gains; no pre/post math performance effect size is reported. The study therefore suggests feasibility for supporting math-task engagement, not demonstrated improvement in numeracy outcomes.
finding.measure: Math task completion during prototype use

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that a virtual agent could help extend or partially replace labor-intensive ADHD camp procedures by automating immediate feedback and reducing the need for extensive staff involvement. This is framed as a potential efficiency benefit for therapy delivery and for parents during homeschooling, but it is not directly tested as an efficiency outcome in a controlled study.
finding.measure: Perceived feasibility of automating feedback and supporting homeschooling; prototype implementation of response-cost feedback
finding.study_size: n=517 parents; clinician/developer prototype work; n=10 children

paper_profiles.title: Increased Coupling in the Saliency Network is the main cause/effect of Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder
paper_profiles.population: Children and adolescents (ages 7-18); includes medication-naive and medication-exposed ADHD subgroups
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks what large-scale resting-state brain connectivity differences characterize attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), using an unbiased brain-wide association study (BWAS) rather than seed-based or ICA approaches. The authors analyzed resting-state fMRI from 502 participants in the ADHD-200 Consortium, including 249 children/adolescents with ADHD and 253 healthy controls, with primary analyses pooling data from Peking University and New York University samples.

The main finding was that the most robust ADHD-associated alteration was increased functional coupling within the salience network, especially between the left anterior insula and anterior cingulate gyrus. Additional altered connections were observed in other circuits, but these were less consistent across validation analyses; voxel-based morphometry found no corresponding gray-matter volume differences in the altered regions. The authors interpret the salience-network hypercoupling as potentially reflecting increased sensitivity to internal/external stimuli and a bias toward executive control, and they report weak or absent correlations with most clinical variables except a small IQ association for one temporal pathway.

Although the paper mentions medication status and reports that psychostimulants were withheld before scanning, it does not test medication effects as an intervention. The study therefore contributes mechanistic evidence about ADHD-related brain connectivity in a pediatric sample, but not treatment efficacy or implementation outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: The paper links ADHD to increased resting-state coupling in the salience network, especially between the left anterior insula and anterior cingulate gyrus, which the authors interpret as greater sensitivity to stimuli and altered switching between internal and executive-control states. This is a mechanistic association study rather than a behavioral intervention study; no symptom-change effect size is reported, and the clinical correlations were described as weak overall.
finding.measure: Resting-state functional connectivity (fMRI) in salience-network circuits; ADHD symptom/phenotype measures were available but weakly correlated
finding.study_size: n=502 total (249 ADHD, 253 controls); subgroup analyses in PU and NYU samples

paper_profiles.title: Simplifying Causal Mediation Analysis for Time-to-Event Outcomes using Pseudo-Values
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a statistical problem in causal mediation analysis for survival and other time-to-event outcomes. The authors argue that standard mediation approaches based on Cox proportional hazards models are difficult to interpret, mathematically inconsistent under mediation, and often unsuitable for decomposing direct and indirect effects.

To simplify analysis, they propose using pseudo-values, which convert censored survival estimands into outcomes that can be analyzed with standard linear regression or existing mediation software. The framework is developed for three estimands: survival probability, restricted mean survival time, and cumulative incidence under competing risks. The paper provides step-by-step guidance, software examples, and influence-function approximations to speed computation.

The method is evaluated in simulation studies across many scenarios, showing unbiased estimation of total, natural direct, and natural indirect effects with appropriate type-I error and coverage. A clinical example from the PARADIGMS trial in pediatric multiple sclerosis shows that the effect of fingolimod on second-year relapse is partly mediated by reduced T1-gadolinium-enhancing lesions at year 1. The authors conclude that pseudo-values provide an intuitive, additive decomposition of treatment effects for time-to-event outcomes and can support surrogate endpoint evaluation in applied research.

finding.finding_summary: The paper proposes a new methodological framework for mediation analysis with time-to-event outcomes and shows that it works across 324 simulated scenarios/estimands. Across simulations, the pseudo-value approach was unbiased for total, natural direct, and natural indirect effects and controlled type-I error at nominal levels, suggesting it is a valid analytic tool for survival mediation research.
finding.measure: Bias, type-I error, and coverage for mediation estimands (TE, NDE, NIE) across survival probability, RMST, and cumulative incidence scales
finding.study_size: 324 simulation scenarios/estimands; 10,000 simulation replicates for bias evaluation

paper_profiles.title: Attitudes of Children with Autism towards Robots: An Exploratory Study
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This exploratory study asks whether children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) have attitudes toward robots, and whether those attitudes and autism-related social impairments are associated with how children interact with a robot versus a person. The paper is motivated by the idea that robots may be especially useful in ASD interventions, but that children may differ in how much they prefer or benefit from robot-mediated interaction.

The study used a convenience sample of 10 boys with ASD aged 6 to 14 years (M=10.20, SD=2.64). Children completed a dual-attitude card task about robots, and parents completed the SRS-2 to assess autism-related social impairments. Children then engaged in brief interactions with QTrobot and with a human, and the researchers compared gazes, imitation, and repetitive/stereotyped behaviors between conditions.

Overall, children showed more positive than negative attitudes toward robots and often preferred robots in specific interaction contexts. Several positive robot attitudes were associated with longer gazes toward the robot and more time looking at the robot, while greater social impairment—especially social communication difficulties and repetitive/stereotyped behaviors—was associated with more repetitive/stereotyped behavior and less gaze toward the robot relative to the person. The authors conclude that these findings are preliminary but may help identify subgroups of children with ASD who might respond more favorably to robot-based interventions.

finding.finding_summary: Children with ASD showed generally positive attitudes toward robots (59% of choices toward robots, 32% against, 9% no preference) and often preferred robot interaction in some contexts. In brief robot-vs-person interactions (n=10), positive robot attitudes were associated with longer gazes and greater gaze duration toward QTrobot, while higher autism-related social impairment—especially social communication and repetitive/stereotyped behaviors—was associated with more repetitive/stereotyped behavior and less gaze toward the robot relative to the person.
finding.measure: Dual-attitude cards toward robots; SRS-2 social impairment scores; gaze measures and repetitive/stereotyped behaviors during QTrobot vs person interaction

paper_profiles.title: The Validity of a Machine Learning-Based Video Game in the Objective Screening of Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder in Children Aged 5 to 12 Years
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether a smartphone-based serious game, FishFinder, can objectively screen for ADHD in children by measuring in-game performance and movement activity during play. The authors argue that current ADHD screening is heavily dependent on subjective parent and teacher reports and that objective, scalable tools are needed for earlier identification and referral.

FishFinder is modeled on continuous performance tests (CPTs) and captures attention, impulsivity, and hyperactivity through game interactions, reaction times, and accelerometer/gyroscope data from the phone. The study tested the game with 52 children ages 5 to 12 years: 26 with clinically diagnosed ADHD and 26 healthy controls in Tehran, Iran. Six ADHD participants were pre-medication at the first psychiatry visit and the remaining participants were on medication but paused treatment briefly before testing; however, the paper does not report a separate medication-effect analysis.

Using support vector machine classification, the system achieved 92.3% accuracy, 90% sensitivity, and 93.7% specificity when combining in-game and movement features. Performance using only in-game features was reported as 96.1% accuracy with 90% sensitivity and 100% specificity, while movement-only features were weaker (88.4% accuracy, 80% sensitivity, 93.7% specificity). The authors conclude that FishFinder is an affordable, accessible, and engaging objective screening method for ADHD, though they note limitations related to small sample size, mixed medication status, and the lack of age- and gender-stratified analyses.

finding.finding_summary: FishFinder was able to classify children with ADHD versus controls with high accuracy, suggesting it could improve screening efficiency and reduce reliance on time-consuming subjective reports. The combined model reached 92.3% accuracy (sensitivity 90%, specificity 93.7%) in a sample of n=52 children aged 5-12.
finding.measure: ADHD screening/classification accuracy using machine-learning model (SVM) on in-game and smartphone motion features

paper_profiles.title: From homemakers to breadwinners? How mandatory kindergarten affects maternal labour market outcomes
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether mandatory kindergarten for four-year-old children changes mothers’ labour market behavior in Switzerland. The policy goal is not only child development, but also to improve compatibility between family and work by requiring kindergarten attendance earlier than in many other settings.

The authors use Swiss administrative population data linked to earnings and insurance records, along with canton-level policy information on the implementation year and birthday cutoff dates. They apply a non-parametric regression discontinuity design around the kindergarten entry cutoff, comparing mothers whose children are just old enough to enter kindergarten in the current year with mothers whose children must wait until the following year. Because kindergarten attendance itself is not observed and parents could potentially delay entry, the estimand is an intention-to-treat effect.

The paper finds no statistically significant effect in the full sample of mothers on employment or earnings. However, effects are concentrated among previously non-employed mothers: mandatory kindergarten increases their employment probability by about 4 percentage points and raises annual income from dependent employment by about CHF 1,030. The authors interpret the null overall effect as consistent with Switzerland’s already high maternal employment rate, half-day kindergarten, and possible crowding out of informal childcare. They also report no robust evidence of manipulation at the cutoff in the main sample and present heterogeneous-effects and robustness checks, including fake-cutoff and donut-RDD analyses.

finding.finding_summary: Mandatory kindergarten changed maternal labor supply only for a specific subgroup, not the full population. In the full sample of mothers, the regression discontinuity estimates are not statistically significant, but among previously non-employed mothers the policy increases employment by 4 percentage points and annual income from dependent employment by about CHF 1,030.
finding.measure: Maternal employment probability and annual income from work / dependent employment under mandatory kindergarten policy
finding.study_size: n=201,993 overall; n=179,895 previously non-employed mothers
finding.effect_size: 4 percentage point increase in employment; CHF 1,030 increase in annual income from dependent employment

paper_profiles.title: The effect of intelligent monitoring of physical exercise on executive function in children with ADHD
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether different physical activity interventions can improve executive function and motor performance in children with ADHD, motivated by concerns about the side effects and limitations of medication-based treatment. The authors specifically compare a specific-skill training program (catching, aiming, balance, coordination, juggling, etc.) with a lower-demand, more general exercise program and a no-treatment control group over a 12-week period.

The study sample consisted of children aged 7-10 years with DSM-IV-diagnosed ADHD, randomly assigned to EG1 (n=13), EG2 (n=14), or control (n=16). Outcomes were assessed with standardized working-memory measures (digit span, letter-number sequencing, Corsi block tapping, verbal fluency) and motor coordination testing (KTK). The paper reports that the specific-skill intervention produced the clearest benefits: it improved catching/aiming performance in the short term and yielded significant longer-term gains in working memory, while the lower-demand exercise group and control group showed smaller or non-significant changes. The authors conclude that targeted physical activity may be a promising non-pharmacological support for children with ADHD, and they note that smart monitoring devices were used to track adherence and progress, though no formal mediation analysis was reported.

finding.finding_summary: The intervention showed positive effects on cognitive skills that can support school functioning, especially working memory. In the 12-week trial, the specific-skill training group (EG1; n=13) showed significant improvement in digit span, vocabulary fluency, and letter-number sequencing tasks, with a reported 15% improvement in working memory on one measure (p<0.05).
finding.measure: Working memory tasks: digit span (forward/backward), letter-number sequencing (HAWIK-IV), Corsi square tapping, and vocabulary fluency

finding.finding_summary: The paper frames physical activity as improving attention, focus, and self-control-related functioning in children with ADHD, but the directly measured outcomes are mainly working memory and motor performance rather than behavioral symptoms. The intervention was associated with stronger engagement/sustained participation in EG1 as tracked by smart monitoring, but no formal engagement scale or symptom rating effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Smart-monitoring tracked activity adherence/engagement; indirect self-regulation-related executive function measures

finding.finding_summary: This is the paper’s core substantive outcome area: executive function, particularly working memory and complex coordination-related control processes. EG1 (n=13) improved significantly on digit span, letter-number sequencing, and verbal fluency after 12 weeks, while EG2 and CG showed smaller or non-significant changes; short-term gains were also seen for catching and aiming accuracy/speed.
finding.measure: Executive function / working memory tasks and motor coordination tasks (digit span, letter-number sequencing, verbal fluency, catching/aiming, balance, manual dexterity, KTK)
finding.effect_size: 15% improvement on working memory reported for EG1; other effect sizes not reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests that smart monitoring devices helped track physical activity intensity, duration, and progress in real time, enabling more tailored intervention delivery, but it does not report formal productivity, workload, or efficiency outcomes. Any operational benefit is therefore indirect and descriptive rather than experimentally quantified.
finding.measure: Real-time smart monitoring of exercise adherence/progress

paper_profiles.title: Efficient Nonparametric Estimation of Causal Mediation Effects
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper develops a new nonparametric method for estimating causal mediation effects. The central problem is how to decompose a total treatment effect into natural direct and indirect effects without relying on multiple parametric regression models for the treatment, mediator, outcome, and confounders.

The authors propose a globally semiparametric efficient estimator based on covariate-balancing calibration weights. For a binary treatment with a mediator and pre-treatment covariates, they derive weighting estimators for potential outcome contrasts and show asymptotic normality, consistency, and efficiency under sequential ignorability. They also extend the approach to multiple mediators and to the natural direct effect among the untreated. The paper is methodological and uses two empirical applications: a job training study and a political framing experiment, mainly to illustrate the estimator rather than to study K-5 educational outcomes.

No educational intervention, student sample, or K-12 ADHD medication effect is analyzed in the paper. The paper’s substantive contribution is statistical methodology for mediation analysis, with applications outside education. Because the empirical sections are not about schooling or student achievement, there are no direct K-12 outcome findings to extract for the requested education knowledge graph.

paper_profiles.title: Dual-task Coordination in Children and Adolescents with Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD)
paper_profiles.population: Elementary (PreK-5th) and Middle School / Early Adolescence (6-16 years)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines whether children and adolescents with ADHD differ from typically developing peers in dual-task coordination, a key executive-function ability involving the simultaneous management of two tasks. The authors also test whether task difficulty changes performance differently for ADHD groups, whether a paper-and-pencil dual-task is comparable to a computerized version, and whether general motor skill and comorbidity explain any observed differences.

The sample included 91 children/adolescents with ADHD and 91 age- and education-matched controls aged 6-16 years. Participants completed computerized and paper-and-pencil versions of a verbal digit-recall plus motor-tracking dual-task, with single-task and dual-task conditions, retest administrations, and manipulated difficulty levels. ADHD diagnoses and subtypes (combined, hyperactive/impulsive, inattentive) were established using DSM-IV-based ratings and multi-informant measures; children with autism symptoms, low IQ, or major neurological/physical impairments were excluded. Parents of ADHD participants were asked to withhold psychostimulants for 24 hours before testing.

Main findings were that overall dual-task coordination was broadly intact in ADHD and did not significantly differ from controls on the paper-and-pencil version; the computerized version showed small, mostly nonsignificant group differences favoring controls. Dual-task performance in controls was associated with better general motor functioning, but this relationship was weak or absent in ADHD, and comorbidity was not a strong determinant of dual-task functioning overall. The authors conclude that children and adolescents with ADHD can perform dual-task coordination adequately, and that task difficulty did not disproportionately impair ADHD participants compared with controls.

finding.finding_summary: The study directly measured dual-task coordination/central executive functioning using digit span plus motor tracking in 182 children and adolescents (91 ADHD, 91 controls). Overall dual-task coordination was available in ADHD and not significantly different from controls on the paper-and-pencil version; the computerized version showed only small, mostly nonsignificant differences favoring controls (e.g., combined μ score 101.51 vs 98.43, p<.066; motor tracking percentage change p<.057).
finding.measure: Dual-task coordination using serial digit recall plus motor tracking; combined percentage change (μ) scores

finding.finding_summary: The paper includes ADHD-related executive functioning and task performance under varying difficulty conditions, but it does not measure motivation, engagement, persistence, or self-regulation with a dedicated social-emotional instrument. Any interpretation for this category is indirect; no clear evidence was reported that ADHD versus control status meaningfully changed these outcomes.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: Altered Oscillatory Brain Networks During Emotional Face Processing in ADHD: An eLORETA–fICA Study
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examined whether adolescents, children, and adults with ADHD show altered oscillatory brain-network activity during inhibitory control tasks that include both neutral and emotional face processing. The authors used EEG source reconstruction with eLORETA combined with functional independent component analysis (fICA) to characterize distributed cortical networks during two parallel Go/NoGo paradigms: a visual continuous performance test (VCPT) and an emotional continuous performance test (ECPT).

The sample included 272 participants total (ADHD n=102, controls n=170), ages 6 to 60, and all participants were unmedicated on the testing day. The analysis identified ten stable independent components spanning temporal, frontal, parietal, and occipital regions. ADHD participants showed statistically significant but small increases in activation in several networks, especially an inferior temporal gamma component (IC3) that was stronger during NoGo trials in ADHD, plus weaker NoGo-selective effects in two other components. One task effect favored VCPT over ECPT for a middle temporal delta component, but no Group × Task interactions were found, suggesting that diagnostic differences were not strongly dependent on emotional versus non-emotional context at the network level.

Behaviorally, ADHD participants had the expected profile of slower reaction times, greater reaction-time variability, and more commission and omission errors, with the emotional ECPT exacerbating deficits. The authors conclude that ADHD-related neural differences during cognitive-emotional inhibition are reliable but modest and embedded in substantial within-group variability. They argue for a dimensional view of ADHD neurobiology and note that these EEG network markers have limited discriminative value at the group level.

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studied inhibitory control and task performance during Go/NoGo paradigms, including an emotional face-processing condition relevant to self-regulation. ADHD participants showed slower reaction times, greater reaction-time variability, and more commission and omission errors than controls (e.g., RTmean Group F=16.20, p≤.001, ges=.05; RTvar Group F=59.72, p≤.001, ges=.15; omission Group F=49.62, p≤.001, ges=.12), with the ECPT further amplifying deficits via Group × Task effects.
finding.measure: Reaction time, reaction-time variability, commission errors, omission errors on VCPT and ECPT Go/NoGo tasks
finding.std_deviation: reported in Table 3, but no single pooled SD

finding.finding_summary: The study examined response inhibition and attention control, which map most closely onto durable skills such as self-regulation and executive control. Across tasks, ADHD participants showed poorer performance than controls, including slower responses, more variable performance, and more errors; for example, the ECPT produced disproportionately worse outcomes for ADHD on reaction time, reaction-time variability, and omissions (Group × Task p<.01 to p<.001).
finding.measure: Behavioral performance on inhibitory control tasks (VCPT, ECPT)
finding.std_deviation: reported in Table 3, but no single pooled SD

finding.finding_summary: Although not a workplace study, the paper measured task efficiency in the form of speed and accuracy on repetitive Go/NoGo performance. ADHD was associated with slower responding and higher error rates than control, indicating less efficient task performance overall (e.g., RT mean Group F=16.20, p≤.001; omission Group F=49.62, p≤.001).
finding.measure: Task performance efficiency metrics: reaction time, variability, commission and omission errors
finding.std_deviation: reported in Table 3, but no single pooled SD

paper_profiles.title: Excessive Screen Time is Associated with Mental Health Problems and ADHD in US Children and Adolescents: Physical Activity and Sleep as Parallel Mediators
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether higher screen time is associated with mental health problems and ADHD in U.S. children and adolescents during the COVID-19 pandemic, and whether physical activity, short sleep duration, and irregular bedtime help explain those associations.
