The authors analyze nationally representative parent-reported data from the 2020-2021 National Survey of Children’s Health (n=50,231) and test both simple mediation models and parallel mediation models, including age-stratified analyses for ages 6-10, 11-13, and 14-17 years.

The main exposure is weekday screen time, categorized as <2 hours, 2-3 hours, and ≥4 hours per day. Outcomes include current anxiety, depression, behavior/conduct problems, and ADHD, as reported by parents/caregivers. The analysis adjusts for child demographics, family factors, insurance, nativity, language, and family resilience/connection, and uses logistic regression plus mediation methods (ExactMed and SEM/LAVAAN) to estimate direct and indirect effects.

The study finds that heavy screen time (≥4 hours/day) is associated with higher odds of anxiety, depression, behavior/conduct problems, and ADHD in adjusted models. In the ADHD model, the adjusted odds ratio for heavy screen time is 1.17 (95% CI 1.05-1.30). Mediation analyses suggest that physical activity is the strongest mediator, with irregular bedtime also contributing and short sleep duration contributing a smaller share. Across age groups, mediation patterns vary somewhat, but the general conclusion is that reducing screen time and supporting physical activity and regular sleep routines may help mitigate mental health problems and ADHD-related risk in children and adolescents.

finding.finding_summary: Daily screen time of ≥4 hours was associated with higher odds of current ADHD in adjusted logistic regression among U.S. children and adolescents aged 6-17 years (n=50,231). The adjusted odds ratio for heavy screen time versus <2 hours/day was 1.17 (95% CI 1.05-1.30), indicating a modest but statistically significant association with ADHD prevalence.
finding.measure: Parent-reported current ADHD diagnosis/condition

paper_profiles.title: Cognitive characteristics of intellectually gifted children with a diagnosis of ADHD
paper_profiles.extended_summary: This paper examines whether intellectually gifted children with a diagnosis of ADHD (“twice exceptional” or 2e-ADHD) show a distinct cognitive profile, whether they are overrepresented in ADHD samples, and whether their pattern of strengths and weaknesses supports the validity of the ADHD diagnosis. The authors use WISC-IV data from a large Italian clinical sample of 1,051 children diagnosed with ADHD, extracting an intellectually gifted subgroup defined by a General Ability Index (GAI) of at least 125 (n=82), and comparing them with average-IQ ADHD peers (n=680) and gifted children with SLD (n=129). They also simulate expected gifted profiles from the overall ADHD distribution to test whether the observed 2e-ADHD profile is simply an extreme tail of the ADHD population.

paper_profiles.title: Multidimensional Social Network in the Social Recommender System
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper studies how user interactions in a multimedia sharing system can be represented as a multidimensional social network and then used for recommending people to one another. The authors focus on Flickr and ask how different kinds of relations—direct contacts, shared tags, groups, favourites, and comments—can be extracted as separate network layers and compared over time.

The approach builds eleven relation layers from Flickr activity data and defines strength formulas for each layer. The paper then compares the layers across two snapshots (2007 and 2008) and also tests a social recommender system that uses these layers, along with system and personal weights, to generate recommendations of users to users.

The studied population is Flickr users, not a school-based sample. The recommendation experiment involved 21,640 downloaded user profiles and eight volunteers who rated recommendation lists before and after the weight-adaptation procedure. Main conclusions are that tag-based relations became increasingly dominant over time, contact and favourite/comment relations reflected more social than semantic ties, and the adaptive recommender produced higher-rated suggestions after personalization.

finding.finding_summary: The paper proposes a recommender system for suggesting people to users in Flickr and shows that the adaptive version improved recommendation quality. In the experiment with eight volunteers, users rated the second recommendation list after personalization about 8% better on average than the initial list, indicating improved usefulness of the system.
finding.measure: User ratings of recommendation lists; average rating before vs. after adaptation
finding.study_size: n=8 volunteers (with 21,640 user profiles downloaded for recommendation generation)

finding.finding_summary: The paper shows that multidimensional social network modeling can improve a social recommender system and that layer-weight adaptation changes which types of relations the system relies on. After adaptation, the social reciprocal-contact layer (Rcoc) and author-opinion layer (Rao) gained importance, while some other layers decreased, suggesting the approach can systematically reshape recommendation behavior.
finding.measure: Change in personal layer weights after adaptation; recommendation ratings

paper_profiles.title: Coordinated Behavior on Social Media in 2019 UK General Election
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper studies how to detect and characterize coordinated behavior on social media, motivated by concerns about information operations, disinformation, and coordinated inauthentic behavior. The authors argue that prior work often relies on binary thresholds that separate accounts into coordinated versus uncoordinated, which oversimplifies coordination as a phenomenon and can hide meaningful structure.

To address this, the paper proposes a network-based framework that builds a user-similarity network, filters it with multiscale backbone methods, and then performs coordination-aware community detection across increasing similarity thresholds. The approach is applied to a large Twitter dataset from the 2019 UK General Election, focused on superspreaders and politically active users. The analysis identifies multiple coordinated communities, including major Labour and Conservative clusters as well as smaller activist groups, and shows that coordination varies continuously across communities rather than being a binary property.

The paper further examines network measures, narratives, and automation indicators as coordination increases. It finds that some communities are strongly coordinated and highly clustered, while others show mixed or weaker coordination patterns; it also finds that coordination and automation are largely orthogonal. Overall, the paper concludes that a non-binary, multiscale approach provides a more nuanced and informative view of coordinated online behavior than fixed-threshold methods.

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studies coordinated behavior in the context of the 2019 UK General Election and argues that such coordination is relevant to online information manipulation and democratic processes. Using a Twitter dataset of 11,264,820 tweets from 1,179,659 users, the authors identify coordinated political and activist communities and show that coordination can be systematically surfaced and characterized with a multiscale network framework. The study does not evaluate a policy intervention, but it does provide evidence about the structure and prevalence of coordination affecting a national electoral debate.
finding.measure: Coordination patterns in Twitter user-similarity networks during the 2019 UK General Election

paper_profiles.title: The effects of gender, age and academic rank on research diversification
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether personal and organizational characteristics shape how much scientists diversify their research portfolios. The authors ask whether gender, age, and academic rank are associated with three dimensions of diversification: extent (number of topics), intensity (share of work outside the dominant topic), and relatedness (how cognitively close diversified work is to the dominant discipline).

The study uses bibliometric data on all Italian professors in the sciences with at least one Web of Science publication from 2004-2008 and a known age at the end of 2008 (n=31,101 for extent; n=26,942 for intensity; n=23,007 for relatedness). It applies OLS regressions with and without controls for total publication output, analyzing the full sample and nine disciplinary UDAs.

The main findings are that younger academics generally diversify more in extent and intensity, while higher academic rank is associated with greater diversification, especially once publication output is controlled for. Gender differences are weaker and inconsistent: men often appear slightly more diversified in simple models, but these differences largely disappear when output is controlled. Relatedness shows similarly weak explanatory power from personal traits, with very low R² values across models. The authors conclude that diversification behavior depends on the dimension analyzed and the disciplinary context, and they caution against treating diversification as a simple explanation for gender productivity gaps.

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studies research diversification as a form of scholarly output behavior and productivity pattern, including extent (ED), intensity (DR), and relatedness (RR). In the full sample of Italian science professors, diversification was common (86.6% diversified; n=31,101 for ED), with higher academic rank associated with greater diversification and younger age associated with greater diversification, but the explanatory power of personal traits was low (e.g., ED model R²=0.089 overall, rising to 0.612 when total output was added).
finding.measure: Research diversification indicators: extent of diversification (ED), diversification ratio (DR), relatedness ratio (RR)

paper_profiles.title: Measuring social spam and the effect of bots on information diffusion in social media
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This chapter-style paper examines how social bots affect information diffusion on Twitter in two settings: political communication during the 2016 U.S. presidential election and social spam campaigns in tobacco-related discussions. The author first reviews bot creation and detection methods, then applies Bot Or Not and SentiStrength to a large election-related Twitter corpus, and finally proposes a dynamical activity-connectivity map to characterize spam accounts in an e-cigarette/tobacco discussion corpus.

In the political case study, the paper analyzes 20.7 million tweets from nearly 2.8 million users and finds that bots are highly active in the conversation and retweet human and bot content at similar rates, suggesting they can effectively diffuse messages into human networks. It also reports that bot-generated pro-Trump content is especially positive, implying bots can amplify perceived grassroots support. In the spam case study, the paper analyzes over 9 million tweets and identifies distinct classes of accounts, including traditional spammers and social spam bots; the latter are characterized by more reciprocal following and network embeddedness, which helps them appear influential despite producing far more tweets than engagement they receive. Overall, the paper concludes that bots can meaningfully shape both political discourse and spam diffusion, and that sentiment and network patterns may reveal coordinated bot strategies.

The work is primarily descriptive and methodological rather than intervention-based. It combines large-scale observational Twitter data collection with bot/spam detection, sentiment analysis, and network-based characterization. The populations studied are Twitter users participating in U.S. election discussion and tobacco/e-cigarette discussions, so the paper is not K-12 focused and does not address classroom or school-level educational outcomes directly.

paper_profiles.title: Comparing Global Tourism Flows Measured by Official Census and Social Sensing
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether location-based social network data can adequately represent global tourism mobility patterns that are traditionally measured through official World Tourism Organization (WTO) survey/census-style statistics. The authors focus on comparing country-level and continent-level tourism flows extracted from Foursquare check-ins with corresponding WTO-derived tourism networks, using network science methods such as centrality rankings, strongly connected components, hierarchical clustering, cross-regional flow matrices, and motif analysis.

The study constructs directed weighted tourism graphs from Foursquare check-ins in 117 countries (April–July 2014) and compares them with WTO tourism flow data analyzed in a prior study. The paper shows that, despite some notable biases—especially Turkey’s disproportionate prominence in Foursquare and weaker representation of some African countries—the two data sources are broadly consistent for many countries and structural properties of the global tourism network. The strongest agreement appears in macroscopic and structural analyses (clusters, components, and motif patterns), while country-specific centrality rankings show more divergence for smaller or less centrally represented countries.

Overall, the authors conclude that Foursquare-based social sensing can satisfactorily approximate many aspects of global tourism mobility, especially for countries with higher social media penetration and stronger representation in the dataset. They also find that most countries have high multidimensional correlation between the two datasets, though a few countries show only moderate or negative correspondence. The paper argues that social sensing is a useful complement to traditional official statistics because it can provide global-scale, low-cost, and fine-grained mobility data.

paper_profiles.title: Attitudes of Children with Autism towards Robots: An Exploratory Study
paper_profiles.population: Elementary (PreK-5th) and Middle School (mixed child sample aged 6-14)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This exploratory study examines whether children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) hold positive attitudes toward robots and whether those attitudes, along with autism-related social impairments, are associated with how children interact with a robot versus a person. The authors focus on preference, gaze behavior, imitation, and repetitive/stereotyped behaviors during brief interactions with QTrobot and an equivalent human interaction.

The study used a convenience sample of 10 boys with ASD aged 6 to 14 years. Children completed an attitude-to-robots task, and parents completed the SRS-2 to measure autism-related social impairments. The researchers then compared children’s behavior during robot and person interactions and correlated those behavioral differences with attitudes and SRS-2 scores.

Results suggested that the children generally held positive views of robots and often preferred robots over people in several scenarios. Positive robot attitudes were associated with longer gaze toward the robot, while greater autism-related social impairments were associated with more repetitive/stereotyped behavior and, in some cases, less favorable gaze patterns in the robot condition. The authors conclude that robot-based interventions may be more suitable for some subgroups of children with ASD than others, particularly those with more positive robot attitudes and fewer social-communication/repetitive-behavior difficulties.

finding.finding_summary: In this exploratory correlational study (n=10 boys with ASD, ages 6-14), children generally showed positive attitudes toward robots and often preferred robots over people (59% of choices toward robots). Positive attitudes such as preferring to work or play with a robot were associated with longer gazes toward QTrobot and greater time looking at the robot, while higher autism-related social impairment scores were associated with more repetitive/stereotyped behaviors in the robot-vs-person comparison.
finding.measure: Children's attitudes toward robots; robot-vs-person interaction measures (gazes per minute, gaze duration, % gaze duration, imitation, repetitive and stereotyped behaviors); SRS-2 social impairment scores

paper_profiles.title: Clustering Memes in Social Media
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of identifying and clustering “memes” in social media streams, with Twitter used as the primary test bed. The authors argue that single tweets are often too sparse to cluster effectively, so they define a meme as a set of related tweets and propose a pre-clustering concept called protomemes based on hashtags, mentions, URLs, and phrases.

The study develops and compares several similarity measures over protomemes, including content, user, tweet overlap, and diffusion-based similarities, and evaluates combinations of these measures with hierarchical clustering and K-means. A manually curated dataset of 5,523 tweets about the 2012 US presidential primaries serves as ground truth, with overlapping topic labels and LFK-NMI used for evaluation.

The main conclusion is that hierarchical clustering outperforms K-means for this task, and that pre-clustering with protomemes substantially improves performance over clustering raw tweets. The best results come from combining heterogeneous similarity signals, especially through a simple pairwise maximum strategy, which performs nearly as well as a tuned linear combination without requiring prior knowledge of the ground truth. The paper’s contribution is methodological and computational: it proposes a scalable, streaming-oriented framework for meme detection rather than studying educational outcomes or interventions.

paper_profiles.title: Kernel-based causal estimators for functional causal effects
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper develops new causal inference estimators for settings where treatments, covariates, and especially outcomes can be functional or path-valued rather than scalar. The core problem is how to estimate causal effects when responses are trajectories over time, which standard ATE and regression methods handle poorly. The authors derive inverse-probability weighted Fréchet mean estimators, kernel ridge regression estimators, and operator-valued kernel estimators to estimate dynamic average treatment effects and dose-response functions in these complex spaces.

The main methodological contribution is theoretical: the paper shows consistency, convergence, and asymptotic normality results under back-door identification assumptions, and it discusses extensions for discretized trajectories, interpolation, and Fisher–Rao alignment for phase-shifted functional data. The empirical section is a simulation study plus an application to Parkinson’s disease digital monitoring data from the Parkinson@Home validation study (50 participants), where the authors estimate effects of levodopa therapy and disease status on functional digital outcomes. The paper reports that higher-dimensional, functional estimators can detect disease-related impacts that standard aggregated measures miss.

Although the application is biomedical rather than K-12 education, the paper is relevant as a causal-effect methodology paper that could be adapted to educational longitudinal or sensor-based settings. It does not study students, educators, or schooling outcomes directly, and it contains no intervention evaluation in education. Its evidence is therefore methodological rather than substantive for the education outcome map.

paper_profiles.title: ROSIE study shows positive impact of treatment
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This newsletter article summarizes first-year findings from the Research Outcomes Study in Ireland (ROSIE), a longitudinal treatment follow-up study of adult opiate users entering treatment services across Ireland. The central question is whether treatment is associated with improved outcomes for people with opiate dependence over one year, including drug use, injecting behavior, health status, social functioning, and crime.

At baseline, 404 opiate users aged 18 years or older were recruited from inpatient and outpatient treatment settings nationwide; 305 were interviewed both at intake and one year later. The article reports substantial reductions in heroin use, polydrug use, injecting, overdose, selected physical and mental health symptoms, and acquisitive crime, alongside increased service contact. Because this is an observational follow-up without a comparison group, the authors explicitly caution that the exact contribution of treatment cannot be isolated from other influences.

The paper is not a K-12 education study and does not examine learning, achievement, classroom functioning, or any mediation pathway linking medication to academic outcomes. It is a substance-use treatment outcome report focused on adult community health and social outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: The article reports that adult opiate treatment was associated with broad improvements at one year, including reductions in heroin use (81% to 48%), injecting (46% to 29%), acquisitive crime (31% to 14%), and overdose (7% to 4%) among the 305 participants followed at both time points. The authors conclude that investment in opiate treatment services produced benefits for the individual, family, and community, although they note that treatment effects cannot be isolated from other influences.
finding.measure: Treatment outcomes in drug use, health, social functioning, and crime among adult opiate users
finding.study_size: n=305 followed at both intake and 1 year

paper_profiles.title: What is essential is visible to the eye: Saliency in primary school ranking and its effect on academic achievements
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper studies whether a student’s rank within a primary school class affects later academic performance, and whether the effect operates through students’ awareness of that rank. The authors focus on Italian students and compare two ranks constructed from the same students’ grade 5 information: a visible rank based on teacher-assigned class grades that students can observe, and an invisible rank based on standardized test scores that students do not receive.

The empirical strategy uses large administrative panel data from Italian public schools, tracking several hundred thousand students from primary school through middle school and high school. The paper argues that the visible rank is much more salient to students and therefore more likely to influence perceptions, motivation, and subsequent achievement, while the invisible rank serves as a placebo. They also use a companion cohort to test whether rank is merely proxying for ability by checking correlations with earlier grade 2 test scores.

The main finding is that visible class rank has a sizeable positive association with later standardized test performance, while the invisible rank is small and usually insignificant once the authors add flexible controls and student fixed effects. A top-versus-bottom rank difference in grade 5 is associated with gains of about 8.5 percentile points in middle school and 7.7 in high school standardized test distributions. The paper also finds evidence that higher visible rank improves students’ self-esteem, perception of school, and perceived peer recognition, and that higher-ranked students are more likely to select into academically stronger high schools. No mediation analysis is presented that links rank to achievement through a formal causal pathway; the paper instead presents mechanism evidence through related survey measures and school choice behavior.

finding.finding_summary: Visible grade 5 class rank had a sizable positive association with later academic achievement. In the main specification with student fixed effects and flexible controls, ranking at the top rather than the bottom of class in primary school was associated with a gain of 8.5 percentile points in grade 8 standardized test performance and 7.7 percentile points in grade 10 performance (about 37,000 ranks nationally).
finding.measure: National standardized test percentile scores in grade 8 and grade 10
finding.study_size: n=387,614 combined across two cohorts (205,123 in 2018 cohort; 182,491 in 2019 cohort)

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that higher visible rank improved several survey-based psychosocial outcomes, including students’ interest in the subjects studied, self-esteem, perceived recognition by peers, and perceptions of school. These are described as potential mechanisms channeling the rank effect rather than as formal mediation estimates.
finding.measure: 2018 student questionnaire on self-esteem, perceived peer recognition, interest in subjects, and school perceptions (Likert-scale survey items)

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that higher-ranked primary school students self-select into high schools with significantly higher average student achievement. This is presented as an institutional/choice outcome showing that rank affects later educational sorting, not just test performance.
finding.measure: High school enrollment choice / average achievement of selected high school peers

paper_profiles.title: The Most Considered Type of Student Characteristics by Primary School Teachers
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal on Integrating Technology in Education (IJITE)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines which student characteristics primary school teachers in Indonesia consider most important when planning instruction, and whether paying attention to those characteristics is associated with better learning achievement. The authors frame student characteristics broadly, including intelligence level, motivation, cognitive style, learning style, prior knowledge, and socio-cultural background.

The study surveyed 37 class teachers from grades 4-6 across seven primary schools. Teachers completed questionnaires about which characteristics they identify and consider most, and researchers also reviewed instructional planning documents to verify how those characteristics were used in practice. Student achievement was then compared using midterm exam scores between classes whose instruction reportedly incorporated student intelligence information and those that did not.

The main finding was that intelligence level was the student characteristic most frequently identified and most strongly considered by teachers. Classes taught with attention to students' intelligence levels showed higher midterm exam averages than classes not taught that way (average 72.67 vs. 68.20; gain reported as 6% overall, with subject-level gains of 3%-10%). The paper does not report a randomized design, confidence intervals, or inferential tests, and it does not include mediation analyses; it only suggests an association between attention to intelligence-related differences and achievement.

finding.finding_summary: Instruction developed with attention to students' intelligence levels was associated with higher midterm exam achievement in primary school. In the comparison reported, the average score increased from 68.20 in classes not developed based on intelligence information to 72.67 in classes that were, with subject-level gains ranging from 3% to 10% (n=37 teachers; student-level n not_reported).
finding.measure: Midterm exam scores across Indonesian Language, Math, Social Science, Natural Science, and Art-Culture-Craft

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively focuses on teacher attention to student motivation as one of the student characteristics considered in instruction, but it does not test a motivation intervention or quantify motivational outcomes. Motivation is discussed as a characteristic related to persistence, engagement, and learning success, and teachers reported identifying it as one of the common characteristics they consider (46% usually identify it; 16% most considered), but no direct effect estimate is reported.
finding.measure: Teacher questionnaire on identifying student motivation as a characteristic

paper_profiles.title: Distance Learning in Primary School During the COVID 19 Pandemic: Results of the “SMART KIDS” Experiment
paper_profiles.venue: L-Person 2021: VI International Workshop on Professional Retraining and Life-Long Learning using ICT: Person-oriented Approach (CEUR Workshop Proceedings)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how primary school distance learning was implemented during the COVID-19 quarantine in Ukraine through the “SMART KIDS” project. The authors focus on the organizational model for distance learning in grades 1–4, built around electronic educational resources (EER) and a virtual teacher’s office, and they discuss the practical conditions needed for online teaching in primary school.

The study reports on a 2020 survey of 94 primary school teachers and involvement of 2,454 students from 12 regions of Ukraine. Teachers described how they used EER to explain new material, practice skills, and monitor independent work, as well as the technical and organizational barriers they faced, including unstable internet, limited device access, and lack of state support for digital resources.

The findings are primarily descriptive and teacher-reported. The paper concludes that EER-supported distance learning can be implemented in primary school and was positively evaluated by teachers, but that its success depends heavily on infrastructure and support. It does not present a causal evaluation of academic achievement, and it does not report mediation analyses linking any intervention to achievement through attention, behavior, or classroom functioning.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports teacher-reported support for using EER to explain new material, practice skills, and monitor student task completion in primary school distance learning. Teachers used EER continuously or periodically in 90.3% of cases; 64.9% used them to explain new material, 74.5% for additional practice, and 50% for monitoring completed tasks, but no standardized academic achievement effect was estimated.
finding.measure: Teacher survey of EER use for instruction and monitoring of student work

finding.finding_summary: The main substantive focus is on the organization and monitoring of distance learning, including the virtual teacher’s office, asynchronous/synchronous communication tools, and checking the quality of independently completed tasks. The paper suggests that these tools supported continuity of instruction and allowed teachers to assign additional tasks when students had difficulties, but the evidence is descriptive and based on teacher reports rather than measured efficiency outcomes.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported implementation of distance learning processes and task monitoring

finding.finding_summary: The paper identifies institutional and system-level barriers to primary school distance learning, including internet interruptions (27% of teachers), lack of devices for students and some teachers (24%), limited government assistance for providing EER (20%), and constrained access to computers when parents were working online. It concludes that sustained implementation depends on infrastructure, digital resources, and policy support.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported barriers and implementation conditions for school-level distance learning

paper_profiles.title: Acoustic Signatures in the Primary Microwave Background Bispectrum
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates the angular bispectrum of the primary cosmic microwave background (CMB) anisotropy as a probe of primordial non-Gaussianity. The authors derive a full-transfer-function formalism for the reduced bispectrum, compare it with the simpler Sachs–Wolfe approximation, and numerically evaluate its acoustic peak structure and signal-to-noise properties for then-forthcoming CMB experiments such as COBE, MAP, and Planck.

The approach is theoretical and simulation-based rather than an empirical study of people or institutions. The paper models a simple local non-Gaussianity parameterized by fNL, then estimates detectability of the primary bispectrum and skewness under realistic noise, beam, and cosmic-variance conditions. It also computes secondary bispectra from Sunyaev–Zel’dovich/weak-lensing coupling and extragalactic point sources to assess separability from the primordial signal.

The main conclusion is that the primary CMB bispectrum has oscillatory acoustic features that make it more powerful than skewness for detecting non-Gaussianity, and that MAP/Planck-era experiments should be able to distinguish the primary signal from secondary contaminants by shape. The paper is about cosmological signal extraction, not education, and contains no K-5 learning, classroom, or achievement outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: Sample Size Estimation using a Latent Variable Model for Mixed Outcome Co-Primary, Multiple Primary and Composite Endpoints
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a statistical design problem: how to estimate sample size for clinical trials that use mixed-outcome endpoints composed of continuous, ordinal, and binary measures. The authors build on a latent-variable framework that models discrete outcomes as thresholded versions of underlying continuous variables, allowing joint analysis of multiple endpoints measured on different scales.

The paper develops sample-size and power methods for three endpoint structures: co-primary endpoints, multiple primary endpoints, and composite responder endpoints. It derives hypothesis tests and power formulas for each case, then illustrates the methods using the MUSE trial in systemic lupus erythematosus (an adult clinical population) and simulation studies exploring how correlation structure and the components driving response affect required sample size.

Main conclusions are that the latent-variable approach can substantially improve efficiency for composite endpoints compared with standard binary analysis, especially when continuous components contribute to response and when outcomes are correlated. For the MUSE example, the authors report much smaller required sample sizes for the composite endpoint than the conventional binary method, and show that sample size behavior differs across co-primary, multiple primary, and composite settings. This paper is methodological and does not study K-12 learning outcomes, classroom functioning, or medication effects on achievement.

paper_profiles.title: Organic direct and indirect effects with post-treatment common causes of the mediator and the outcome
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a methodological problem in causal mediation analysis: how to define and identify direct and indirect effects when there is a post-treatment variable that affects both the mediator and the outcome. The author notes that standard natural direct/indirect effects typically assume no such post-treatment mediator-outcome confounder, and proposes an intervention-based alternative called organic direct and indirect effects that can accommodate this setting.

The paper develops two versions of the framework, one aligned with natural-effect style mediation and one closer to Baron and Kenny-style decomposition. It defines conditions under which an intervention on the mediator is considered “organic” and proves identification formulas for the mean potential outcomes under randomized treatment, with one formula for interventions after A=1 and another for interventions after A=0. The results show how to express these effects using observable quantities involving the outcome regression and the mediator and post-treatment covariate distributions.

The paper is methodological and does not study an education intervention, student sample, or K-12 learning outcomes. Its main contribution is theoretical: it extends mediation methods to settings with post-treatment common causes of the mediator and outcome and provides guidance for estimation and interpretation. The examples and discussion are generic and focus on causal inference applications rather than any specific educational population.

paper_profiles.title: Bounds on direct and indirect effects under treatment/mediator endogeneity and outcome attrition
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper develops a sensitivity-analysis framework for causal mediation analysis when treatment assignment, mediator choice, and outcome observation may all be endogenous, and when outcomes are missing for a nonrandom subset of cases. The authors derive bounds on natural direct and indirect effects using inverse-probability weighting perturbed by entropy-based deviations from the estimated propensity scores, and solve the resulting identification problem with linear programming.

The paper is methodological rather than an intervention study. It applies the approach to the National Longitudinal Survey of Youth 1979 (NLSY79), using adult wage outcomes for individuals aged 35 to 43 in 2000 to decompose the gender wage gap into direct and indirect components operating through mediators such as education, occupation, employment history, and related labor-market variables. The application is designed to show how sensitive the decomposition is to violations of conditional exogeneity and sample-selection assumptions.

The main conclusion is that the direct and indirect wage-gap components are often fairly robust to moderate relaxations of identifying assumptions, but certain omitted confounders—especially those affecting mediator-outcome relations or selection into employment—can widen the bounds substantially and in some specifications render effects less precise or statistically insignificant. The authors also show that the choice of link function (logit vs probit) can matter for the sensitivity bounds. No K-5 educational learning or achievement outcome is studied in this paper.

finding.finding_summary: The paper develops a general sensitivity-analysis method for mediation models with treatment, mediator, and outcome-selection endogeneity, then applies it to wage-gap decomposition. In the NLSY79 application (n=6,658), the method shows that estimated direct and indirect gender-wage components are sensitive to omitted confounding and selection assumptions, with some bounds widening enough that statistical significance can disappear under stronger relaxations.
finding.measure: Bounds on natural direct and indirect effects in a wage-gap decomposition; sensitivity of identified sets under alternative entropy parameters and link functions
finding.confidence_interval: Reported in tables as 95% subsampling CIs for bounds; exact interval varies by specification

paper_profiles.title: Exploring Programming Task Creation of Primary School Teachers in Training
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 2023 Conference on Innovation and Technology in Computer Science Education V. 1 (ITiCSE 2023)
paper_profiles.population: Adult (preservice primary school teachers in training)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates how preservice primary school teachers create Scratch programming tasks for primary school children and whether a static analysis tool, LitterBox, supports that process. The authors motivate the work by arguing that teachers often need to prepare example code for young learners, but may lack sufficient programming knowledge to produce high-quality code and task scaffolds.

The study combines a pre-study and a main A/B study with 59 teachers in training in Germany (plus 26 in the pre-study). All participants were asked to create a Scratch task package for primary school children; the treatment group used LitterBox during task creation, while the control group did not. Data included task texts, starter/solution programs, code metrics and pattern counts, and open-ended survey responses about the creation process and tool evaluation.

The main findings are that teachers in training typically began with brainstorming or programming before writing the task text, and that tool support was associated with fewer bugs and smells in the produced Scratch programs and with more hints/scaffolding in the task texts. Participants generally viewed LitterBox positively, especially for detecting code patterns and suggesting improvements, though they also noted usability and comprehension limitations and suggested features such as automatic refactoring. The paper concludes that automated analysis tools can help inform teacher training and improve the quality of educational programming tasks.

finding.finding_summary: Using LitterBox reduced the number of code issues in the Scratch tasks created by preservice teachers. In the main study (n=59; 56 programs analyzed), the treatment group inserted significantly fewer bug patterns (p=0.034, A12=0.66) and smells (p=0.022, A12=0.68), suggesting faster or more effective task-creation support through automated feedback.
finding.measure: Scratch program code quality metrics: bug pattern count, smell count, bug density, smell density
finding.effect_size: A12=0.66 for bugs; A12=0.68 for smells

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly examines teachers' task-creation procedures, including brainstorming, setting learning objectives, and iterative task design, which are metacognitive/design-oriented durable skills. The treatment group reported significantly fewer programming difficulties (p=0.038, A12=0.66), and many participants described iterative or parallel approaches to creating code and task text.
finding.measure: Self-reported task-creation procedure and reported programming difficulties

paper_profiles.title: Educational Robotics in Online Distance Learning: An Experience from Primary School
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of continuing educational robotics (ER) instruction for primary school students during Covid-19 school closures, when access to robots, programming interfaces, and in-person interaction was limited. The authors ask whether ER activities can be adapted for online distance learning in an age-appropriate way using low-tech materials and common communication tools.

The intervention is a four-week online ER activity for 13 Swiss primary school students aged 9–12, of whom 9 participated through the full sequence of tasks. The activities used a pen-and-paper simulation of Bee-Bot robots (paper triangles, grids, and programming strips) plus email/post delivery of materials, smartphone messaging, and weekly video conferences for feedback, discussion, and collaboration. Students solved 12 progressively challenging tasks from home, submitted solutions as photos, and received teacher feedback via text, audio, and video.

The paper is primarily descriptive and reflective rather than an achievement study. The reported outcomes emphasize engagement, feasibility, collaboration, and reduced screen time, with students responding positively and the approach enabling continued ER learning during closures. The authors conclude that the hybrid synchronous/asynchronous, paper-based approach can support primary-school ER online, but they explicitly note that more exhaustive studies are needed to confirm learning benefits and generalize the approach to other contexts.

finding.finding_summary: Students showed high engagement with the online ER activities and were described as eagerly awaiting the teacher’s video recordings of Bee-Bot behavior. The paper reports that students evaluated the experience as mainly positive, but no standardized engagement scale or effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Observed engagement and student/teacher evaluation of the ER online activity

finding.finding_summary: The activity was designed to foster collaboration, communication, and reflection through peer feedback in group chats, synchronous video conferences, and a delayed pen-and-paper feedback loop. The paper argues that these structures supported collaborative problem solving and reflection, but it does not report quantitative learning or skill gains.
finding.measure: Collaborative participation, peer feedback exchanges, and reflective problem-solving behavior

finding.finding_summary: Math class time was part of the context in which ER activities were implemented, but the paper does not report any mathematics achievement measure, test score, or learning outcome. Therefore, there is no empirical evidence of an effect on mathematical numeracy in this paper.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: The effect of primary school education on preventive behaviours during COVID-19 in Japan
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether hygiene education received in primary school has a lasting association with adult preventive behaviors during the COVID-19 pandemic in Japan. Specifically, the authors examine whether adults who report having been supervised by teachers to wash hands in primary school were more likely to engage in hand washing, mask wearing, or staying at home during the pandemic.

The study uses repeated monthly online survey data from the same Japanese adults across 26 waves from March 2020 to September 2022 (n=996, 25,896 observations). The key explanatory variable is retrospective report of primary-school hand-washing education, with school-uniform experience as an additional control. Ordinary least squares models with time fixed effects and demographic/economic controls are used to estimate associations with three preventive behaviors.

The main findings are that childhood hand-washing education is positively associated with hand washing and mask wearing in adulthood, but not with staying at home. The association is strongest for hand washing (coef. 0.197, 95% CI 0.126–0.267) and smaller for mask wearing (coef. 0.109, 95% CI 0.051–0.167); staying at home is not statistically significant (coef. 0.072, 95% CI -0.032–0.186). The authors conclude that school hygiene education may form durable preventive habits, but the paper does not study academic achievement, classroom functioning, or mediation pathways to learning outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that primary-school hand-washing education is associated with more sustained COVID-19 preventive behavior in adulthood, suggesting that childhood school practices can have long-run public-health effects at the population level. In the full panel analysis (n=996; 25,896 observations), the association is statistically significant for hand washing and mask wearing, but not for staying at home.
finding.measure: Adult self-reported preventive behaviors during COVID-19 (hand washing, mask wearing, staying home)
finding.effect_size: coef.=0.197 for hand washing; coef.=0.109 for mask wearing; coef.=0.072 for staying home
finding.confidence_interval: hand washing: 0.126–0.267; mask wearing: 0.051–0.167; staying home: -0.032–0.186

paper_profiles.title: A Note on Entanglement Entropy for Primary Fermion Fields in JT Gravity
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a theoretical physics note about Jackiw-Teitelboim (JT) gravity coupled to primary massless fermion fields in an asymptotically AdS2 spacetime. The authors derive equations of motion for the fermion-gravity system, solve for a particular fermion wave function outside the extremal black hole horizon, and determine the dilaton profile in the JT background.

The paper then computes two-point correlators for primary fermion fields under Weyl transformations and uses the resolvent technique to derive entanglement entropy for massless Dirac fields. First, it reviews the standard derivation in flat 2D Minkowski space, then extends the calculation to conformally flat JT gravity by rescaling the fermion field with the conformal factor. The main conclusion is an analytic expression for the renormalized entanglement entropy in JT gravity, with emphasis on its relevance for modular flow and island-based black hole information arguments.

This is a purely theoretical, field-theory/gravity paper with no human participants, no educational intervention, and no K-12 outcomes. It does not study learning, behavior, or academic achievement, and it contains no mediation analysis related to education or medication.

paper_profiles.title: Instrumental Learning in ADHD in a Context of Reward: Intact Learning Curves and Performance Improvement with Methylphenidate
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines whether children with ADHD have impaired instrumental learning and whether methylphenidate (MPH) improves learning from reward-based feedback. The authors also explored whether oppositional defiant disorder (ODD) symptoms moderated task performance. The central question was not academic achievement in the school sense, but rather whether children could learn stimulus-response mappings from informative versus probabilistic feedback in a laboratory task.

Fifty children aged 8 to 12 participated: 23 with ADHD and 27 typically developing controls. Children with ADHD completed a five-week double-blind placebo-controlled medication sequence that included baseline, placebo, low-dose MPH, medium-dose MPH, and high-dose MPH weeks. The learning task measured accuracy and response latency across four task blocks under informative and probabilistic feedback conditions.

Results showed intact learning curves for children with ADHD relative to controls: both groups improved over time, and there were no significant group differences in accuracy or latency. Exploratory analyses suggested that higher parent-rated ODD symptoms were associated with lower accuracy. MPH improved performance relative to placebo, with the clearest benefits at the high dose, yielding higher accuracy and faster responses. The study concludes that children with ADHD can learn adequately in structured reward-rich contexts, and that MPH can enhance laboratory learning performance, though the findings do not address distal academic achievement outcomes such as reading or math attainment.

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly measured instrumental learning over time, a learning/adaptation process related to self-regulation and performance adjustment. Children with ADHD showed intact learning curves versus controls (n=50 total; ADHD n=23, controls n=27), with accuracy improving over task blocks (F(3,46)=3.88, p=0.02, ηp²=.20) and response latency decreasing over time (F(1,48)=6.59, p=0.01, ηp²=.12).
finding.measure: Instrumental learning task accuracy and response latency across 4 task blocks under informative vs probabilistic feedback
finding.effect_size: ηp²=.20 for accuracy over blocks; ηp²=.12 for latency over blocks

finding.finding_summary: The study also assessed feedback-related performance sensitivity and ADHD/ODD symptom associations, which are more closely tied to self-regulation than academic achievement. Parent-rated ODD symptoms were associated with lower accuracy (e.g., ADHD+ODD subgroup M=.67 vs ADHD without ODD M=.77 and controls M=.79), while parent-rated hyperactivity/impulsivity correlated with slower latency (r=.54** with one latency-related association reported).
finding.measure: Task accuracy/latency; parent- and teacher-rated DBD ADHD and ODD symptoms
finding.study_size: n=23 ADHD for correlation analyses; subgroup n=10 ADHD+ODD, n=13 ADHD without parent-rated ODD
finding.effect_size: r=.54, r=-.46; subgroup accuracy difference reported, effect size not_reported

finding.finding_summary: Medication improved task efficiency on the laboratory learning task. Children with ADHD became faster on methylphenidate than on placebo, with a linear dose effect (Wald χ2(1)=6.30, p=0.01), and the high dose produced a significant placebo comparison (p=0.008).
finding.measure: Response latency (ms) on instrumental learning task

paper_profiles.title: Identifying resilience promoting factors and sex differences in youth with ADHD across the transition to middle school
paper_profiles.population: Elementary (5th grade) to Middle School (7th grade) youth with ADHD
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This article is a study protocol for the Resilience in Student Education (RISE) study, a two-site prospective longitudinal cohort study of youth with ADHD as they transition from fifth grade through seventh grade. The paper addresses a gap in ADHD research that has largely emphasized risks and deficits, by instead focusing on promotive and protective resilience factors that may support academic and socio-emotional functioning during the transition to middle school.

The study will recruit 300 children with ADHD, approximately equally divided by sex, from school and community settings near two academic medical centers. Using a multi-informant, multi-method design, the study will collect caregiver, teacher, and child ratings across five timepoints, plus school records and standardized academic achievement testing at baseline and seventh-grade follow-up. Measures include student engagement, motivation, social support, school connectedness, ADHD symptoms, executive functioning, behavior, grades, attendance, homework performance, and standardized achievement.

Analytically, the protocol plans latent growth curve and multivariate latent curve models with structured residuals to examine reciprocal relations between promotive factors and academic/socio-emotional outcomes, and to test whether sex moderates these associations. Medication use will be monitored and can be controlled for, but the paper does not propose a mediation analysis linking medication to achievement through attention, behavior, or classroom functioning. Because this is a protocol, it reports no empirical results; the main contribution is the planned design, measurement strategy, and analytic framework for identifying resilience-promoting mechanisms in school settings.

finding.finding_summary: This is a protocol paper and reports no results. It does specify that academic outcomes are a primary focus of the planned longitudinal study, including grades, attendance, homework performance, classroom performance, and standardized academic achievement (WIAT-4 subtests: reading comprehension, spelling, word reading, and math fluency) assessed in a sample of n=300 youth with ADHD across fifth to seventh grade.
finding.measure: Grades and school attendance; Classroom Performance Survey; Homework Performance Questionnaire; Wechsler Individual Achievement Test, Fourth Edition (reading comprehension, spelling, word reading, math fluency)

finding.finding_summary: This protocol centers on student attitudes/engagement, social support, school connectedness, and related socio-emotional functioning as core outcomes and predictors. No outcomes are reported yet; the planned sample is n=300, and the study will test reciprocal relations among promotive factors and academic/socio-emotional adjustment over five timepoints.
finding.measure: Behavioral-Emotional Cognitive School Engagement Scale; Student Subjective Wellbeing Questionnaire; Social Emotional Health Survey; Self-Regulation Strategy Inventory; Friendship Quality Questionnaire; Multidimensional Scale of Perceived Social Support; School Climate Measure; Teacher Engagement Report Form

finding.finding_summary: The protocol includes some durable-skill-related constructs, especially self-regulation, studying habits, motivation, and cognitive/behavioral engagement, but these are part of the planned measurement battery rather than reported findings. No empirical effects are available because the study has not yet been conducted.
finding.measure: Self-Regulation Strategy Inventory; Patterns of Adaptive Learning Survey-Revised; Implicit Theories of Intelligence Scale-Revised; Academic Competence Evaluation Scales

paper_profiles.title: Working Memory Training in College Students with Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder/Learning Disabilities
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This dissertation examines whether computerized working memory (WM) training can improve cognitive functioning and related academic/symptom outcomes in college students with comorbid attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder and learning disabilities (ADHD/LD). The work is motivated by evidence that WM is central to learning, attention, and academic performance, and by the possibility that WM training may produce durable gains beyond simple practice effects.

Participants were college students registered with disability services and randomized to either a Cogmed WM training program or a wait-list control group. The dissertation focuses on training gains on near-transfer WM outcomes, potential transfer to academic measures and symptom ratings, and 2-month maintenance of effects. Primary WM outcomes included WAIS-IV Digit Span and CANTAB Spatial Span; additional outcomes included self-reported ADHD symptoms, daily cognitive failures, and academic measures such as reading and math comprehension.

The main conclusion is that WM training produced significant improvement on trained/near-transfer WM measures and was associated with fewer self-reported ADHD symptoms and daily cognitive failures relative to controls. Gains in WM were maintained for at least 2 months among follow-up completers. The text also suggests that academic transfer was of interest and that reading/math comprehension were selected because of their link to WM, but the excerpt provided does not report clear strong evidence of distal academic achievement effects or mediation analyses linking symptom change to achievement.

finding.finding_summary: WM training led to significantly greater improvements on criterion WM measures in college students with ADHD/LD compared with a wait-list control. The primary near-transfer outcomes were WAIS-IV Digit Span and CANTAB Spatial Span; the abstract reports significant gains, but the excerpt does not provide exact effect sizes or confidence intervals.
finding.measure: WAIS-IV Digit Span; CANTAB Spatial Span

finding.finding_summary: Participants who received WM training self-reported fewer ADHD symptoms and fewer daily cognitive failures than the wait-list control group. These are proximal self-regulation/attention-related outcomes rather than academic achievement outcomes; the excerpt does not report exact effect sizes or sample size for these comparisons.
finding.measure: Adult ADHD self-report/symptom ratings; Cognitive Failures Questionnaire or similar daily cognitive failures measure

finding.finding_summary: The dissertation discusses reading comprehension as a theoretically relevant transfer/academic outcome and notes that reading measures were selected because of their strong link to working memory. However, in the provided excerpt, no clear statistically reported improvement in literacy/reading achievement is given; the text primarily states rationale rather than a demonstrated effect.
finding.measure: Reading comprehension / literacy outcome measures

finding.finding_summary: Math comprehension/calculation was also selected as an academic outcome because of its association with working memory, but the excerpt does not report a clear statistically significant improvement on math achievement measures. The available text emphasizes rationale and prior literature rather than a quantified math-transfer finding.
finding.measure: Math comprehension / calculation outcome measures

paper_profiles.title: Impact of EEG biofeedback on event-related potentials (ERPs) in attention-deficit hyperactivity (ADHD) children.
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether EEG biofeedback (neurofeedback) changes event-related potential (ERP) measures in children with ADHD. The authors focus on whether training alters neural markers associated with attention and decision-making, especially the P300 component, and whether it also changes error rates on an auditory oddball task.

The study prospectively compared 16 unmedicated children with ADHD who received 30 neurofeedback sessions over 6 weeks with 23 unmedicated ADHD children who did not receive treatment. Children were 10-12 years old, so the sample is elementary-aged, although the outcomes are laboratory neurophysiological measures rather than academic tests. The treated group showed significant improvements in P3 latency and amplitude and lower omission/commission errors relative to the untreated group. However, the paper does not measure reading, math, grades, or other academic achievement outcomes, and it does not report any mediation analysis linking neurofeedback to academic achievement through attention, behavior, or classroom functioning.

finding.finding_summary: EEG biofeedback was associated with improved attention-related performance on an auditory oddball task in 10-12-year-old children with ADHD. In the treated group (n=16), P3 latency decreased from 465.94 to 417.31 ms and P3 amplitude increased from 6.87 to 9.81 after 30 sessions over 6 weeks; omission errors fell from 5.13 to 2.38 and commission errors from 4.5 to 0.88. These changes were significantly better than the untreated group (n=23) for several outcomes, but the study assessed laboratory attention/impulsivity markers rather than classroom behavior or achievement.
finding.measure: ERP indices of attention/executive functioning (P3 latency/amplitude) and omission/commission errors on an auditory oddball task
finding.effect_size: partial eta squared = .858 for P3 latency, .81 for P3 amplitude, .596 for omission errors, .351 for commission errors

paper_profiles.title: Teaching Physics in the first years of Elementary School to children with ADHD
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper describes a science-fair-based learning experience developed at Colégio Pedro II in Rio de Janeiro with a small group of 8 children ages 8–12 diagnosed with ADHD. The authors’ main question is how a hands-on physics project, framed within a science, technology, and society (STS) approach, can support scientific literacy and also help stimulate executive-function-related behaviors such as planning, organizing, and prioritizing tasks.

The intervention took place in the school’s Learning Laboratory and physics lab over about six weeks. Students researched electricity and energy, built and tested batteries and circuits, created banners and a quiz-board “fabric robot,” kept a journal of their learning, and presented the project at a school science fair. The paper is descriptive rather than experimental: it reports observations that students were able to explain the circuit and energy ideas clearly and confidently during the fair, and that they appeared engaged in planning and executing the project.

The authors conclude that the experience was positive and suggest that such inclusive, interest-based science activities may help children with ADHD participate more successfully in school science and develop early physics understanding. However, the paper does not include a comparison group, formal pre/post achievement measures, or statistical analyses, so its claims are based on qualitative observation and author interpretation rather than causal evidence.

finding.finding_summary: The authors report that the eight ADHD students were able to explain how the electrical quiz board worked and showed solid understanding of energy storage and transformation during the science fair presentation. This is presented as qualitative evidence of learning science concepts, but no formal test scores, effect sizes, or pre/post measures are reported.
finding.measure: Observed explanation and demonstration of energy/electric circuit concepts during science fair presentation

finding.finding_summary: The project was intended to stimulate executive function, and the authors observed students organizing, defining, and prioritizing tasks over the six-week preparation period. They also describe the students as participating confidently and with sustained engagement, but these are informal observations without standardized behavior measures.
finding.measure: Observed executive-function-related behaviors, engagement, and confidence during project work and presentation

finding.finding_summary: The paper centers on developing planning, time management, and task organization as part of the science-fair workflow. The authors characterize the activity as a successful opportunity to exercise these durable skills, but provide no quantitative assessment or comparison condition.
finding.measure: Observed planning, prioritizing, and task-management behaviors during project completion

paper_profiles.title: Visual Attention Network
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper proposes a new computer vision backbone called Visual Attention Network (VAN) built around a novel attention module, Large Kernel Attention (LKA). The main technical question is how to obtain self-adaptive, long-range feature interactions for vision tasks without the quadratic cost and 2D-structure limitations of standard self-attention.

The authors decompose a large-kernel convolution into depth-wise convolution, depth-wise dilated convolution, and pointwise convolution to form LKA, then stack these modules in a hierarchical four-stage backbone. They evaluate VAN on a broad set of vision benchmarks, including ImageNet-1K and ImageNet-22K classification, COCO object detection and instance segmentation, ADE20K semantic segmentation, COCO panoptic segmentation, pose estimation, fine-grained classification, and saliency detection.

The paper reports that VAN generally outperforms comparable CNN, MLP, and transformer backbones at similar model scales, often with better accuracy-throughput trade-offs. However, this is a methods paper in computer vision, not an education study, and it does not examine K-5 learners, classroom outcomes, achievement, or any mediation relationship involving attention, behavior, medication, or academic achievement.

paper_profiles.title: Attention Debiasing for Token Pruning in Vision–Language Models
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (computer vision / vision-language models; no human study population)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper studies a technical problem in vision–language model (VLM) inference: attention-based visual token pruning is often misled by systematic attention bias. The authors argue that language-to-vision attention is distorted by two effects inherited from large language models—recency bias, which over-favors later visual tokens, and attention sink behavior, which inflates scores on padding tokens—causing pruning methods to keep irrelevant visual content.

To address this, they propose two lightweight, training-free debiasing steps: positional debiasing, which normalizes attention by a fitted exponential recency-bias trend, and padding attention suppression, which zeros out padding-token attention. The method is designed to be plug-and-play with existing attention-based pruning frameworks and is evaluated on multiple VLM backbones (LLaVA-v1.5-7B/13B) and several pruning methods (e.g., FastV, PyramidDrop, SparseVLM, HiMAP, TokenCarve, iLLaVA).

The evaluation is conducted on image question answering, video question answering, and related multimodal benchmarks, not on educational or K-5 learner populations. Across these benchmarks, the debiasing approach consistently improves accuracy and GPT-based scores, with the largest gains appearing when token budgets are tighter. The paper concludes that correcting attention bias can make token pruning more reliable and efficient, while also showing that both recency bias and padding-induced attention sinks are measurable and harmful to pruning performance.

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studies inference efficiency for vision–language models by improving attention-based visual token pruning. Across ten image benchmarks and three video QA benchmarks, the proposed debiasing method consistently improves pruning-based performance while keeping token budgets fixed (e.g., 128 visual tokens for images, 512 video tokens), indicating more effective token selection and less wasted computation on irrelevant tokens.
finding.measure: Vision–language benchmark accuracy / GPT-based QA score under fixed token budgets; pruning effectiveness

paper_profiles.title: A Spatio-Temporal Attention-Based Method for Detecting Student Classroom Behaviors
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of accurately detecting student classroom behaviors from video, with the goal of improving classroom status analysis and teaching efficiency. The authors argue that existing image-based and video-based classroom behavior detection methods struggle with accuracy, especially under long-tail class imbalance and multi-person occlusion in classroom scenes.

To address this, the paper proposes BDSTA, a video behavior detection model built on SlowFast and augmented with a spatio-temporal attention module (TCS3D) plus an improved focal BCE loss (FBce). The model operates on a newly constructed student classroom behavior dataset, STSCB, collected from 20 students and containing eight behavior classes such as sitting, reading/writing, raising-hand, talking, and using the phone. The study evaluates model variants using mAP, false detection rate, and missing detection rate, showing that FBce substantially improves performance over the baseline and that combining FBce with TCS3D provides the best overall results.

The paper is a technical computer-vision study rather than an educational outcomes study. Its primary endpoint is behavior detection accuracy on classroom video, not student learning, academic achievement, or instructional outcomes. The reported improvements are on detection metrics for classroom behavior classes, with no mediation analysis and no direct measurement of K-5 learning or achievement outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: The proposed BDSTA model improves classroom behavior detection efficiency and accuracy on the STSCB video dataset. Compared with the baseline SlowFast model, the best configuration (FBce + TCS3D) improved mAP from 73.61% to 82.55% and reduced missing detection rate from 12.72% to 4.66% while lowering false detection rate from 24.11% to 19.11%.
finding.measure: mAP@0.5 IOU, missing detection rate, false detection rate for classroom behavior detection

paper_profiles.title: Gated Sparse Attention: Combining Computational Efficiency with Training Stability for Long-Context Language Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the computational and training challenges of long-context language models. The authors note that dense attention is expensive at long sequence lengths, while sparse-attention methods improve efficiency but do not fix training instability or attention-sink behavior, and gated-attention methods improve stability and sink mitigation but retain quadratic cost.

To combine the strengths of both approaches, the paper proposes Gated Sparse Attention (GSA), which uses a gated lightning indexer, adaptive sparsity, and dual gating at the value and output stages. The model is evaluated in large-scale language-modeling experiments with 1.7B-parameter models trained from scratch on 400B tokens, using perplexity, downstream benchmark accuracy, long-context retrieval (RULER), sink-attention statistics, training stability, and throughput as outcomes.

Results indicate that GSA improves efficiency and model quality relative to dense, sparse-only, and gated-only baselines. It achieves substantial speedups at 128K context, lowers perplexity, improves downstream benchmark scores, reduces attention to the first token and loss spikes, and maintains strong long-context performance. The paper concludes that sparse selection and gating are complementary and that their combination yields better long-context language modeling than either method alone.

finding.finding_summary: GSA substantially improves computational efficiency in long-context inference and training. The paper reports roughly 12–16× speedup at 128K context relative to dense attention, with prefill cost reduced to 0.09× and decode cost to 0.13× of standard attention in Table 9.
finding.measure: Throughput, latency, memory at 128K context
finding.study_size: n=4 model variants (standard, sparse only, gated only, GSA)

finding.finding_summary: The model improves language modeling quality and downstream benchmark performance. Perplexity drops from 6.03 to 5.70 on WikiText-103 and from 7.82 to 7.38 on C4, while average downstream accuracy increases from 54.7 to 57.1 across five benchmarks.
finding.measure: Perplexity and downstream benchmark accuracy (MMLU, GSM8K, HumanEval, HellaSwag, C-Eval)

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports improved long-context retrieval and reasoning performance, which is closest to durable-skill style outcomes such as multi-step reasoning. RULER scores at 128K context rise from 31.7 for standard attention to 62.2 for GSA, indicating substantially better long-context retrieval/reasoning behavior.
finding.measure: RULER benchmark scores at multiple context lengths

finding.finding_summary: GSA improves training stability, which the paper operationalizes through fewer loss spikes and higher allowable learning rates. Loss spikes fall from 12.3 to 0.3 per 100K steps compared with the standard baseline, and the maximum stable learning rate increases from 4e-3 to 8e-3 in Table 8.
finding.measure: Loss spikes per 100K steps; maximum stable learning rate
finding.effect_size: loss spikes 12.3→0.3 per 100K steps; max LR 4e-3→8e-3

paper_profiles.title: First De-Trend then Attend: Rethinking Attention for Time-Series Forecasting
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates how self-attention behaves in time-series forecasting when attention is computed in different representational domains: time, Fourier, and wavelet. The authors ask whether these domains have equivalent representation power under linear attention, and whether the softmax nonlinearity changes their empirical behavior on data with seasonality, trend, and noise.

The paper introduces a new forecasting architecture, TDformer, which first decomposes an input time series into trend and seasonal components. It uses an MLP to forecast trend and Fourier-domain attention to forecast seasonality, then combines the two predictions. The work is evaluated on synthetic time-series experiments and benchmark forecasting datasets (electricity, exchange, traffic, weather, ETTm2), all in adult/computational settings rather than education settings.

The authors find that time, Fourier, and wavelet attention are mathematically equivalent under linear assumptions, but softmax creates meaningful performance differences in practice. Fourier attention is strongest for strongly seasonal and spiky data, wavelet attention helps when seasonality varies, and attention-based models are generally weak on trend extrapolation. TDformer, which separates trend from seasonality, achieves better forecasting accuracy than the compared baselines on the benchmark datasets.

paper_profiles.title: Structural Brain Asymmetries in Youths with Combined and Inattentive Presentations of Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder
paper_profiles.population: Youths / adolescents with ADHD and age-matched controls
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether structural brain asymmetries differ across ADHD presentations, specifically inattentive (ADHD-I) and combined (ADHD-C), relative to typically developing youths. The authors focus on asymmetry indices derived from structural MRI across 13 subcortical and 33 cortical regions, using volumetric, surface area, and cortical thickness measures.

The study analyzes preprocessed T1-weighted MRI data from the ADHD-200 repository, excluding medicated or medication-unknown participants and other ineligible cases, leaving n=413 youths across four sites. A linear mixed-effects model was used to compare asymmetry patterns by diagnosis and age while accounting for site heterogeneity.

Results indicate several significant differences in brain asymmetry between ADHD presentations and controls, as well as between ADHD-I and ADHD-C, with notable age-by-presentation interactions. The paper concludes that structural asymmetry differences vary by ADHD subtype and age, and that some regions may show normalization or compensatory developmental trajectories. The study is neuroimaging-focused and does not evaluate learning, academic achievement, classroom functioning, or medication effects on achievement.

paper_profiles.title: SSRepL-ADHD: Adaptive Complex Representation Learning Framework for ADHD Detection from Visual Attention Tasks
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of detecting ADHD from EEG signals collected during visual attention tasks. The authors propose a self-supervised representation learning and transfer learning framework, SSRepL-ADHD, built with LSTM and GRU layers, and compare it against a random forest baseline and a lightweight DNN variant.

The dataset consists of EEG recordings from 120 children ages 7 to 12: 60 children diagnosed with ADHD and 60 typically developing children. The ADHD group had reportedly been treated with Ritalin for up to six months, but medication effects were not analyzed as an outcome. The task was a visual attention picture-identification activity, and model performance was evaluated with classification metrics rather than educational or academic outcomes.

Results showed that SSRepL-ADHD achieved the best classification performance, with accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score all reported at 81.11%, compared with 78.01% for random forest and 73.67% for the lightweight DNN. The study concludes that the proposed architecture may be useful for ADHD detection from EEG, but it does not measure learning, classroom behavior, or academic achievement, and it does not include mediation analyses linking medication to achievement through attention or behavior.

paper_profiles.title: Grounded Text-to-Image Synthesis with Attention Refocusing
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of improving controllability in text-to-image generation when prompts describe multiple objects, attributes, or spatial relationships. The authors diagnose failures in diffusion-model cross-attention and self-attention, where tokens or pixels can attend to irrelevant regions, causing missing objects, blended attributes, or incorrect spatial composition.

They propose a training-free framework called attention refocusing that adds two losses during sampling: Cross-Attention Refocusing (CAR) and Self-Attention Refocusing (SAR). CAR encourages attention to concentrate inside the correct bounding boxes and away from background regions, while SAR discourages pixels inside each region from attending to unrelated regions. The method is applied to existing diffusion models such as Stable Diffusion, GLIGEN, Attend-and-Excite, MultiDiffusion, and ControlNet, and can also use GPT-4 to generate layouts from text prompts.

Experiments are conducted on text-to-image benchmarks including HRS, DrawBench, TIFA, COCO2014 FID evaluation, and a mask-guided dataset. Results show consistent improvements in counting, spatial composition, and attribute alignment, while largely preserving image quality. The paper is about computer vision and generative modeling rather than education, and it does not study K-5 learning outcomes, classroom functioning, or any mediation from attention/behavior to achievement.
