paper_profiles.title: Beyond Self-attention: External Attention using Two Linear Layers for Visual Tasks
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper proposes a new attention mechanism for computer vision called external attention. The authors argue that standard self-attention is computationally expensive because it has quadratic complexity in the number of input positions and only models relationships within a single sample. Their alternative uses two small, learnable, shared memory units implemented as two linear layers plus normalization, yielding linear complexity and lower memory cost.

The paper evaluates external attention across a broad set of visual tasks, including image classification, object detection, semantic segmentation, instance segmentation, image generation, point cloud classification, and point cloud segmentation. Experiments are conducted on standard computer vision benchmarks such as ImageNet, COCO, PASCAL VOC, ADE20K, Cityscapes, CIFAR-10, ModelNet40, and ShapeNet. Across these tasks, the authors report that external attention is generally comparable to or better than self-attention and several variants, while being much more efficient.

The work is methodological and does not study education, schools, learners, or instructional outcomes. It contains no K-5 learning or academic achievement endpoints, no classroom-function outcomes, and no mediation analyses relevant to education. Its conclusions are entirely about efficiency and performance in visual machine learning models.

paper_profiles.title: Differential Effects of Atomoxetine on Executive Functioning and Lexical Decision in Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder and Reading Disorder
paper_profiles.venue: Journal of Child and Adolescent Psychopharmacology
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether atomoxetine improves executive functioning and reading-related performance in children with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), reading disorder (RD), or both conditions together. The study was motivated by prior evidence that ADHD and RD share some executive-function weaknesses, and by the possibility that a medication effective for ADHD might also improve reading-related outcomes in children with RD or comorbid ADHD+RD.

The authors conducted a randomized, placebo-controlled crossover trial in 102 children aged 8–12 years, including 16 with ADHD, 20 with ADHD+RD, 21 with RD, and 26 normal controls. Children received 28 days of atomoxetine and 28 days of placebo in counterbalanced order, with neuropsychological testing at baseline and after each treatment period. Outcomes included ADHD symptom ratings, visuospatial working memory, response inhibition, and lexical decision/decoding tasks.

Atomoxetine reduced ADHD symptoms overall and produced its clearest cognitive benefit in the comorbid ADHD+RD group. In that group, atomoxetine improved visuospatial working memory and showed a marginal improvement in inhibition, but it did not improve lexical decision. The ADHD-only and RD-only groups did not show meaningful cognitive gains from atomoxetine. The findings suggest that atomoxetine’s neuropsychological effects may differ by diagnostic subgroup, with the strongest benefit observed in children who have both ADHD and reading disorder.

finding.finding_summary: Atomoxetine did not improve reading-related performance on the lexical decision task. Across groups, lexical decision accuracy (d') and decoding speed (mean reaction time for pseudowords and valid words) were not meaningfully improved by atomoxetine compared with placebo in this 28-day crossover trial.
finding.measure: Lexical decision accuracy (d'), mean reaction time for valid words, mean reaction time for pseudowords
finding.study_size: n=57-58 (task analyses; 102 enrolled, with one child missing lexical decision data and group-specific analyses varying by measure)

finding.finding_summary: Atomoxetine reduced ADHD symptom ratings across the ADHD and ADHD+RD groups. On the ADHD Rating Scale-IV, symptoms diminished compared with placebo (F[1,34]=6.91, p<0.013, partial eta squared=0.16), indicating a modest but meaningful improvement in ADHD-related self-regulation/behavioral control.
finding.measure: ADHD Rating Scale-IV parent/investigator ratings

finding.finding_summary: Atomoxetine improved visuospatial working memory, especially in the ADHD+RD subgroup. For the Corsi Block Tapping task, atomoxetine increased the number of correct sequences versus placebo (F[1,54]=8.21, p=0.006, partial eta squared=0.13), and the subgroup effect was significant only for children with ADHD+RD.
finding.measure: Corsi Block Tapping task (Number Correct Sequences)

finding.finding_summary: Response inhibition on the Stop Signal Paradigm showed no overall treatment effect, but there was a group-by-treatment interaction. Children with ADHD+RD showed faster stop-signal reaction times after atomoxetine than placebo, with a near-significant paired test (p=0.07), whereas ADHD-only and RD-only groups did not improve.
finding.measure: Stop Signal Reaction Time (SSRT) on Stop Signal Paradigm

finding.finding_summary: Although the paper focused partly on reading-related cognition, atomoxetine did not improve lexical decision, and the authors explicitly concluded that the medication did not enhance reading performance as assessed by this task. This reading-specific finding is directly relevant to school-related academic functioning but not to literacy achievement tests per se.
finding.measure: Lexical decision task (d' and reaction time for words/pseudowords)

paper_profiles.title: Differential Effects of Atomoxetine on Executive Functioning and Lexical Decision in Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder and Reading Disorder
paper_profiles.venue: Journal of Child and Adolescent Psychopharmacology
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial examined whether atomoxetine improves executive functioning and reading-related performance in children with ADHD, reading disorder (RD), or both conditions. The study was motivated by evidence that ADHD and RD share some executive-function weaknesses, and it asked whether a noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor might benefit visuospatial working memory, response inhibition, and lexical decision beyond symptom reduction.

The sample included 76 children aged 8–12 years (16 ADHD, 20 ADHD+RD, 21 RD, and 26 normal controls), recruited from outpatient clinics and community sources in the Netherlands and Belgium. Participants received 28 days of atomoxetine and 28 days of placebo in counterbalanced order, with neuropsychological testing after each period. Outcomes included ADHD symptom ratings, visuospatial working memory (Corsi Block Tapping), inhibition (Stop Signal Paradigm), and lexical decision tasks.

Atomoxetine reduced ADHD symptoms overall and improved visuospatial working memory primarily in the ADHD+RD group; inhibition showed only marginal benefit in that same group. Atomoxetine did not improve lexical decision performance and had no detectable benefit in the ADHD-only or RD-only groups on the executive-function outcomes. The findings suggest that atomoxetine may have selective neuropsychological benefits for children with co-morbid ADHD and reading disorder, but not broad reading gains.

finding.finding_summary: Atomoxetine did not improve lexical decision accuracy or speed in children with ADHD, ADHD+RD, or RD. Lexical decision accuracy (d0) and reaction times for pseudowords and valid words showed no significant placebo-versus-atomoxetine benefits; the authors concluded that reading-related performance was not influenced by atomoxetine in this sample (n=76 randomized; lexical decision n=75 with one missing child).
finding.measure: Lexical decision task: d0 accuracy, mean reaction time for valid words, mean reaction time for pseudowords
finding.study_size: n=76 randomized; n=75 for lexical decision

finding.finding_summary: Atomoxetine improved visuospatial working memory, but only in the ADHD+RD group. The primary outcome on the Corsi Block Tapping task (Number Correct Sequences) increased after atomoxetine compared with placebo, with a significant group-by-treatment interaction; the authors report the effect as specific to the ADHD+RD subgroup (n=20).
finding.measure: Visuospatial working memory: Corsi Block Tapping task (Number Correct Sequences)
finding.effect_size: Zp2=0.13 for placebo vs atomoxetine; group-by-treatment Zp2=0.16

finding.finding_summary: Atomoxetine reduced parent/clinician-rated ADHD symptom severity on the ADHD Rating Scale-IV. Across the ADHD and ADHD+RD groups, symptoms diminished after atomoxetine compared with placebo (F[1,34]=6.91, p<0.013), indicating a modest but statistically significant benefit on ADHD symptomatology in this elementary-school-age sample.
finding.measure: ADHD symptom ratings: ADHD Rating Scale-IV
finding.study_size: n=36 with ADHD or ADHD+RD for symptom analysis

finding.finding_summary: There was some evidence that atomoxetine improved response inhibition, but the effect was limited to children with ADHD+RD and did not clearly reach conventional significance. On the Stop Signal Paradigm, the ADHD+RD group showed faster stop-signal reaction times after atomoxetine versus placebo, with a nearly significant paired test (p=0.07), while the ADHD-only and RD-only groups showed no benefit.
finding.measure: Response inhibition: Stop Signal Paradigm (Stop Signal Reaction Time, SSRT)
finding.effect_size: Zp2=0.09 for the atomoxetine vs placebo contrast by group

paper_profiles.title: Cross-cultural Adult ADHD assessment in 42 countries using the Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale Screener
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines adult ADHD symptoms in a large cross-cultural sample and evaluates the psychometric performance of the Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale (ASRS) Screener across languages, countries, and gender groups. The authors analyze whether the screener shows acceptable reliability, dimensionality, and measurement invariance, and whether symptom severity and screening positivity vary by sociodemographic factors such as age, gender, socioeconomic status, and mental/physical/sexual health.

The study uses data from the International Sex Survey collected online in 42 countries, with 72,627 adults after data cleaning. The ASRS Screener showed acceptable internal consistency (α=.73, ω=.82) and a largely stable one-factor structure, with partial measurement invariance across languages and countries and partial invariance across gender. The paper also reports substantial between-country differences in screening positivity and higher ASRS scores among women and especially gender-diverse individuals, along with small negative associations with age and socioeconomic status and positive associations with self-reported mental illness and sexual problems.

Although the paper does not study medication treatment or elementary-aged children, it is relevant to ADHD subgroup differences because it reports no major measurement bias across gender, language, and country groups and provides correlational evidence of differential symptom severity by sociodemographic characteristics. The authors caution that the ASRS is a screener, not a diagnostic tool, and that the observed prevalence estimates may overstate true ADHD prevalence due to false positives and convenience sampling.

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not directly study school engagement or self-regulation in educational settings, but it does assess adult ADHD symptom severity and its associations with age, gender, socioeconomic status, and comorbid self-reported mental health problems. Higher ASRS scores were associated with worse self-rated life circumstances (r=-.10, p<.001), suggesting a small but meaningful relationship between ADHD symptoms and broader functioning; the study also found strong subgroup differences by gender (women and especially gender-diverse individuals scoring higher).
finding.measure: Adult ADHD symptom severity on the ASRS Screener; self-rated life circumstances; self-reported mental illness

finding.finding_summary: The study provides cross-cultural measurement evidence for the ASRS Screener across 42 countries and 26 language versions, which is relevant to assessment standardization and diagnostic practice. The authors report partial measurement invariance across languages and countries and partial invariance across gender, supporting cautious use of the screener in international and multicultural contexts.
finding.measure: Measurement invariance of the ASRS Screener across language, country, and gender groups

paper_profiles.title: Interventions for Substance Use Disorders in Adolescents: A Systematic Review
paper_profiles.venue: Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality Comparative Effectiveness Review No. 225
paper_profiles.population: Adolescents and young adults (primarily ages 12-20; pharmacologic studies up to 25)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This AHRQ comparative effectiveness review synthesizes evidence on behavioral and pharmacologic interventions for adolescents and young adults with problematic substance use or substance use disorders. The review was designed to inform clinicians, policymakers, and an AACAP guideline update by evaluating which interventions help reduce or stop use, improve functioning, and reduce substance-related harms.

The review included 118 randomized controlled trials and related systematic reviews, with most studies focused on alcohol and cannabis use and a smaller number on opioids and psychiatric comorbidity treatment. Behavioral interventions were grouped into brief (1–2 sessions) and nonbrief/intensive (3+ sessions) approaches, and pharmacologic studies were separated into medications for substance use disorders versus medications for psychiatric comorbidities. Meta-analyses showed that brief motivational interviewing reduced heavy alcohol use days, alcohol use days, and substance-related problems, while not reducing cannabis use days. Among intensive interventions, family-focused therapy was most effective for reducing alcohol use days, but no intervention clearly reduced cannabis use days.

For pharmacologic treatment of opioid use disorder, longer buprenorphine/buprenorphine-naloxone courses were more effective than shorter courses for abstinence and opioid-use reduction. Evidence for medications targeting alcohol or cannabis use disorders, and for medications used to treat psychiatric comorbidities, was limited. The review also reports that subgroup analyses by sex, race/ethnicity, socioeconomic status, and family characteristics were sparse or absent, limiting conclusions about differential response patterns.

finding.finding_summary: Brief motivational interviewing improved substance-use related problems in adolescents, with a standardized mean difference of 0.5 versus treatment as usual. The review notes this outcome included problems such as missing school or work or getting into trouble, and the effect was based on meta-analyzed randomized trials.
finding.measure: Substance use problem scales / substance-related problems

finding.finding_summary: Brief motivational interviewing reduced alcohol use frequency and heavy use among adolescents with problematic substance use. Compared with treatment as usual, it reduced heavy alcohol use days by 0.7 days per month and alcohol use days by 1.2 days per month in meta-analysis, indicating improved day-to-day functioning related to substance use behavior.
finding.measure: Days of heavy alcohol use; days of alcohol use

finding.finding_summary: Brief motivational interviewing reduced overall substance use problems relative to treatment as usual, consistent with improved self-regulation and reduced substance-related consequences. The review reports a standardized mean difference of 0.5 across randomized studies, but does not provide subgroup-specific estimates.
finding.measure: Overall substance use problems

finding.finding_summary: Family-focused therapy was the most effective intensive behavioral intervention for alcohol outcomes in adolescents. Across trials, it reduced alcohol use days by 3.5 days per month compared with treatment as usual, while intensive interventions did not clearly reduce cannabis use days.
finding.measure: Alcohol use days

finding.finding_summary: The review states that substance-use related problems included outcomes such as missing school or work, which are relevant to school functioning, but it did not report a separate academic outcome estimate. Brief motivational interviewing improved the composite problem scale (SMD=0.5), suggesting potential downstream benefits for school attendance or disciplinary problems, though this was not isolated as an academic endpoint.
finding.measure: Substance use problem scales (includes school/work-related problems)

paper_profiles.title: The effect of intelligent monitoring of physical exercise on executive function in children with ADHD
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether structured physical activity can improve executive function and motor performance in children with ADHD, addressing the broader problem that ADHD-related cognitive deficits can affect academic and daily functioning. The authors frame exercise as a non-pharmacological alternative or complement to medication, motivated by concerns about medication side effects and the need for safer interventions for children.

The study randomized children aged 7-10 with diagnosed ADHD into three groups: a specific skill training group (EG1), a lower-demand exercise group (EG2), and a control group, with intervention delivered twice weekly for 12 weeks. The paper used standardized cognitive and motor measures including digit span, letter-number sequencing, Corsi square tapping, and the KTK motor coordination test; it also describes use of smart monitoring devices during training. Baseline groups were similar in age and BMI, and all participants were not receiving medication or systematic behavioral intervention before the study.

Results suggest that the targeted skill-training condition produced the clearest benefits. EG1 showed immediate gains in catching/aiming tasks and longer-term improvements in working memory, including significant group-by-time effects on digit span, vocabulary fluency, and letter-number sequencing, while EG2 and the control group showed smaller or non-significant changes. Balance and manual dexterity did not improve significantly over the short intervention window. The paper concludes that targeted, coordination-heavy physical activity may improve both motor and executive function outcomes in children with ADHD, but it does not present subgroup analyses by grade band, sex, socioeconomic status, or ADHD comorbidity; it explicitly notes the need for future studies to examine subtype differences and other individual differences.

finding.finding_summary: The study reports that a 12-week specific skill training intervention improved working-memory-related cognitive performance in children with ADHD, which the authors link to learning-relevant functions rather than direct academic achievement. EG1 showed significant group × time interaction effects on digit span, letter-number sequencing, and vocabulary fluency, with 15% improvement reported for working memory in the abstract. Sample sizes were small (EG1 n=13, EG2 n=14, CG n=16), and the paper does not provide effect sizes or confidence intervals.
finding.measure: Working memory tasks (digit span forward/backward, letter-number sequencing, Corsi square tapping); vocabulary fluency task

finding.finding_summary: This was the paper's central outcome area: executive function and related cognitive control skills in children with ADHD. The specific skill training group (EG1) showed significant improvements in working memory and task-related cognitive performance after 12 weeks, including significant group × time interactions on digit span, vocabulary fluency, and letter-number sequencing, whereas the lower-demand exercise group and control group improved less. The abstract reports a 15% working-memory improvement in EG1 (p<0.05), but the paper does not report standardized effect sizes or 95% CIs.
finding.measure: Executive function / working memory tasks (digit span, letter-number sequencing, vocabulary fluency); implied cognitive flexibility and self-regulation-related performance

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses executive-function-related self-control, concentration, and engagement as important targets, and it reports improved sustained engagement in the smart-monitored specific skill training group. However, these are secondary to the main cognitive and motor outcomes, and the paper does not present direct measures of motivation, behavior, or emotional functioning beyond performance-based tasks.
finding.measure: Observed sustained engagement via smart monitoring; indirect self-regulation-related performance on executive function tasks

finding.finding_summary: The paper repeatedly states that executive function deficits in ADHD affect academic performance, but it does not directly measure grades, test scores, literacy, or school achievement. Any academic implication is indirect, inferred from improvements in working memory and related cognitive control processes rather than from an academic outcome measure.
finding.measure: Indirect academic relevance via executive function / working memory tasks

paper_profiles.title: Revitalizing Sex Education for Chinese Children: A Formative Study
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the current state of sex education for Chinese children and asks why school- and family-based sex education remains limited, restrictive, and culturally difficult to deliver. The authors are not evaluating an intervention; rather, they conduct formative research to understand stakeholder needs, barriers, and design opportunities for future sex education supports.

The study combines semi-structured interviews with 11 participants across stakeholder groups—children, young adults, parents, and education practitioners—with a qualitative content analysis of 333 Sina Weibo posts about children’s sex education in China. The context is broadly K-12, with specific attention to primary-school-aged children, junior-high students, and family settings in relatively developed regions of Eastern China, plus wider public discourse online.

Findings show that school sex education is scarce, often superficial, and constrained by exam pressure, censorship, and policy/political interference. Parents often feel embarrassed, lack pedagogical and sexuality knowledge, and struggle to answer children’s questions accurately. The paper concludes that sex education in China needs to be earlier, more comprehensive, and better supported through culturally situated approaches, including games and other educational technologies, as well as co-education of parents and children.

finding.finding_summary: The study finds that sex education in China is systemically constrained by exam-oriented schooling, political interference, censorship, and lack of institutional support. Across interviews (n=11) and 333 Weibo posts, participants described school sex education as scarce, restrictive, and often displaced by tested subjects; the paper argues that these institutional conditions prevent comprehensive sex education from being implemented.
finding.measure: Interview themes and qualitative content analysis of social media posts about school, family, and policy conditions for sex education

paper_profiles.title: Tinkering in Primary School: From Episode to Science Practice
paper_profiles.venue: The Primary School as a Playful Space
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This chapter examines how tinkering, a constructionist and playful making practice, can be integrated into primary school science learning without reducing it to a conventional, teacher-directed activity. The authors propose a model called TIDE (Tinkering, Ideas generation, Disciplinary connection, Exploration) to connect open-ended tinkering with curricular learning objectives, especially in physics education.

The paper reports on a multi-school implementation in Bologna involving 13 primary classrooms, 24 teachers, and approximately 300 students, alongside teacher questionnaires and analysis of fishbowl documentation protocols. Teachers received professional development and access to a resource library, but were largely free to choose how to connect tinkering to classroom learning. The authors find that tinkering often increased student engagement and surfaced authentic scientific questions, including questions about light and color, but teachers frequently felt unprepared to pursue those questions scientifically.

A second major finding is that tinkering changed teachers’ perceptions of students: children who struggled in conventional instruction often participated enthusiastically and took on leadership roles, while some high-achieving or highly school-oriented students experienced frustration in the open-ended setting. The authors conclude that tinkering can re-engage marginalized learners and reveal hidden strengths and vulnerabilities, but that successful integration into formal schooling requires stronger disciplinary support for teachers and more deliberate documentation practices.

finding.finding_summary: Tinkering repeatedly surfaced authentic scientific questions and supported inquiry into physics concepts such as light, color mixing, and reflection. In the reported classroom cases, students generated and pursued research questions during workshops, but the paper does not provide quantitative effect sizes for learning gains; the evidence is qualitative and based on teacher documentation and fishbowl protocol analysis (n=20 teachers; approximately 300 students in the broader project).
finding.measure: Teacher reports, fishbowl documentation, classroom observations of scientific questioning and inquiry

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that tinkering increased student engagement, participation, motivation, and cooperative behavior, especially after the post-pandemic period when students had struggled with collaboration. In the questionnaire, 70% of teachers said tinkering revealed unexpected or partially expected behaviors, often noting that previously disengaged students became enthusiastic and that even reluctant students participated more actively.
finding.measure: Teacher questionnaire responses about engagement, participation, motivation, collaboration, and classroom behavior

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests that tinkering supported collaboration, shared problem solving, and the development of agency and perseverance in the face of frustration. Teachers noted that students learned to manage failure, focus on process, and work in pairs or groups more effectively, though some school-oriented students initially experienced setbacks in the open-ended task.
finding.measure: Teacher narrative responses coded into themes about collaboration, frustration tolerance, agency, and persistence

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that tinkering can become part of formal primary schooling through the TIDE model, but only if schools provide methodological support, documentation structures, and disciplinary preparation for teachers. The study also suggests that documentation practices like fishbowl protocols can help make learning visible and guide future co-design, although the implementation was constrained by pandemic-related disruptions.
finding.measure: Implementation experience with TIDE, teacher feedback on integration into curriculum, documentation protocol use

paper_profiles.title: Comparison of the Gamma-Ray Burst Sensitivity of Different Detectors
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how to compare the sensitivity of different gamma-ray burst detectors using a common, instrument-independent metric. The author argues that detector teams report thresholds in inconsistent energy bands and with different burst-intensity measures, which makes it difficult to compare which burst populations different missions can detect.

The paper proposes using the threshold peak photon flux integrated over 1–1000 keV, paired with the burst spectral peak energy Ep, and derives a method for calculating the threshold flux FT as a function of Ep for a given detector and trigger configuration. The approach is then applied to several missions and instruments, including BATSE, BeppoSAX WFC and GRBM, HETE-2 WXM and FREGATE, Swift BAT, GLAST GBM, and proposed EXIST.

Using published detector areas, efficiencies, mask open fractions, backgrounds, and trigger thresholds, the paper compares maximum sensitivity curves across instruments. The main conclusion is that low-energy-sensitive detectors such as Swift BAT, FREGATE, and EXIST are better for soft bursts, while BATSE and GBM are less sensitive to low-Ep bursts; the paper also shows that trigger energy band and detector efficiency strongly shape relative sensitivity.

paper_profiles.title: Impact of EEG biofeedback on event-related potentials (ERPs) in attention-deficit hyperactivity (ADHD) children
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines whether EEG biofeedback (neurofeedback) changes event-related potential (ERP) measures and response-error performance in children with ADHD. The authors focus on whether treatment alters early ERP components (N1) and later cognitive components (P3/P300), which they interpret as reflecting attention, selection of action, and decision making.

The study prospectively included 39 unmedicated children with combined-type ADHD aged 10-12 years. Sixteen children received 6 weeks of neurofeedback (30 sessions), while 23 comparable children did not receive treatment. ERP recordings and omission/commission error rates were collected before and after the treatment interval. The design is nonrandomized and compares a treated subgroup with an untreated subgroup, making it a quasi-experimental comparison rather than an RCT.

Results showed improvements in the treated group on later ERP measures: P3 latency decreased and P3 amplitude increased after neurofeedback, and omission and commission errors also improved. The untreated group showed some time-related changes as well, but treatment-by-condition interactions were significant for several outcomes, especially P3 latency, P3 amplitude, omission errors, and commission errors. The authors conclude that neurofeedback can affect later stages of cognitive processing in children with ADHD, particularly processes related to action selection and decision making. The paper does not report subgroup analyses by sex, socioeconomic status, comorbidity, or grade band beyond a narrow age range; it also does not study academic achievement directly.

finding.finding_summary: Neurofeedback was associated with improved attention-related performance in children with ADHD. In the treated group (n=16), omission errors decreased from M=5.13 (SD=1.59) to M=2.38 (SD=0.89) and commission errors decreased from M=4.5 (SD=2.31) to M=0.88 (SD=0.89) after 6 weeks; both treatment-by-condition interactions were significant (omission errors F(1,37)=19.421, p<.0001, partial eta squared=.344; commission errors F(1,37)=37.515, p<.0001, partial eta squared=.503). These outcomes reflect changes in attention/impulsivity and task performance rather than academic tests.
finding.measure: Omission errors and commission errors on auditory oddball ERP task
finding.effect_size: partial eta squared=.344 (omission errors), partial eta squared=.503 (commission errors)
finding.std_deviation: treated: omission SD pre=1.59, post=0.89; commission SD pre=2.31, post=0.89

finding.finding_summary: The intervention improved ERP markers the authors interpret as reflecting cognitive control, action selection, and decision making. In the treated group (n=16), P3 latency decreased from M=465.94 ms (SD=33.73) to M=417.31 ms (SD=22.51), and P3 amplitude increased from M=6.87 (SD=2.03) to M=9.81 (SD=1.87) after neurofeedback; treatment-by-condition interactions were significant for both outcomes (latency F(1,37)=22.698, p<.0001, partial eta squared=.38; amplitude F(1,37)=44.044, p<.0001, partial eta squared=.543). These are physiological proxies for attentional resource allocation and executive processing, not direct academic performance measures.
finding.measure: ERP P3 latency and amplitude during auditory oddball task
finding.effect_size: partial eta squared=.38 (P3 latency), partial eta squared=.543 (P3 amplitude)
finding.std_deviation: treated: P3 latency SD pre=33.73, post=22.51; P3 amplitude SD pre=2.03, post=1.87

paper_profiles.title: When Children Program Intelligent Environments: Lessons Learned from a Serious AR Game
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether children aged 7-12 can understand and program an Intelligent Environment (IE) using a serious augmented-reality game called MagiPlay. The research asks two main questions: whether children comprehend the concept of IEs and whether they can create trigger-action rules that control smart artifacts in the environment.

The intervention/approach is a block-based, gamified AR spatial coding prototype in an Intelligent Living Room simulation. Fifteen children interacted with four progressively harder levels requiring them to create and deploy trigger-action rules such as turning off lights when a door closes or controlling multiple devices with AND logic. The study used observation, behavioral notes, interaction-error tracking, and post-session questions to gather qualitative and quantitative evidence.

The authors report that all children were able to complete the tasks, with only a small number of errors and minimal help, suggesting that the trigger-action/block-based paradigm was understandable for this age group. Children also appeared engaged and enthusiastic, and many could transfer the idea to their own homes. The paper concludes that children 7-12 can understand and program IEs, and that AR plus gamified block-based programming may be a promising approach for child-facing end-user programming tools. The study is exploratory and emphasizes design implications rather than controlled causal effects.

finding.finding_summary: Children showed high engagement, enjoyment, and motivation while using the game-based AR system. The authors report that 70% of children requested to play again after the session, and observers noted smiles, excitement, and no clear signs of boredom or frustration.
finding.measure: Observer notes, post-study comments, and requests to replay the game

finding.finding_summary: The study found that children could understand the trigger-action programming logic and apply it to create rules for intelligent artifacts, indicating gains in computational thinking and problem-solving. All 15 children completed the four levels, and most could transfer the rule concept to imagined home scenarios; however, the paper does not report a formal effect size.
finding.measure: Successful completion of rule-creation tasks; correctness/errors in block-based programming; verbal explanations of rules

finding.finding_summary: The paper frames programming as a learning activity and reports that children were able to learn the basic logic of block-based coding in the context of an AR serious game. The main evidence is that all participants completed the programming tasks and demonstrated understanding of programming concepts such as sequencing and conditional logic, but no standardized academic achievement measure was used.
finding.measure: Task performance on programming levels; observations of understanding of coding concepts

paper_profiles.title: Kinsey Reporter: Citizen Science for Sex Research
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces Kinsey Reporter, a global mobile citizen-science platform for collecting anonymous survey data about sexual behavior and related experiences. The authors focus on the system’s design constraints: preserving contributor anonymity, preventing deanonymization, and enabling public exploration of aggregated data while avoiding free-text responses and tightly controlling location/time resolution.

The paper describes the app’s survey structure, anonymization protocol, and early usage statistics from about 8,300 reports across 32 countries. It also presents preliminary descriptive analyses of report co-occurrence patterns, such as relationships between sexual activities and relationship description, to illustrate the kinds of questions the platform can support. The authors emphasize that these are early, largely descriptive findings intended to motivate future research rather than to establish causal effects.

The paper is not an education study and does not investigate instructional interventions, student outcomes, or school-based populations. Its substantive contribution is methodological and infrastructural: it demonstrates how a privacy-preserving mobile platform can collect sensitive data at scale and surface aggregate patterns for future sex research.

paper_profiles.title: Detecting a Proxy for Potential Comorbid ADHD in People Reporting Anxiety Symptoms from Social Media Data
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether social media text can be used to identify people who present with anxiety symptoms and later begin posting in an ADHD forum, using that posting trajectory as a proxy for possible comorbid ADHD. The motivation is clinical: anxiety and ADHD frequently co-occur, and ADHD may be overlooked when anxiety is the presenting complaint. The authors argue that detecting a systematic textual difference between these groups could help illuminate how anxiety and ADHD presentations overlap.

The study uses Reddit data from the Anxiety and ADHD subreddits collected between February 2020 and November 2022. Users were filtered into two groups: those who only ever posted in the Anxiety subreddit, and those who first posted in Anxiety and later posted in ADHD; for the latter group, only Anxiety posts at least 6 months before the first ADHD post were retained. The task was to classify Anxiety subreddit posts into these two groups using baseline keyword-based models and a fine-tuned RoBERTa model.

Results showed that logistic regression and Naive Bayes performed only modestly above chance (54% and 58.6% accuracy, respectively, with a 50% base rate), while RoBERTa achieved 76% accuracy. The authors conclude that the signal is more complex than keyword matching and that transformer models can detect patterns associated with later ADHD-related posting. However, the paper is exploratory and observational, relies on Reddit behavior as a proxy rather than clinical diagnosis, and does not report subgroup analyses by grade band, sex, socioeconomic status, or comorbidity beyond the broader anxiety-ADHD relationship.

paper_profiles.title: Enhancing Primary Teacher Training through Academic Portfolios in Advanced Mathematics Courses
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether academic portfolios can improve the preparation of primary-school teacher candidates in advanced university mathematics courses. The core problem is the disconnect between abstract mathematical content and the practical demands of teaching elementary mathematics, which can reduce engagement and make assessment feel disconnected from future classroom practice.

The intervention was the integration of academic portfolios into two undergraduate courses in algebra and number systems within a primary teacher education program at Pontificia Universidad Católica de Chile. The portfolio model included a negotiated learning contract, structured reflection, drafts with feedback, rubric-based assessment, presentations or discussion tables, and an emphasis on connecting theory to teaching practice. The study followed 37 mostly female preservice teachers across four course cohorts from 2022 to 2024.

Findings were based on course records, surveys, reflective writing, and peer evaluation. The paper reports higher attendance, more digital engagement, improved grades across semesters, strong self-reported gains in time management, self-study, understanding of course content, and reduced mathematics anxiety. Overall, the authors conclude that portfolios are a promising assessment and learning tool for teacher education, but they also caution that the evidence is preliminary and confounded by cohort and contextual changes, so causal claims are not established.

finding.finding_summary: Portfolio implementation coincided with higher course grades in advanced mathematics teacher-preparation courses. In MAT2920, the average grade rose from 4.43 the prior semester to 5.89 when portfolios were introduced, then to 5.71 and 6.44 in later semesters; in MAT2925, grades increased from 5.52 to 5.80 and then 6.44. The paper does not report inferential statistics or effect sizes, and it explicitly notes that cohort differences and other instructional changes may have contributed.
finding.measure: Course grades in Algebra and Number Systems I and II (MAT2920, MAT2925) on the Chilean 1.0–7.0 scale

finding.finding_summary: The portfolio approach was associated with higher engagement, sustained attendance, and reduced mathematics anxiety. Attendance remained above 70%, no absences were recorded for assessed activities, and 11 of 12 survey respondents (91.7%) said alternative assessment methods such as portfolios helped mitigate feelings related to mathematics anxiety. Responses also suggested greater motivation and ownership of learning, but the study is descriptive and does not estimate causal effects.
finding.measure: Attendance, participation, self-assessment survey items on motivation and mathematics anxiety

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests portfolios strengthened durable skills such as self-regulation, time management, reflection, and critical evaluation. In self-assessments, 100% of respondents reported improved time organization and 85.7% reported improved self-study; peer evaluations also indicated strong organization, detailed explanations, and thoughtful reflections in portfolio work. These outcomes are based on self-report and qualitative evidence rather than controlled comparison.
finding.measure: Self-assessment surveys, peer evaluations, reflective paragraphs
finding.study_size: n=37 overall; self-assessment survey proportions reported for n=7 and n=12 subgroups in the paper text

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports improved assessment efficacy and smoother portfolio-based course management, with teachers noting that the portfolio and rubric structure made expectations clearer and assessment more meaningful than traditional exams. However, this is presented mainly through qualitative commentary and perceptions; no workload metrics, time savings, or efficiency effect sizes are reported.
finding.measure: Instructor and student perceptions of assessment efficacy and organization

paper_profiles.title: Teaching Physics in the first years of Elementary School to children with ADHD
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper describes a science-fair-based learning activity implemented at Colégio Pedro II in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, for a small group of elementary-aged students diagnosed with ADHD. The authors frame the work around two goals: promoting early physics/scientific literacy and supporting students’ executive functioning, especially time management, planning, and task prioritization.

The intervention consisted of a six-week sequence in a Learning Laboratory and physics lab in which eight students ages 8–12 researched, built, tested, and revised hands-on electricity/energy activities, ultimately creating a “fabric robot” with a quiz board and presenting it at a school science fair. The authors emphasize student interest, collaboration, planning, and public explanation of the project rather than formal assessment instruments.

The paper’s main conclusion is descriptive and celebratory: the authors report that students appeared confident in explaining the circuit and energy concepts, and that the experience positively supported scientific literacy and executive-function practice. No controlled comparison, pre/post testing, or subgroup analysis is reported, so the paper does not provide evidence about differential effects by grade band, comorbidity, sex, socioeconomic status, or medication status.

finding.finding_summary: The authors report that the eight ADHD students (ages 8–12) were able to explain how the electric circuit quiz board worked and showed apparently solid understanding of energy storage and transformation during the science-fair presentation. This is presented as a qualitative positive learning outcome, but no formal test score or effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Observed student explanations and science-fair presentation performance on electricity/energy concepts

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that organizing, defining, and prioritizing science-fair tasks was a useful opportunity to stimulate executive function in ADHD students, particularly time management and planning future tasks. The evidence is observational and anecdotal, based on classroom participation over six weeks, with no standardized self-regulation measure reported.
finding.measure: Observed executive-function-related behaviors during project planning and completion

finding.finding_summary: The intervention was explicitly designed to strengthen planning, prioritization, and task management as students prepared the science-fair project. The authors describe improved ability to organize tasks and explain the project to visitors, but do not report quantitative measures or comparative data.
finding.measure: Observed planning, organization, prioritization, and public explanation of project work

paper_profiles.title: Cognitive characteristics of intellectually gifted children with a diagnosis of ADHD
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether children who are both intellectually gifted and diagnosed with ADHD (“twice exceptional,” or 2e-ADHD) show a distinctive cognitive profile, and whether they appear to be misdiagnosed because of giftedness-related boredom or uneven performance. The authors analyzed WISC-IV data from a large Italian clinical sample of 1,051 children with ADHD, identifying 82 children with a General Ability Index (GAI) of at least 125 as 2e-ADHD. They compared these children with children with ADHD of average intelligence and with gifted children who had SLD but not ADHD.

The study focused on WISC-IV subtests and derived indices, especially the contrast between verbal/perceptual reasoning abilities and working memory/processing speed. The authors also tested whether 2e-ADHD children with and without comorbid SLD differed, and whether the observed 2e-ADHD profile matched a simulated profile predicted from the broader ADHD distribution. They found that gifted children with ADHD were overrepresented relative to what would be expected from a normal distribution, that their profiles still showed the typical ADHD-related weaknesses in working memory and processing speed, and that these patterns closely resembled those seen in gifted children with SLD. No meaningful differences emerged between 2e-ADHD children with versus without SLD.

The paper does not study ADHD medication effects, subgroup response to medication, or academic achievement outcomes directly. Instead, it provides descriptive and modeling evidence about cognitive profiles and diagnostic interpretation. The main practical implication is that clinicians and educators should interpret giftedness and ADHD carefully, as high reasoning ability does not rule out genuine ADHD-related cognitive weaknesses; the findings support individualized educational support rather than assuming misdiagnosis.

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not measure academic achievement directly, but it addresses academically relevant cognitive functioning in children with ADHD and giftedness. Across 82 2e-ADHD children, the profile showed strong verbal/perceptual reasoning with persistent weaknesses in working memory and processing speed (e.g., GAI=130.24, WMI=97.37, PSI=95.88), suggesting a mixed cognitive profile that may affect school performance. The authors argue these weaknesses help explain why intellectually gifted children can still have academic difficulties.
finding.measure: WISC-IV cognitive indices and subtests (verbal comprehension, perceptual reasoning, working memory, processing speed)
finding.study_size: n=82 (2e-ADHD); comparison groups n=680 average ADHD and n=129 gifted SLD
finding.std_deviation: reported in table; group SDs vary by index

finding.finding_summary: This was the central outcome focus: the study characterized executive/cognitive skills relevant to learning, especially working memory and processing speed. The 2e-ADHD group showed pronounced weaknesses relative to their reasoning abilities, with mean WMI=97.37 and PSI=95.88 compared with GAI=130.24; these weaknesses were similar to those of gifted children with SLD and were interpreted as reflecting ADHD-related deficits rather than misdiagnosis. No meaningful differences were found between 2e-ADHD children with and without SLD (all p>.24; Cohen’s d mostly 0.01–0.29).
finding.measure: WISC-IV Working Memory Index, Processing Speed Index, and subtests (Digit Span, Letter-Number Sequencing, Coding, Symbol Search)
finding.study_size: n=82 (2e-ADHD); subgroup comparison n=32 without SLD vs n=35 with SLD
finding.effect_size: d≈0.01 to 0.29 for subgroup differences; large within-group discrepancy between GAI and WMI/PSI described qualitatively
finding.std_deviation: reported in table; e.g., WMI SD=11.54, PSI SD=15.24 in 2e-ADHD

paper_profiles.title: Dual-task Coordination in Children and Adolescents with Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether children and adolescents with ADHD differ from typically developing peers in dual-task coordination, a working-memory/executive-function ability involving simultaneous performance of a verbal recall task and a motor tracking task. The authors also test whether task difficulty changes performance disproportionately in ADHD, whether a computerized and paper-and-pencil dual-task version yield comparable results, and whether performance differences are explained by motor functioning or comorbidity.

The study included 91 children/adolescents with ADHD and 91 age- and education-matched controls aged 6-16 years from schools and a pediatric neurology clinic in Tbilisi. Participants completed computerized and paper-and-pencil dual-task paradigms, with repeated single-task and dual-task trials, plus standardized assessments of IQ, motor skills (MABC-2), ADHD symptoms, autism symptoms, and comorbid conduct/oppositional disorders. Parents of ADHD participants were asked to withhold psychostimulants for 24 hours before testing.

Overall, the findings suggest that dual-task coordination is broadly preserved in ADHD and that increased task difficulty does not disproportionately impair ADHD relative to controls. The paper-and-pencil version produced broadly similar results to the computerized version, although the computerized task showed some statistically significant or near-significant differences favoring controls. The authors also report that general motor functioning relates to dual-task performance in controls but not in ADHD, and that comorbidity and sex can modulate computerized performance in some analyses; however, there was no clear evidence of a robust ADHD subtype effect on the main dual-task outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: The main dual-task coordination outcome showed little to no ADHD-related deficit overall. In the computerized version, the group effect was small and only modestly significant for motor tracking (F(1,179)=5.642, η2=.031), while the combined dual-task μ score difference was only near-significant (control M=101.51, SD=10.34 vs ADHD M=98.43, SD=12.01; one-tailed p<.066). In the paper-and-pencil version, no significant group, task, or interaction effects were found, and the authors conclude that dual-task coordination is available in children/adolescents with ADHD.
finding.measure: Dual-task coordination / combined μ score; serial digit recall plus motor tracking performance
finding.effect_size: η2=.031 for computerized motor tracking group effect; μ difference not otherwise reported
finding.std_deviation: computerized μ: control SD=10.34, ADHD SD=12.01; paper-and-pencil μ: control SD=9.97, ADHD SD=13.02

finding.finding_summary: Task difficulty did not disproportionately impair ADHD relative to controls. Across the 2-group × 3-difficulty ANOVAs, the authors report significant main effects of task difficulty but no clear interaction indicating that ADHD participants were more sensitive to harder tasks than controls. The results suggest broadly similar sensitivity to task demands across groups, with overall lower performance in ADHD but without a consistent differential-response pattern.
finding.measure: Performance across easy, standard, and difficult dual-task conditions on motor tracking and digit recall

finding.finding_summary: The paper-and-pencil dual-task was intended as a more practical clinical/educational alternative to the computerized version, and the authors found it produced comparable results in most analyses. However, the paper-and-pencil μ scores did not significantly differ between groups and showed no significant associations with motor functioning or sex, suggesting usability and consistency, but not a clear efficiency advantage in outcomes.
finding.measure: Agreement/comparability between computerized and paper-and-pencil dual-task performance; test-retest reliability and cross-version correlations
finding.effect_size: cross-version correlation r=.26; test-retest r=.36 computerized, r=.37 paper-and-pencil

paper_profiles.title: School value-added models for multivariate academic and non-academic outcomes: A more rounded approach to using student data to inform school accountability
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether school accountability systems that rely almost exclusively on academic attainment can be broadened to include non-academic outcomes. The authors argue that schools shape not only achievement but also attendance and exclusions, and that using a single outcome gives an incomplete and potentially misleading picture of school performance.

To investigate this, the paper develops and applies a multivariate, mixed-response, multilevel value-added model that jointly analyzes student attainment, absences, and exclusions. The analysis uses administrative data from England’s National Pupil Database for a random sample of 300 mainstream secondary schools (n=45,103 students) who completed GCSEs in 2017/2018. Models progressively adjust for prior attainment, prior absences, prior exclusion, student background (including sex, ethnicity, EAL, SEN, FSM, summer-born status), and school characteristics.

The main conclusion is that schools differ meaningfully across the three outcomes and that those differences are only weakly aligned once student intake and background are adjusted for. In the most adjusted model, the school-effect correlation between attainment and log absences is only -0.12, suggesting that a school effective at raising achievement is not necessarily effective at reducing absenteeism or exclusions. The paper concludes that school accountability would be more holistic and fair if it incorporated multiple outcomes, especially non-academic ones such as attendance and exclusions.

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s central academic outcome is GCSE Attainment 8, analyzed in a multivariate value-added framework. After adjustment for prior attainment and student background, school-level variance in attainment dropped from 0.192 to 0.059, with the final model explaining 56% of the variance; the correlation between attainment and log absences at the school level fell to -0.12 in the contextual value-added model, indicating that academic and non-academic school effects are only weakly aligned.
finding.measure: Attainment 8 (GCSE summary attainment score)
finding.effect_size: school variance 0.059 in Model 3; school-effect correlation with log absences rho=-0.12

finding.finding_summary: Absences were modeled as a school outcome and were substantially predicted by prior absences and student background, but school effects on log absences were modest. School-level variance was 0.050 unadjusted and 0.037 in the final contextual model, with the contextual model explaining 28% of variance; the school-effect correlation with attainment was only -0.12, showing attendance is related to but distinct from achievement.
finding.measure: Total student absences over secondary school, log-transformed
finding.effect_size: school variance 0.037 in Model 3; R-squared=0.28; school-effect correlation with attainment rho=-0.12

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s policy conclusion is that school accountability systems should incorporate multiple outcomes rather than rely on attainment alone. It shows that excluding attendance and exclusion data would miss substantively different dimensions of school performance, and that school effects are only weakly correlated across outcomes after adjustment, supporting broader accountability and inspection practices.
finding.measure: Multivariate school value-added estimates for attainment, absences, and exclusions; school characteristics; school-effect correlations
finding.effect_size: correlation between attainment and log absences in Model 3 rho=-0.12; correlation between attainment and exclusions in Model 1 rho=-0.52

paper_profiles.title: Pediatric brain tumor classification using digital histopathology and deep learning: evaluation of SOTA methods on a multi-center Swedish cohort
paper_profiles.population: Children and young adults with pediatric brain tumors (ages 0-20 years; mean 8.5 years)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of classifying pediatric brain tumors from digitized histopathology slides, a task that is difficult because pediatric brain tumor datasets are small, heterogeneous, and spread across centers with different scanning workflows. The authors ask whether modern weakly supervised deep learning methods can accurately classify tumor category, family, and type from whole-slide images, and whether histology-pretrained foundation-model features generalize better than ImageNet-pretrained features.

The approach uses a multi-center Swedish cohort of 540 children and young adults with 564 unique subject-diagnosis cases and 1,449 whole-slide images from six university hospitals. Patch-level features were extracted with three encoders—ResNet50, UNI, and CONCH—and aggregated with two MIL methods, ABMIL and CLAM, for patient-level classification. Models were evaluated on three hierarchical tasks and also in a generalization setting where two centers were used for training and four for testing.

Results show that histology-pretrained encoders, especially UNI and CONCH, substantially outperform ResNet50 across all tasks. The best performance was obtained with UNI + ABMIL, with MCCs of 0.76 for tumor category, 0.63 for tumor family, and 0.60 for tumor type. Generalization to out-of-site data remained fairly strong, with limited and inconsistent performance drops across feature extractors and aggregation methods. Attention maps broadly aligned with neuropathologist-identified diagnostic regions, suggesting the models learn clinically meaningful morphology, though the study also highlights persistent difficulty in fine-grained distinctions between histologically similar tumor entities.

paper_profiles.title: Increasing Systemic Resilience to Socioeconomic Challenges: Modeling the Dynamics of Liquidity Flows and Systemic Risks Using Navier–Stokes Equations
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of how to model liquidity flows and systemic financial risk in modern economies under conditions of shocks, volatility, and nonlinear interactions. The authors argue that traditional financial models such as CAPM, VaR, and GARCH are insufficient for capturing extreme events and dynamic instability, and propose an alternative framework based on an economic interpretation of the Navier–Stokes equations.

The study develops a mixed-method modeling approach combining econometric testing, Fourier analysis, stochastic simulation, simulation-based sensitivity analysis, and AI-based tuning. It integrates multiple macroeconomic and financial variables, including GDP, inflation, Gini index, CDS spreads, and liquidity coverage ratio, and calibrates the model using Georgian data from 2010–2024. The paper reports that the adapted Navier–Stokes framework can represent liquidity diffusion, systemic stress, and cyclical behavior, and that a dynamic residual term helps restore balance when discrepancies arise.

The empirical context is the Georgian financial system, with simulations and parameter estimates grounded in national and international macro-financial datasets. The main conclusion is methodological rather than educational: the model is presented as a novel tool for forecasting crises, analyzing systemic risk, and informing countercyclical policy. There is no study of students, schools, ADHD medication, or academic outcomes in the K-12 sense.

paper_profiles.title: Comparison of the Gamma-Ray Burst Sensitivity of Different Detectors
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a measurement and comparison problem in gamma-ray burst (GRB) astronomy: different detectors have different energy responses, trigger bands, and background conditions, so their reported sensitivities are not directly comparable. The author proposes a common comparison framework based on threshold peak photon flux over the 1–1000 keV band and the burst spectral peak energy Ep, allowing detector capabilities to be expressed on a shared FT-versus-Ep plane.

The paper develops a simple analytic method using a Band-function spectral model, detector effective area and efficiency, coded-mask geometry, and trigger significance thresholds. It then applies this method to several past, current, and planned GRB instruments, including BATSE, BeppoSAX WFC/GRBM, HETE-2 WXM/FREGATE, Swift BAT, GLAST/GBM, and EXIST.

The main conclusion is that detector sensitivity depends strongly on both instrument design and burst spectral hardness. Soft-burst sensitivity is improved by low-energy response and lower trigger bands (for example, FREGATE and Swift BAT for low Ep events), while larger detector area improves sensitivity for harder bursts (for example, EXIST relative to Swift and BATSE). The paper is comparative and methodological rather than an educational intervention study; it does not address ADHD medication, academic outcomes, or subgroup effects in children.

paper_profiles.title: Altered Oscillatory Brain Networks During Emotional Face Processing in ADHD: An eLORETA–fICA Study
paper_profiles.extended_summary: This study examines whether individuals with ADHD show altered large-scale oscillatory brain network activity during inhibitory control tasks that include both neutral and emotional face processing. The authors focus on cognitive and emotional Go/NoGo paradigms (VCPT and ECPT) and use EEG source analysis (eLORETA) combined with functional independent component analysis (fICA) to identify frequency-specific cortical networks.

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studies emotional face processing and inhibitory control in ADHD during an emotional Go/NoGo task. ADHD participants showed small but statistically significant neural differences, including stronger inferior temporal gamma activation during NoGo trials (IC3: F(1,268)=9.49, p≤.01, η²_G=.02) and a Group × Condition interaction indicating disproportionately stronger NoGo-related activation in ADHD. Behaviorally, ADHD showed slower responses, greater variability, and more errors, especially in the emotional ECPT (e.g., RT mean ADHD ECPT 467.28 ± 98.71 vs control 415.27 ± 94.57).
finding.measure: EEG network activation during emotional face processing; reaction time, reaction-time variability, commission errors, omission errors
finding.effect_size: η²_G=.02 for IC3 Group effect; d=.3 for NoGo-related IC3 contrast; RT mean group effect ges=.05; RTvar group effect ges=.15; omission group effect ges=.12
finding.std_deviation: reported in Table 3 for behavioral outcomes

finding.finding_summary: The paper assesses response inhibition and task performance in Go/NoGo paradigms, which are closely related to self-regulation and executive control. ADHD participants performed worse than controls across tasks, with significant group effects for reaction time (F=16.20, p≤.001, ges=.05), RT variability (F=59.72, p≤.001, ges=.15), commission errors (F=12.04, p≤.001, ges=.03), and omission errors (F=49.62, p≤.001, ges=.12), plus several Group × Task interactions.
finding.measure: Go/NoGo performance: reaction time, reaction-time variability, commission errors, omission errors
finding.std_deviation: reported in Table 3 for behavioral outcomes

paper_profiles.title: What is essential is visible to the eye: Saliency in primary school ranking and its effect on academic achievements
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper studies whether a student’s relative class rank in primary school affects later academic performance, and whether the effect depends on whether the rank is visible to students. The authors motivate the work by noting that prior rank-effect studies may confound rank with underlying ability and peer composition, so they propose a new identification strategy using two rankings: a visible rank based on teacher-assigned class grades and an invisible rank based on standardized test scores that students do not see.

Using panel data on several hundred thousand Italian public-school students observed in grade 5, grade 8, and grade 10, the paper compares the effects of visible and invisible rank on later standardized test performance. The visible rank has a large positive association with later outcomes, while the invisible rank is near zero once extensive controls and student fixed effects are included, supporting the interpretation that salience/perception matters rather than rank per se. In the main specification, moving from bottom to top of the primary-school class rank distribution is associated with gains of about 8.5 percentile points in middle school and 7.7 percentile points in high school.

The paper also examines heterogeneity by gender, immigration status, SES, class size, peer ability, and individual ability. It finds no statistically significant differences in the visible-rank effect across these groups, and no meaningful variation by class size or peer/individual achievement. The authors further show that higher-ranked students self-select into higher-achieving high schools and report stronger school perceptions and self-esteem, suggesting a psychological mechanism. Overall, the paper concludes that salient rank in primary school can shape later academic trajectories, but that the competitive quality of peers remains beneficial even after accounting for rank.

finding.finding_summary: Primary-school visible rank has a sizable positive association with later math-related academic performance as measured by national standardized test percentiles. In the main specification, moving from the bottom to the top of the class rank distribution in grade 5 is associated with a gain of 8.5 percentile points in grade 8 and 7.7 percentile points in grade 10; the invisible rank is close to zero and not significant.
finding.measure: National standardized test percentiles (Italian and math combined academic outcomes; paper reports grade 8 and grade 10 percentile distributions from Invalsi tests)
finding.study_size: n=387,614 total in the two main cohorts after sample selection (205,123 in 2018 cohort; 182,491 in 2019 cohort)

finding.finding_summary: Higher visible rank improves students’ perceptions and self-reported non-academic attitudes. Using the 2018 questionnaire, the authors find that a higher visible rank improves interest in studied subjects, self-esteem, perceived recognition by peers, and perception of school; the invisible rank remains close to zero. The paper interprets these patterns as evidence of a psychological/perception channel.
finding.measure: Student questionnaire Likert-scale responses on self-esteem, perceived peer recognition, interest in subjects, and perception of school

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that visible rank influences later academic achievement beyond the specific math/literacy subject comparison by affecting overall standardized test performance and school trajectories. Higher-ranked students also self-select into high schools with higher average student achievement, indicating a persistent academic-pathway effect.
finding.measure: Later academic performance and high-school track/peer-achievement composition

finding.finding_summary: The study has institutional implications for how school grading and rank salience shape student trajectories within the Italian school system. It argues that teacher-assigned, publicly salient grades create meaningful rank effects, while unreported standardized scores do not, implying that school practices around grade visibility can alter academic outcomes and sorting into later schools.
finding.measure: Rank salience via teacher grades vs. unreported standardized scores; later school selection and academic tracking

paper_profiles.title: Classification of ADHD and Healthy Children Using Multi-Band and Spatial Features of EEG
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of automatically classifying children with ADHD versus healthy controls using EEG signals. The authors argue that early and accurate ADHD identification is important for intervention, and they investigate whether multi-band EEG features can distinguish the two groups reliably.

The study uses a benchmark EEG dataset containing 61 children with ADHD and 60 healthy controls, ages 7 to 12, recorded during a visual attention task. EEG from 19 channels was filtered into five frequency bands, and power spectral density and spectral entropy were extracted as features. These features were then classified using SVM and XGBoost; the best result was obtained with an RBF-kernel SVM, reaching 99.2% cross-validation accuracy (std=0.0079), with XGBoost performing slightly worse at 96.92% accuracy.

The main conclusion is that multi-band spatial EEG features are highly effective for distinguishing ADHD from controls in this dataset. The paper presents this as support for non-invasive, data-driven diagnostic tools, but it does not evaluate treatment effects or learning outcomes. It also does not report subgroup analyses by grade band, comorbidity, sex, or socioeconomic status beyond noting that the sample included both boys and girls.

finding.finding_summary: The study is not an intervention study on student skills, but it does directly model ADHD-related attentional control using EEG during a visual attention task. The reported classification performance was very high for distinguishing ADHD from healthy children, with SVM-RBF achieving 99.2% mean cross-validation accuracy (std=0.0079) on n=121 children aged 7 to 12, suggesting the feature set captured attention-related differences relevant to self-regulation/attention processes.
finding.measure: ADHD vs healthy child classification accuracy on EEG features during a visual attention task

paper_profiles.title: Leveraging contact network structure in the design of cluster randomized trials
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how to design cluster randomized trials in infectious disease settings when there is meaningful contact between clusters. The central question is whether trial designs can use knowledge of contact network structure to both improve epidemic control and preserve statistical power to detect intervention effects.

The authors propose a family of connectivity-informed cluster randomized trial designs, including Static Rank and Adaptive Rank variants, plus parallel, stepped-wedge, and holdback options. They evaluate these designs with network-based agent simulations of an Ebola-like epidemic in a 20-cluster synthetic population, comparing epidemic outcomes such as cumulative incidence, time to epidemic end, and power to detect vaccine effects.

Across 1,000 simulated epidemics, connectivity-informed designs reduced cumulative incidence by about 20% and lowered peak infectiousness compared with standard designs, but generally reduced power to detect treatment effects. Adding a brief holdback period recovered much of the lost power. The paper concludes that incorporating cluster connectivity can improve public health impact in outbreak trials, though it trades off against power and complicates causal estimation.

finding.finding_summary: The paper shows that trial design choices using network connectivity can improve population-level outbreak control while retaining some ability to evaluate intervention effects. In 1,000 simulated epidemic trials, connectivity-informed designs reduced cumulative incidence by about 20% compared with traditional staggered CRTs, though they generally reduced power; adding a brief holdback recovered much of the lost power.
finding.measure: Cumulative incidence, time to epidemic end, time to Re<1, and statistical power in simulated cluster randomized trials
finding.study_size: n=1000 simulation iterations; 20 clusters; 200 individuals per cluster
